div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

A Famous Singer.—The musical world has sustained a great loss by the death of Madame Belle Cole, who, like Antoinette Sterling was at her best in such songs as " The Lost Chord," and " The Better Land." She was , an American by birth, but her success over here when she first appeared under the late Sir Joseph Barnby was I so great,that she decided to settle down in this country. I Madame Belle Cole was forsome years in the front rank orsingers,but in spite of her fame,she was entirely with- out conceit' and was a very genial woman. Climate, she thought, had a great deal to do with the voice, and she , used to say that many of the negroes on the plantations ' in her native country, had as good a voice as she had. A Famous Actress.—Mrs. Patrick Campbell is a great favourite with American audiences, and her many admirers on both sides of the Atlantic will regret the unfortunate accident, as a result of which, she has been , compelled to abandon her tour in the States. Instead of being a famous actress, Mrs. Campbell might very well have been a professional musician, as her abilities as a pianist would at any time justify her appearance in the concert room. There used to be at one time a very marked distinction in the social scale, between the dramatic stage and the lyric stage. A woman who became an actress was liable to be looked upon by her friends as being sadly misguided, though she might safely become a singer, or professional musician without it being regarded as a dangerous proceeding. But in recent vrsars, the social status of the dramatic stage has vastly improved and "actresses" are no longer shunned by leading lights in society. It was however more by accident than otherwise, that Mrs. Campbell passed from an amateur to a professional actress, as she never trained with the idea of going on the stage. Concerning Things Musical.—Japanese music is well to the fore this winter, and those performers who are searching after effective yet somewhat easy pieces, should not fail to secure a spirited Japanese March " Banzai," by Stepan Esipoff. "Yo San," a pretty, realistic Japanese Dance, by Leslie Smith is another charming little piece—(Leonard Sc Co.) In the matter of new songs, we are well off just now, especially in those little "scrappy " ones, usually so much more appreciated by the average audience than the larger and sometimes monotonous varieties. " A Memory," the words by Lilian Scott, and the music by Katharine Barry, is an exquisite touching little song. "Times Roses," the words by Alice E. Gillington, the music by Katherine Berry, is another one to get, while yet another—" Two Eyes of Grey "—written and com- posed by Daisy McGeoch (Leonard Sc Co.) will appeal to all lovers of the pathetic. A Gruesome Entertainment.—Patients will think twice before submitting to an operation at the hands of a certain eminent Parisian surgeon, who, for the benefit of hospitals, colleges, and the generations to come, has been having all his more important exploits cinemato- graphed. His sole idea was to serve the ends of science, but the fact that he failed to secure exclusive posses- sion of the films led to one of those incidents in which the reality is stranger than fiction. The occasion was a select dinner party, after which the company sat down to watch a cinematograph display. One of the scenes presented was the carrying out of an operation by this eminent surgeon, which may have been very amusing andi entertaining to the company in general, but one can hardly imagine the horror of a lady guest amongst them, who at once recognised herself as the subject of theoperation. Troubles have ensued which remain to be adjusted between the different parties, but the sym- pathy of the public will he with the lady, who would naturally object to have her sufferings displayed in grue- fome detail for the sport of a vulgar crowd, either at select dinner parties, or at the country fairs. The Causes of Adpendioitis.—lt has been suggested before that the prevalence of appendicitis is due in no smallimeasure to the modern habit of swallowing aperient waters or pills, and a well-known physician, writing in the" Nineteenth Century "is entirely of this view. The notion that appendicitis is only an old desease under anew namedoes not dispose of the fact that it is much more prevalent than it used to be, and this physician says that its three principal causes are neglect of chills, hurried meals with imperfect mastica- tion, and dosing oneself with purgatives. America would seem to furnish evidence that this theory is correct, as the Americans are proverbially given to bolting their food, besides taking large quantities of aperient medicines, and nowhere is appendicitis so common as across the Atlantic. It would therefore be well to take note of ,the three warnings which this physician conveys, and avoid above all, the swallowing of unmasticated food, not only for this reason but also for the sake of the general health. Trying to put Down Confetti Throwing.—There have been many and various complaints of the use of confetti at weddings and a Sussex Vicar announces that in future he will make a substantial addition to the marriage fees for clearing it away. He hopes by these means to induce wedding parties to dispense with it. Several of the Railway Companies have also announced that they will take strong measures against those who litter the carriages and stations with paper cuttings, but in spite of these warnings it does not appear that the practice of throwing confetti is dying out. It is less dangerous than rice, and will not cause a black eye, like the heel of an old shoe, but it was an unfortunate mischance that is said to have led to the introduction of confetti. According to the story, the work girls in a paper mill were engaged in punching eyelet holes in a quantity of stationery, and amused themselves in throw- ing the refuse cuttings over one another. It was from their fun ,that the idea caught on, and led to confetti throwing as a regular cust4m. Costly Umbrellas.—Formerly costly jewels were reserved for evening wear, but now they make their appearance at all hours of the day. One extravagance leads to another, and not only are gloves and shoes decorated with sparkling gems, but equally expensive ornamentation is also bestowed upon umbrellas. These may be seen with costly fitted handles, which are works of art, embellished with diamonds, rubies, and pearls, but of course such expensive articles only come within the means of those women to whom money is no object. It is however only the very few who are in this happy position, and for ordinary people a very expensively finished umbrella is a mistake, as it only becomes a worry, lest it should be lost. The Alteration of Sleeves.—Tho complete change in

the fashioning of sleeves is causing considerable anxiety among those women who are forced to make gowns and blouses last more than one season. Already even the late autumn sleeves—with the sole exception of those placed in neaetailor-made coats,—look out of date,and in those cases where a length of the necessary fabric is not forthcoming despair reigns supreme. But therg is one way out of the difficulty, that so far does not seem to have occurred to the home worker, namely, the simple process of turning the sleeve upside down. Where we had scantiness we now have an abundance of fabric, and vice versa, and byl taking out the sleeve and hanging it upside down,we get what Dame Fashion insists upon—a sleeve that is full above, and tightly fitting below the elbow. The sleeve will need slopiniz underneath at the top, to fit the armhole, of course, and it should be lined a little way down with tailor's canvas, so as to afford to the shoulders the once more approved square appearance Concerning Lace.—According to leading modistes, it seems more than probable that entire lace gowns will again find favour for garden party, race, wedding and evening wear when the summer days arrive and it would therefore seem to be a wise proceeding to secure lengths of some of the lovely laces that are now being offered at greatly reduced figures at some of the sales. Even if the prediction should fail in fulfilment, good lace is always usable in some form or other. MAD GE.

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

Excitement continues to be intense concerning the decision of the French Automobile Club to run the Grand Prix at the same time and over the same course as the Gordon-Bennett. One of the English manufac- turers, it is stated, has declared that he will withdraw his entries if the proposal is to be seriously entertained; but, unless the other countries agree to stand down also, it is hardly to be supposed that all the English entrants will take the same view and not make a fight in the coveted Cup.

Many motorists do not seem to comprehend fully what takes place when a car begins to falter in going op-hill and are apt to advance the ignition. This is. of course. quite wrong. As the engine is pulling slower, the igni- tion should be retarded, (assuming, of course, that it had been considerably advanced),or otherwise the explo- sion will take place when the piston is in a wrong posi- tion, that is to say, before it has reached the top of the stroke. The result of this error' of judgmentm will be readily seen, may be very serious, and many a bent crank-shaft owes its origin to this.

The right time for the explosion of the mixture to occur is when the piston has reached the top of its stroke and is just beginning the descent. in order, therefore,,always to time this correctly, it is necessary to so alter the ignition laver that the explosion will , always take place just as the piston is descending. Up !hill the motor is pulling more slowly, and, conse- quently the piston takes a slightly longer time in com— pleting each stroke. But the careful retlrding of the spark and the admission of a slightly richer mixture to the carburetter will often help her up an awkward rise, where, otherwise, a changing down of gear might have been necessitated, or, perhaps, when the engine would have stopped altogether.

Some misguided person is urging upon impecnniou womanhood the wisdom of training as motor drivers.s Why? Where would they train, and who in the world would employ them? Are they expected to take a long course of engineering lessons, both in theory and practice—for which they would obviously have neither the time, money, nor, it may be added, the, natural aptitude, or does their well-wisher merely intend them to learn how to steer a car? This latter course would take, perhaps, half-an-hour; and what then? How about the repairs, the breakdowns, the knowledge of what was wrong, and the ability to put it right? No, woman has surely encroached far enough upon man's preserves in business already; she had better be content to leave him in sole possession of the workshop bench, the oil-saturated overalls, and the motor that won't ' mote because the silly carburetter is choked, or the idiotic clutch is slipping.

div.head: WORK FOR ST,. HELENS UNEMPLOYED,.
div.p: WORK FOR ST,. HELENS UNEMPLOYED,.

At St. Helens Water Committee meeting on Wednes- day, the Mayor (Councillor Martin) said that the com- mittee had in several places where they were putting down new water mains decided to abandon the old pipes, because it would cost as much to get them up as they were worth. He suggested, however, that in order to give employment for those out of work, the pipes in such places as Sherdley-road might be dug up. It was resolved to start the work.

DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
TnE REVIVED 1830 Gown.

A very pretty damsel made quite a sensation the other night, says the Queen, by appearing in a dress of that day, made in soft crêpe, short enough to show her sandaled shoes. All round the skirt a soft fold of the material had been festooned and caught up with bows at every point; there was a band of velvet round the waist, a full puffed sleeve, which ended above the elbow, a low, full bodice, and a perfectly plain-cut fichu of the material, with an embroidered bunch of roses on one side. The fan was attached to a chain carried round the neck, and a bow of ribbon fastened the front, -

div.head: LATEST MALADY.
div.p: THE LATEST MALADY.

"Bicycle back," "lawn-tennis arm," "type-writer's wrist," "motor-car cold," and many more ailments which come from a special amusement or employ- ment, now have a new companion in the "bridge eye"!. It appears that almost every woman who devotes much time to playing at bridge gets an anxious look in the eyes which in many cases is not becoming.

div.head: CHILD'S PARTY DRESS.
div.p: CHILD'S PARTY DRESS.

A party dress is a great delight to a tiny maiden. One that could not fail to charm the most fastidious little person is shewn in the accompany- ing sketch. There is so great a variety of suitable materials for children's wear. A fine spotted muslin, with lingerie embroidery for trimmings, and a soft Japanese silk are both especially pretty; or we would suggest a cream eolienne, with Cluny lace trimmings. The frock was made with a deep yoke tucked in groups of two; a small square of lace insertion outlines the neck. The skirt is very

full, and gathered on to the yoke, and is finished at the bottom by a deep hem and insertion. The pretty little sleeves are gathered above the elbow to form a fussy frill; a ribbon is tied round the arm into a bow at the side; and a wide sash is worn high up on the frock and fastens under a bow, the long end being edged with fringe. The colour chosen for sash and ribbons will depend on what is most becoming to the little weare:, but an eav-de-nil will be found to be very generally becoming.

div.head: "FLAPPER."
div.p: THE "FLAPPER."

This nondescript being, who has hitherto been kept in the seclusion of the schoolroom, treated with contemptuous indifference by her family, and wholly ignored by those outside its circle, is cer- tainly shewing a marked tendency to emerge from her hiding-place out of due season, writes "Ambrosia "in the World. Time was when her existence was not even recognised, and guests often came to and went from her home in complete ignorance that there was such a person. Nowadays Baby is the fashion. It is ala mode to have it in evidence, and without doubt it is well to the fore at present. Since this innovation has obtained, the "flapper" has been steadily gaining ground. Mothers are no longer profusely apologetic if they take out a girl answering to this description, and, indeed, she is even finding her way into ballrooms. The "boy and girl" dance has ceased to be a mere figure of speech, and this winter mixed dances of grown-ups, "flappers," and corresponding male creatures have been very general. There have even been one or two instances of engagements among the species. Among last season's brides, in fact, there was one who practically came straight from the schoolroom to the saw:. And one may well ask where the "flapper" will next appear, and what will be the effect of her presence every-where ? I incline to the opinion that the "flapper" will lose by her premature advent into the social arena. She will be denied the delights of anticipation, have her complexion ruined before she has had time to attain her full height, and be robbed of that invalu- able asset, youth, long before she has been able to realise what it means.

div.head: SMART SATIN BLOCSE.
div.p: SMART SATIN BLOCSE.

Most effective and dressy blouses can be achieved fn glossy-surfaced materials, such as satin or Oriental satin, merv, or brilliant. Oriental satin has been chosen for the realisation of our sketch. The transparent yoke is of cream piece lace outlined round the neck with silk Teneriffe wheels. The pointed berthe is gathered on to the yoke with a tiny heading, and is likewise outlined with silk Teneriffe wheels. The bodice is rucked at intervals to draw

the fulness close to the figure, and then disappears beneath a deep folded belt made with a very long point in front. The sleeves puff to the elbow, where they are finished with pointed frills edged with wheels like the berthe. These Teneriffe wheels are very simple to make, being worked over tiny round frames, which can be obtained at any fancy- work shop, and when worked they form a most effective trimming for dainty blouses.
IN THE MOVEMENT.

To be really up-to-date one must collect, or at least affect, the old. To acquire the modern is possibly to incur social reproach, while to possess anything "Victorian"—other than the Order— would be almost a blot on one's escutcheon—it one could be troubled with such a thing in these democratic days. You must be not a day later than "Georgian," declares the World of Dress, if you want the right people to call on your day-at- home. .

div.head: To-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: To-DAY'S RECIPE.

- - FILLET OF BICEF MILANAISE. —Lard and braise about 31b. or 41b. of filltt of beef, with onions, carrots, a good bouquet, some whole pepper- corns, and salt, moistening it with about one and a-half pint of stock and oue gill of eau de ,le; then place it on a baking-tin in the oven, brush it over with glaze, and leave it there for a few minutes to crisp; meanwhile, strain its liquor, take off all the fat, and boil it up sharply till reduced a full third. Have ready some spaghetti, previously boiled in stock, toss this with a little butter, loz. or 2oz. of grated Parmesan cheese, and a good dash of freshly-ground black pepper, with a little more stock to swell the macaroni thoroughly. When ready there should be little moisture left. Place a good layer of this on a hot dish, set the fillet on it, pour the gravy round, and serve,

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, January 14, 1905. SCIENCE NOTES AND GLEANINGS.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, January 14, 1905. SCIENCE NOTES AND GLEANINGS.
A TEST FOR DEATH.

Dr. Icard has given a new test for death by Injecting a solution of fluoresceine deeply into the cellular tissues. If circulation exists, the neigh- bouring akin becomes yellow and the eye green. If there is no circulation, one sees no coloration. A revival of circulation brings out the coloration.
MAGNETIC STREAMS FROM THE SUN.

Mr. E. W. Maunder, the astronomer, has come to the conclusion that disturbances of the earth's magnetism, observed at Greenwich, are associated with certain areas in the sun. Their action on our magnetism is not radiated like heat or light, but restricted to definite lines. These magnetic streams from the sun are, he thinks, analogous to the long rays of the corona.

div.head: ALBUMEN IN WINTER DIET.
div.p: ALBUMEN IN WINTER DIET.

In cold weather the system appears to require more albumen in food. Annamite labourers worked less in winter on rice containing carbon hydrates, but little albumen, than they did when albumen was added to the diet. A good ration was biscuit 100 grammes, rice 800, beet 300, fat 15, salt 10, tea and condiments.

div.head: CURIOUS INSECT.
div.p: A CURIOUS INSECT.

Takiranambois " is the Indian name for a curious insect of the Amazon, and means venomous serpent. Instead of being a serpent it is really a species of cricket six to eight centimkres long, of a greenish- yellow colour, with a yellow spot on the wings; and it is quite inoffensive. Another mistake is that it yields a light from its head, but the uncouth prolongation of its forehead appears to be a resonator, and not a lantern.

div.head: PERSONAL ORIENTATION.
div.p: PERSONAL ORIENTATION.

Experiments made by M. Fere with the ergo. graph of Mosso, and communicated to the Societe de Biologie, France, go to prove that the orienta- tion of a person, or his position with respect to the north, has an influence on the quality and quantity of his work and his nervous reaction. Something of this kind has been suspected in case of sleep and the positions of the bed. It is not easy to see why, unless the magnetic field of the earth or its motion in space is concerned. The human body is a conductor of electricity, and conductors moving across the lines of a magnetic field generate elec- tricity, which may affect the nerves, or blood, &c. It has been suggested that an effect of this kind may operate in the orientation of animals, such as homing pigeons or ants.

div.head: COLDEST PLACE ON EARTH.
div.p: COLDEST PLACE ON EARTH.

Werchejansk, Siberia, is considered the northern pole of cold, or place of greatest cold in the northern hemisphere. A temperature of 69.8 deg. Centigrade below zero (the freezing-point of water) has been observed there; but the Russian painter, Borissow, has found a temperature of 70deg. C. below zero registered on a minimum thermometer left by an Austrian exploring expedition in 1872 in the Straits of Matotchkin, Nova Zembla. Another maximum thermometer registered 14deg. above zero Centigrade as the highest temperature since 1872. Apparently the place has a good title to be regarded as the pole of cold.

div.head: EFFECTS OF POISONS ON THE HEART.
div.p: EFFECTS OF POISONS ON THE HEART.

According to Professor Carlson, of the University of Chicago, digitalin and nicotin (a principle of tobacco) dissolved in sea-water (one part of the alkaloid to 100 of water) contract the muscle of the heart. Atropin, curare, and pilocarpin of the same strength do not, but they stimulate the ganglion cells and increase the beats of the heart. Nicotin, digitalin, veratrin, and aconite paralyse, by over stimulation, the ganglion cells. Chlorides of barium, rubidinum, potassium, and sodium depress the activity of the ganglions. His experiments, described in Science, were made on the heart of the "Limulus."

div.head: FAMINES AND SOLAR CYCLES.
div.p: FAMINES AND SOLAR CYCLES.

Dr. Lockyer having shewn that periodic droughts and famines may arise from the cycles of the sun, Professor O'Reilly, of Dublin, remarks that inundations like that which caused the Zuyder Zee might occur at periods of maximum solar activity. He remarks that the Etruscan cycle was 122.2 years, or about eleven solar cycles of eleven years, and thinks it might begin from some flood or cold attributable to solar activity.

div.head: SATURN'S NINTH SATELLITE.
div.p: SATURN'S NINTH SATELLITE.

Professor Pickering has given the elements of the ninth satellite of Saturn, from which it appears that Phcebus is 12,703,000 kilometres from the planet, and takes 546 days 5 hours to go round it. Phcabus is about 3.25 kilometres in diameter, and appears less bright than a star of the fourteenth magnitude.

div.head: CURIOUS FIRe. ALARM.
div.p: A CURIOUS FIRe. ALARM.

An improvised and very sensitive fire alarm has been brought out by a Danish inventor. It only acts when a sudden wave of heat is generated. A U-tube 4in. high is filled with mercury, the upper parts containing sulphuric ether, and both ends being closed. One side of the tube is covered with anon-conducting material. An even and gradual rise of temperature warms the entire apparatus; but a sudden heat, as in fire, vaporises the ether under the unprotected glass, forcing down the mercury, and ringing an electric bell by the closing of a local contact.

div.head: RADIUM AND ITS PRODUCTS.
div.p: RADIUM AND ITS PRODUCTS.

In an interesting article in Harper'; Magazine, Sir William Ramsay has given some of the results which have been obtained in the chemical examina- tion of the products of change of radium. Summing up he says: The work is merely begun, but it leads to a hypothesis as regards the constitution of radium and similar elements, which was first put forward by Rutherford and Soddy. It is that atoms of elements of high atomic weight, such as rAclium, uranium, thorium, and the suspected eloments polonium and actinium, are unstable; that they undergo spontaneous change into other forms of matter, themselves radioactive, and them- selves unstable; ,and that finally elements are pro- duced which, on account of their non-radioactivity, are, as a rule, impossible to recognise, for their minute amount precludes the application of any ordinary test with success. The recognition of helium, however, which is comparatively easy of detection, lends great support to this hypothesis. The natural question which suggests itself is: Are other elements undergoing similar change? Can it be that their rate of change is so slow_that it cannot be detected? Professor J. J. Thomson has attempted to answer this question, and he has found that many ordinary elements are faintly radioactive; but the answer is still incomplete, for, first, radium is

div.head: SO ENORMOUSLY RADIOACTIVE
div.p: SO ENORMOUSLY RADIOACTIVE

that the merest trace of one of its salts in the salt of another element would produce such radio- activity; and, second, it is not proved that radio- activity is an invariable accompaniment of such change; or again, it may be evolved so slowly as to escape detection. A lump of coal, for example, is slowly being oxidised by the oxygen of the air; oxidation is attended by a rise of temperature, but the most delicate thermometer would detect no difference between the temperature of a lump of coal and that of the surrounding air, for the rate of oxidation is so slow.

- Another question which arises is: Seeing that an element like radium is changing into other sub- stances, and that its life is a comparatively short one, it must be in course of formation, else its amount would be exhausted in about 2,500 years. An attempt has been made by Soddy to see if uranium salts, carefully purified from radium, have reproduced radium after an interval of a year: but his result was a negative one. Possibly some other form of matter besides uranium contributes to the synthesis of radium, and

FURTHER EXPERIMENTS in this direction will be eagerly welcomed. Lastly, the experiments of Ramsay and Cook on the action of the 0-rays appear to foreshadow results of importance. For while radium, during its spon- taneous change, parts with a relatively enormous amount of •energy, largely in the form of heat, it is a legitimate inference that if the atoms of ordinary elements could be made to absorb energy, they would undergo change of a construc- tive, and not of a disruptive, nature. If, as looks probable, the action of 0-rays, them- selves the conveyers of enormous energy, on such matter as glass, is to build up atoms which are radioactive, and consequently of high atomic weight; and if it be found that the par- ticular matter produced depends on the element on which the 0-rays fall, and to which they impart their energy—if these hypotheses are just, then the transmutation of elements no longer appears an idle dream. The philosopher's stone will have been discovered, and it is not beyond the bounds of possibility that it may 'lead to that other goal of the philosophers of the dark ages—the elixir vitae. For the action of living cells is also dependent on the nature and direction of the energy which they contain; and who can say that it will be impossible to control their action, when the means of imparting and controlling energy shall have been investigated?

THE WINNING OF FRIDA.
BY COMRIE COLQUHOUN, Author of "The Finger of Fate," "ha Better Self," "A Son of the South," Sco.

I had always been told that country-bred folk, when they came to settle in London, did not take kindly to restaurants. My experience was quite different, as the regularity with which I patronised a certain restaurant in a certain street off the Strand went to prove. _ _

Not that this restaurant was particularly famous for high-class fare. I selected it because there was an air of quietness about it (it was out of earshot of the roaring, rushing life of the Strand) and because the prorr;etor, a Frenchman, did his utmost to make his customers comfortable.

The place was a popular rendezvous, not only with the proprietor's compatriots, but with other foreigners—Germans, Italians, Swiss and Spaniards. I found it an interesting occupation to watch these people day after day as I ate the grilled chop and chip potatoes, and drank the light wine, on the excellence and cheapness of which old Henri, the proprietor, was never weary of dilating. I had been a customer of old Henri for two years, and nothing had occurred to interfere with the regularity of my diurnal visits. One day, however, an unusual incident occurred. so unusual that it changed my life, and has led to my telling this story. I went to the restaur tnt two hours after my accustomed time. That is to say, about thre o'clock in the afternoon. There was not a single customer in the place. The two foreign waiters, taking advantage of the lull, were chatting at the farthest end of the room, and old Henri was deep in the Petit Journal, his favourite paper, which he secured every day from the French paper-stand e the Strand. He appeared to be not at all piety*. with the aspect of affairs ; for the first time &a many a week his daily beam of recognition as I entered the door was lacking. But I was not the sole occupant of the place for long. I had scarce got half-way through my lunch when two men entered, and seated themselves at the marble-topped table in near neighbourhood to me. They were foreigners—Germans, as I soon made out—and so far as I could remember, this was their first visit to the restaurant.

They had come to talk as well as to eat, and the subject of their conversation was so engrossing that they apparently forgot the presence of the Englander—myself. Strange-looking men they were—widely different from the usual run of old Henri's customers. Their clothes were in the seedy stage. They were fair of complexion, and wore pointed beards with long moustaches ; their hats were alike, dark brown in colour and of soft felt, with the crowns crushed in.

Their looks were certainly not prepossessing. Their gestures and the furtive glances of their eyes were such as to engender suspicion. I, at least, suspected them, and consequently became more observant than usual.
"How many did you say are left, Rudolf?" asked the more talkative of the two, whol gathered was called Fritz.
"Five," answered his companion, "and they are only waiting for an opportunity to leave." "Ach " groaned the first speaker. "So we are smashed up. And to think of the excellent start we had."
"An excellent start, truly. Twenty members, and all eager to do what was expected of them." "And only you and Karl have found your way here ? "
"That is so. Five in Paris, six in Brussels, one in Rome, Karl, you and I here, and five left behind."

"Mein Gott! I feel myself possessed of a demon's fury against Judge Holz." "Calm yourself, comrade. Judge Holz will have reason to regret having pursued us so relentlessly." "What do you mean ? " "When I found you out I told you that I had something of the utmost importance to communicate. Listen."

Here the speaker looked over to where I sat. His cautious glance evidently convinced him that the Englander was oblivious of everything save his chop, and that I hadn't the remotest idea of what was being said, for he at once resumed: "When the fact was borne in upon us that the Freedom Club would be dissolved, we swore to be revenged on the man who had found us out. It was Flowed that the revenge should not be directed against himself, but against one to whom he was as much attached as to life itself—his only child. Lots were drawn, and it fell out that Karl and I had to accomplish the task. We have performed it, thanks mainly to Karl's wife. A clever womas is Fran Heimal. Herr Flolz's daughter is now London. Karl and his wife are with her now. The effect on the man to whom all this was told was strange to behold. He jumped up from the table, and grasped his companion's hand. "Bas geht gut camerad he exclaimed. I myself was not less astonished at this sensa- tional ending of a German secret society. Involun- tarily my knife and fork became silent, and I found myself looking eagerly at the Germans. There was that in my glance which disturbed them ; their voices dropped to undertones, and a few moments later they left the restaurant. A German secret society dissolved ; its members either prosecuted or compelled to flee the Father- land through the instrumentality of a zealous judge ; the abduction of that judge's daughter by way of revenge—this, briefly, was what I had learnt. My friends who know me best say that im- petuosity is a leading trait in my character—that lam quick to act without counting the consequences. I acted up to my reputation now. Jumping up, I paid old Henri what I owed him, and reached the Strand at the same time as the Germans. They entered a hansom, which wss crawling along. I followed suit.
"Follow that hansom wherever it goes," I shouted to the driver, pointing in front of me. "Make no mistake; the driver is wearing a. white hat."
"Right, sir," answered the-driver, promptly. It turned out to be a short chase, oaly along the Strand and over Waterloo l3ridge. to Waterloo Station.

The two men went to the third-class booking °Mee, and then passed to No. 6 platform. [followed closely behind, and selected a com- partment immediately to the rear of that which they had entered. They left the train at Queen's-road, and then turned up a quiet street off the main thoroughfare. So far they had not perceived me. I felt that their mission boded no good, and I resolved to act cautiously in order to get at the bottom of what appeared to me tc be a strange proceeding. I therefore took due note of the house they had entered, and after the lapse of a few minutes, made my way to an arch almost opposite, access •to which could be had by making a circuitous tour. I must have loitered up and down this arch for fully half-an-hour, keeping a sharp eye on the house across the road. But there was not the least indication that anyone was within, and the fear that I had come on a wildgoose chase was fast laying hold of me. , Suddenly the door of the house opened, and the men I had followed appeared.

Simultaneously a Ytce appeared at an upper window. It was the face of a girl, a face which told of acute distress of mind as plain as words could. It was a face of death-like pallor, and there was a haunted, fear-stricken look about the eyes that aroused my compassion at cnce. So engrossed was I with this face at the that I had for the moment forgotten the men who I had followed. Those dark, lustrous eyes had a mesmeric effect upon me. I stood as one spell- bound until she left the window. It was then too late to follow the men, Fritz andfßudolf, and I returned to the Strand, be,tring with me the vision of the beautiful, sad-eyed captive.. For a certain period every day 1 visited the arch. More often than not the face appeared at the window, but only for a few minutes, and always when the men were leaving the house. Late one afternoon, when my vigil was longer than usual, another man besides Fritz and Rudolf left the house. The third I took to be Karl, the girl's keeper. They had scarce reached the end of the street when the face again shewed itself. But there was a wholly different expression in the eyes now. They wer6 keen and feverish. I knew it well, for their gaze rested upon me. I was recognised. _ _ . _ _ •

Instantly I placed my fitic.,,erg to my lips. She interpreted my signal for caution, for pressing her cheeks to the window-pane. she glanced furtively below. Then stealthily and silently she opened the window, and the next moment a billet fluttered La the pavement.
ran and picked it up, returned to the arcn, and read this in German:
"Save me, but as you pity me and value your own life, be careful.

I looked up at the window, intending to assure her by signs that she possessed a friend in me, but the face I sought was not there. Instead there was another face—the face of a fearsome-looking woman with coal-black eyes, and a large, sensuous mouth.

I was amazed at this sudden metamorphosis, and drew further into the arch for a few moments. The black eyes looked right and left and below—every- where except in the arch—and then this face vanished too.

"This evil-looking woman must be Karl's wife," I thought. "A woman with a face like that will stop at nothing." I fell to thinking how I could save the girl. "Save me, but as you pity me and value] your own life, be careful.

I pored over the slip of paper containing these words as the train bore me to Waterloo. " Be careful." What reason was there for this injunc- tion ? " I asked myself. "There must be a reason," I concluded, and decided to watch the house more closely than ever. The necessity for doing so did not arise, however, for the following evening, after the street lamps were lit, great was my surprise to see the men I had seen in the restaurant, and Karl, leave the house, follcwed a few moments later by the woman with the coal black eyes and the captive. The men kept in advance till the station was reached, and I followed closely in the wake of the women.

It was another case of dogging their movements when Waterloo was reached. The darkness made this extremely difficult, but I was again fortunate in my cabman, who set me down in a street in Soho, a few paces from a house with which he said he was familiar, having driven innumerable fares thither.

I did not attempt to enter the place just then, but loitered about. By-and-bye I became aware of its character. Men and women in evening dress drove up to the house and entered it; it was a fashionable night-house. "Whoever goes there once goes again," I told Irself, and went home.

4'ln 'following evening I was amongst those who sought admission to the house. To the porter's mind my attire constituted my bona fides; he con- cluded that I had come there to spend money. A thrill shot through me after my first glance round the place. At the top of the gorgeously decorated and magnificently lighted room was she whom I sought. Never before had my eyes beheld so beautiful a creature. Her dress was a dream of loveliness. Diamonds flashed on her bosom and in her hair. Men buzzed round her, but a woman stood nearest her, a woman sumptuously dressed, and whose ample bosom was bejewelled with vulgar prodigality. She was none other than the woman with the coal- black eyes. . . _ . .
My heart sank within me as I watched the young and beautiful face which had haunted me ever since I first beheld it at the window.

There was no death-like pallor, no sorrow-laden eyes now. She was chatting gaily, and distributing smiles to the men who hung about her. I turned away in disgust, and was about to leave the place when my eye fell on Fritz and Rudolph, who had emerged from another room. There was that about their movements which arrested my attention. They were in evening dress, and diamonds sparkled in their shirt-fronts. They fussed about a great deal, and spoke to many of the men and women, pointing now and again to the door of the room from which they had come. rt was the gambling room, and these men Ensilaged it.
„ My gaze again sought the girl, and what I saw made me hurry towards her. She sat on a lounge with her hands on her knees. The sad look had returned to her eyes, the pallor to her cheeks.
"Do you recognise me ? " I asked, gently, in German.

She looked up hurriedly, and instantly a look of joy overspread her face. She would have grasped the 'hand I held out towards her, but on second thoughts withdrew hers hurriedly, and with fear in her eyes glanced nervously about her. "I have followed you here," I continued. "I want to save you." Again she looked round. "Oh, thank you, thank you I" she said. "But beware—oh, beware of Frau Heimal." "Frau Heimall" I said. "Who is she ? "

There was no need for her to answer, for the next moment the woman with the coal-black eyes appeared at her side. Instantly the girl's demeanour changed. Her eyes, instead of being filled with sadness now shone with a coquettish light. Her glance was the glance of the charmer, her voice the voice of the siren. There was no withstanding the appeal in the dulcet tones.

"Do you play ? " she asked. I was too much astounded at this sudden trans- formation to ',answer at once. Whereupon Frau tieimal, concluding that I had not understood what the charmer had said, repeated the question in broken English. "Oh, yes," I replied, resolving to blindfold this woman. "I have come purposely to play." "Den you will hare much pleasure here," she said, pointing to the gambling room. I took the hint, as the other men who had spoken to the girl had done, and entered the gambling hell. But not to play; rather to think. Several ideas coursed through my brain as I sank into a luxurious arm-chair, but one clung tenaciously to me. It was this. I was convinced Frau Heimal had some occult influence over the girl. That influence had been exercised in her abduc- tion, and it was now employed to lure men with money to squander in this night house. In other words, the girl was a decoy—a tool in the hands of this terrible woman, whose hypnotic influence caused her to smile and cozen in a way to turn the heads and empty the pockets of foolish men. The play, which was of an exciting character, had no allurement for me. The sight of the players with their feverish faces, of the cards, money and cheques, were abhorrent to me. "Cannot you be induced to play, sir ? " I looked up. It was Karl, the husband of the hypnotist and the tout of the gambling room, who spoke. "Presently," I answered, indifferently, and returned to my thoughts.

_ I now made an important discovery. I was possessed of something more than a feeling of pity for this poor girl. Pity alone would have induced me to try to save her, but love was mixed with compassion nrm.. Those beautiful eyes with sad glances h. d lone for m • They held meicapt ye i 11 save hr at all cost," I cried, veheinentiy. The gamblers were too much engrossed with their cards to hear me, but the managers of the place, the men I had seen in the restaurant, came hurriedly forward. "Is the gentleman unwell ? " asked Fritz.

I was abut to mutter some sort of excuse when a strange thing happened. Frau Heirnal rushed into the room, her black eyes almost starting out of her head. "Cease playing!" she shouted to Fritz. "Hide the cards ! Clear the tables of money! The police are here!" _ _

Sure enough the police had come to make one of those raids which were not uncommon in Soho at that time. A raid on this particular establishment, how- ever, was never expected, for the reason that it was understood to be well conducted, that drinking and dancing were all that went on in the place. In the confusion which prevailed I hurried to the girl's side. Freed from the hypnotic spell of Fran freimal, who was now otherwise engaged, she seized my hand and looked inquiringly into my face. She wanted to know what this confusion meant. "Pray keep calm," I entreated. "Trust in me." She repaid me with a glance which sent the hot Mood to my face. Meanwhile the Germans were being severally questioned by the police officers.

, "We have secured more than we bargained for," I heard one officer remark to another. "Look at these." And he pulled five photographs from his pocket. Four were photographs of the three men who managed the club and Fran Mims]. Those personages having been identified, the officer looked round the room until his eye rested on the girl at my side. "Ah," he exclaimed, unable to conceal the pleasure he felt at his discovery. "She is here." -"Friiiilein Frida Holz, I presume ?" he said, advancing forward and holding up the fifth photograph. She bowed her head.

At this juncture Frau Heitnal came forward with flashing eyes. and sought to interpose hers6lf between the girl and me. Fraulein Holz held up her hands appealingly. "Don't leave me!" she cried, "Oh, don't leave
"Back woman!" 1 shouted. devilish arts."
"Away with your

And taking hold of the girl's hand I led her into the midst of the officers and told my story, beginning with what I had heard in the restaurant, what I had seen in the quiet street in. the Queen's- road, and ending by giving the reasons for my visit to the night house. My statement was believed. "Friedrich Schwerin, Rudolf Hermann, Karl and Hermione Heimal," began the chief officer, "you are not only arrested on a charge of permitting gaming on these premises, but also on an extradition warrant charging you with having kept the Free- dom Club, at Hamburg, for an unlawful purpose, and with being concerned in the abduction of Friiulein Frida Holz, daughter of Judge Holz, from her home at Blankenese."

The principals were taken to Marlborough-street, and the next day only formal evidence was given, and a remand for a week granted. Meanwhile, Scotland Yard authorities were in frequent communication with the German police, with the result that, after two further remands, the English charge of keeping a gaming house was adjourned sin.e die—in other words, in this instance, dropped. The culprits were next taken to Bow. street, and in due course committed for extradition to Germany to answer the graver charge preferred against them there. But they seemed' to possess endless resources. They availed themselves to the utmost of the various forms which the legislature in its wisdom has placed on the statute ly_iok for the protection of the oppressed against the oppressor, and they appealed against the magistrate's decision. But forensic ingenuity was of no avail, and to Germany they were despatched. Friiulein llolz was restored to her parents. With her departure it seemed as though I had passed out of her life. She had rot passed out of mine, how- ever, for never a day, never an hour, elapsed since the final scene in the police-court, that I did not think of her. I pictured her with her parents, saw her no longer sad, but joyous-hearted and more biautiful than ever, and soon to be married, proba- bly to a rich Hamburg merchant, or a man learned in the law like her father.

But my imaginings were brought to a sudden conclusion one morning. A packet from Marl- borough-street Police-court enclosing letters from Judge Holz and Frida herself was handed to me. These missives not only overwhelmed me with thanks, but strongly invited me to pay the judge a visit, as soon as I conveniently could. Do you wonder that I jumped at the opportunity' There was not a happier passenger on the steamer from London to Hamburg than myself. And as was the case during the voyage across the North Sea, so up the Elbe to Blankenese, where Frida resided, and where the Hamburg folk, with oppor- tunities for holidaying, resort in the summer months. Many of the passenzers. vming men and maidens, chatted gaily about. jiuent in store for them in the dancing saloon at the top of the Sullberg, which overlooks the broad bosom of the Elbe. As for myself, I was enjoying in anticipation the sight of Frida's happy and beautiful face. It was not a difficult matter, from the minute description supplied to me at Hamburg, to pick out the large white house in which Judge Holz resided. It stood distinct from those villas embowered in foliage on the north bank of the river.

What need to describe the reception accorded to me. Let it suffice to say that my visit to Frida's home extended longer, much longer, than I had, anticipated. It was not my last visit either. When next I sailed up the Elbe and ascended the hill to the white house, it was to ask the- judge for Frida's hand. When the farewells came to be said, the worthy judge and his wife laughingly accused me of abducting their daughter and of carrying her off to, London. Frida smiled, and shot a loving glance at me. And so with Goethe slightly varied, it was then, and has remained till this day, a case of: "Hand in Hand und Lipp auf Lippe, Liebes Madchen bleibt treu." [Liz END:I

NATINAL CONFERENCE ON, THE EDUCATION

ACTS. A conference of unusual importance is now being organised by the National Council of the Evangelical Free Churches. On Thursday, February 2nd, immedi- ately before the opening of Parliament, Representative Free Church Educationalists will meet in the Memorial Hall to confer on the practical working of the Educa- tion Acts. These representatives will come from every part of England and \Vales and will consist of men and women actually engaged in the administration of our present educational system, such as County, Borough and District Councillors, members of Education Com- mittees and managers of schools. All Members of Parliament representing English and Welsh constitu- encies and prospective candidates known to be Free Churchmen will also be invited to attend. The after- noon will be devoted to a practical Conference when some of the real grievances of Nonconformists, as seen in the working of the Acts will be dealt with. There will be a Representative Protest Meeting in the even- ing. It is expected that Mr. Augustine Birrell, Mr. Lloyd George. M.P., Dr. Fairbairn, Rev. C. Silvester Horne, M.A., Dr. Horton' Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., Dr. Clifford, Rev. J. Scott Lidgett, M.A., and other prominent leaders will take part.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
NORTHERN LEAGUE.
First Division.
Warrington Win at Halifax.

The Warrington team paid a visit to Halifax on Satur- day, minus such men as Fish, Dickenson, and Harris. Halifax were, however in a worse plight,Little,Nettleton, Hadwen and Morley being the principal absentees. There was only a small attendance, the weather being cold and unfavourable. Tennis: Halifax—Homer, back; Hartley, Williams Joe Riley, and Marshall, three-quarter backs ; Atkins and Gledhill, half backs ; Bulmer, Jack Riley, Langhorn, Mallinson, Winskill, Morton Hammond,and H. Morley, forwards. Warrington—Hallam, back; Short, Isherwood, Brooks and Kenyon, three-quarter backs; Davies and Hocken- hall, half backs; Boardman, Preston, Thomas, Belton, Jolley, Swift, Harrier, and Shugars, forwards. Referee. Mr. W. McCuteheon, Oldham ; touch judges Mr. F. Clegg, Bradford, and Mr. Tattersall, Normanton. Isherwood came late, and during the first twenty-five minutes of the game Warrington had only 14 players. Thomas left the pack and played threequarter. War- rington more than held their own however, and Preston twice nearly lowered the Halifax goal with penalty kieks. Williams several times kicked a great length,but the Halifax back play, taken all round, was disappoint- ing. At half-time neither side had scored. Warrington went off with a rush after the intervaLand were soon dangerous. A passing bout ended in Short getting possession near the line, but he dropped the ball when a score seemed a certainty. Kenyon did the same thing at the other corner. Halifax then took up the attack, but several chances were made poor use of. Warrington cleared, and eventually Brooks snapped up the ball, after Joe Riley had made a bad pass to Williams. and made for the line. Finding his way barred, he passed to Hockenhall, and after Preston had handled the ball Davies ran over and scored a try. Hockenhall kicked a goal. The remaining play was in favour of Warrington, and Short added a try, from a cross-kick, which Preston converted. Result :—War- rington 2 goals, 2 tries (10 points), Halifax nil. LEEDS v. HUNSLET.

_ There was great popular interest in this game, and a crowd of 20,000 spectators witnessed a fluctuating con- test in which victory finally rested—as it deserved to do on the play.—with the Leeds team. A score was forthcoming in the first three minutes. Leeds were defending when Huuslet were penalised, and after the free kick Brayshaw cleverly punted across to Evans. It was a forward, however, who took the ball on, and after his final kick Llewellyn beat Guy in the race for the ball, and scored a try close to the corner flag, Little- wood's kick, though a good one, failing. Hunslet imme- diately made the scores level through a fine passing round cpmmenced by A. Goldthorpe. This movement also ended in a cross kick for the wing man, Ward, who with a very fast run completed the try. The goal-kick was unsuccessful, but a few minutes later A. Goldthorpe gave his side the lead with a penalty goal. Leeds attacked fiercely after this, and just before the interval Naylor got over at the corner and made the half-time score 6 points to sin favour of Leeds. Towards the close the game went strongly in favour of the home team, and seven minutes from the end Naylor scored his second try in clever fashion. No goal was kicked, and the final score was :—Leeds, 3 tries (9 points), Hunslet, 1 goal and 1 try (5 points). LEIGH V. WAKEFIELD TRINITY.

- -- At Leigh, before 2,000 spectators. For a time Leigh had to defendl the Wakefield) backs making good use of the wind. The interval arrived without any score. In the opening stages of the second half, Leigh took up a strong attacking position, and Dunbavin punted across to his right wing, and Messer dribbled over the line and scored a try. Dunbavin made a poor attempt at road. Play was kept atthe Wakefield end,the visitors' efforts to attack being very crude. Moreover,the Leigh forwards were now overplaying their opponents and getting the ball from almost every scrummage, and at last Whittaker passed to Johnson, who dodged the Wakefield backs one after the other, and scored near the corner. Result:—Leigh 2 tries (6 points), Wake- field nil.

div.head: BRADFORD v. WIDNES: SIX TRIES BY DECHAN.
div.p: BRADFORD v. WIDNES: SIX TRIES BY DECHAN.

At Park Avenue, before about 5,000 spectators. No detailed description of the match is necessary, since Bradford easily triumphed over a disorganised Widnes team, and scoring was so frequent as to become mono- tonous. In the first half Dechan—well fed by Mosby— scored 5 tries and Connell one. Mosby kicked a couple of goals, and Eagers close on half-time dropped a goal from near the centre line. Halftime :—Bradford, 3 goals 6 tries (24 points); Widnes, nil. The game had scarcely been re-started before Barker scored for Bradford, and McCarthy with a clever drop registered Widnes' only score, a goal. Barker was the next to add a try, and then Dechan put on his sixth try ofithe match. None of the place kicks were successful this half. Resultl:—Bradford, 3 goals 9 tries (33 points), Widnes, 1 goal (2 points). HULL v. SALFORD: GRAND WORK BY THE

div.head: HULL FORWARDS.
div.p: HULL FORWARDS.

This match was played on the Boulevard Ground, before about 8,000 pspectators. Eventually the home forwards broke through the Salford defence, and, thanks to a mull by Lambert, Hall picked up the ball and dashed over in a nice place, so that Goodfellow added the goal points. There was more scoring in the second half, and, like the first, the play was brilliant. Salford played a fine game, Lambert being in grand form, but Jenkins scored the second try, which Goodfellow failed to convert, but the latter player soon afterwards added several points for his side. tie dropped a goal from a penalty near midfield; he scored a try near the corner, which he failed to improve, and he finished by breaking in almost single-handed, and scoring and converting Result 3 goals 4 tries (18 points), Salford, nil - - - -

div.head: , – OLDHAM v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.
div.p: , - OLDHAM v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.

Played at Oldham, in showery weather, before an attendance of some 4,000 persons. In the first half Oldham, playing against the wind, had decidedly the Worst of the play. The game after the interval was a complete contrast. Oldham adopted a rushing forward game, which proved completely successful. From a scrummage near the line A. Lees passed to Dixon, who dashed over. Ferguson failed at goal. Passing between Cash and Lewis ended in the last-named scoring a try. Though the kick was at a difficult angle, Ferguson brought it off. A grand forward rush ended in Ellis scoring, Ferguson failing to add a couple of points. Result :—Oldham 1 goal and 3 tries (11 points), Hull Kingston Rovers nil.
RUNCORN Y. BATLEY.
At Runcorn, before 2,000 spectators. Jolley, Watton, and Moran gained ground for Runcorn with passing,and

eventually from a scrummage Jolley passed to Watton, who was successful ir scoring a fine try. Houghton failed at goal. Play was even for a time, until a line round of passing between Oakland, Goodall, Shackleton and Abbott ended in the last-named scoring in a good position. Wattie Davies added a goal. Half-time score :—Batley 1 goal and 1 try (5 points), Runcorn 1 try (3 points). After the interval Runcorn were soon on the attack, but Oakland, Goodall, and Abbott returned to the centre. Houghton replied with a lofty kick. Harrison followed up, and getting hold, trans- ferred to Williams, who scored. Jolley failed at goal. Houghton landed a goal from a mark, and shortly after Jolley dropped a goal. Play had hardly resumed when Jolley again got possession and dropped a second goal. Batley were now sorely pressed, and with difficulty kept their opponents out. Just before the finish Jolley passed out to Moran, who dodged round the 13atley backs and scored a try. The same player added a goal. Result :—Runcorn 4 goals and 3 tries (17 points), Batley 1 goal and 1 try (5 points). WIGAN v. ST. HELENS.

These teams opposed each other at Wigan, where about 8,000 persons assembled. Wigan displayed the better movements, particularly at three-quarters, but there was little to choose between the two contingents during the first half, in which Harris registered a try for Wigan after a brilliant run, the succeeding kick by Mason being successful, and Traynor, as a result of a wide pass from Edmunds, gained a try for the visitors, the scorer failing at goal from an easy position. In the second half Wigan managed to further increase their lead by 10 points. b The extra points came as a re- sult of a forward rush,which enabled Whittaker to score, Mason landing the goal, and from a magnificent dribble nearly the whole length of the field by Leytham, Mason again adding the goal points. Result :—Wigan 3 goals, 2 tries (15 points), St. Helens 1 try (3 points).

div.head: BROUGHTON RANGERS v. SWINTON.
div.p: BROUGHTON RANGERS v. SWINTON.

Seven thousand spectators witnessed this match at Broughton in miserable weather. From the start the Rangers always held the upper hand, and pressed severely. Wilson threw away a splendid opportunity by selfish play, but early on Swinton were penalised, and Harris placed a goal. Molyneux made a couple of dashing runs for Swinton, but the visitors were seldom danger- ous, and from a cross kick by Harry Smith scored for the home side, and Harris kicked a goal. At the interval the score was—Broughton Rangers 2 goals, 1 try (7 points), Swinton nil. On resuming the visitors attacked, and after Horton had been so badly hurt that he had to leave the field fbr the rest of the game, Flynn placed a goal. This was the extent of the visitors' success for the Rangers, despite being a man short, played magnificently. Wilson was tackled on the line, and then Hogg scored at the corner. Harris failed at goal, and the next try came from Beetham, who scored under the posts. Harris improved, and subsequently Woodward, after a magnifi- cent run from half-way, scored the try of the day. No goal resulted, and the final result was :—Broughton Rangers 3 goals, 4 tries (18 points), Swinton 1 goal (2 points).

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES.

WARRINGTON " A " V. SALFORD ST. BARTHOLOMEW'S. For the second time this season Warrington met the Salford organization at the Wilderspool enclosure on Saturday. Interest centred in the match owing to the fact that a trial was given to a threequarter hailing from South, Wales. Play was even in the opening stages, but eventually strong runs by Berry and Jordan landed the home men close to their opponents' line. After Berry had been pulled up on the line, the sang e player accepted a pass from Roberts and got in near the posts, for Knight to place a goal. The' Saints " retaliated, and excellent loose work caused Warrington to fall back on the defence. Fine fielding by Knight was fol- lowed by a weak kick, and from the ensuing scrummage the visitors scored, the try being unimproved. Salford continued to attack, and came near scoring on several occasions, but Jordan eventually got the Warringtonians out of a tight corner, and play again took an even turn. Warrington rallied, and vigorous forward work almost ended in a score. Half-time :—V7arrington five points ; Salford St. Bartholomew's, three points. On resuming Warrington soon rattacked and Berry scored at the corner, Knight landing the goal. Another fine move- ment by the backs in which the new man distinguished himself, saw Berry score a third try. In the last few minutes Knight placed a penalty goal. Resuß, : War- rington " A " 15 points ; Salford St. Bartholomew's 3 points. ORFORD V. PADGATE JUNIORS. These teams met al, Orford. The Orford forwards, heeling out well, gave their backs plenty of chances, and Taylor starting a passing bout resulted in Birchall scoring a fine try. In the second half Padgate were outplayed, and tries were scored by Taylor, Clare, and Higham, Phillips adding goals. Cottom intercepted a pass, and scored for Padgate, Chamberlain adding the goal. Final : Orford, three goals, four tries ; Padgate Juniors, one goal, one try.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, January 14, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, January 14, 1905.

FIRST DIVISION. CROSFIELD'S V. LA.TCHFORD BRITANNIA. These teams tried conclusions on the former's ground on Saturday. Midfield play ensued for the first few minutes, but the home men soon got to work,land forced a fruitless corner. The visitors now attacked, but Strettle, who throughout played splendidly, sent them back. Crosflelds were awarded a free kick, but nothing Iresulted. Later on Strettle scored from a penalty, and afterwards Dickenson sent in a shot at thirty yards' range which proved effective. Even play now ensued, neither side having the advantage. Half-time score : Crosfleld's, two goals; Latchford Britannia, nil. There was no addition to the score in the second half.
Berths lay awake oue whole night thwareg et all this, and in the morning she rose up, deter- mined on a certain course of action.
"I am going to build a house," she announced at breakfast. •• What .?" almost screamed Miss Lizabeth.

"To get a house built rather. And I'll get it done without losing a penny of my own or any- one else's by it," she said, anticipating the ob- jections that were rising to Miss Lizabeth's lips. To all the aunt's questions she would only give the information that this was a fancy of hers, that she would have it built on the portion of the freehold belonging to herself, and that she meant to commence the work forthwith. She had some ready money in the bank to use in the beginning. This she would replace later on, with the in- terest that should have accrued on it.

It was an extraordinary whim Miss Lizabeth thought, but Bertha was no child to be thwarted, or pushed away from any project that she seri- ously entertained, and the aunt could see that this was a very well defined plan, however aston- ishing in its nature. There was nothing for Miss Lizabeth to do but to let her niece take the mat- ter in hand and go through with it as she woahl. At the rear of the Hoffmann residence, there was a disused storehouse fitted up with shelves and bins that had been empty since the time of the house's occupancy by the minister with seventeen children. To make this place into a very presentable shop was a work of very little labour or expense. In a week it was stored with a full supply of teas, sugar, candles, cottons. shoes, &c.—all the modest requirements of a general shop's customers in such a town as Kil- cullen. People wondered at this but it was set down after the usual nine days' discussion as a " frake " of one of the notoriously " frakish " genteel folks—to do " siuseless " things was the privilege of the prosperous. But it was soon dis- covered that the 'frake was not quite so senseless as it had at first appeared. Miss Bertha hal interviews with sundry quarrymen, masons, carpenters, Sm., resulting in very general satisfaction to those long idle crafts- men. She engaged them at fair wages for the work on the building of which she was to be architect and contractor-general. The one cor.di- tion attached to their employment was that they should agree to buy from her (Miss Bertha's) shop everything they wanted of the kind sold therein. Any infringement or disregard of this agree- ment was to be met by instant dismissal. As may be surmised of people who had for months been on the brink of starvation, they were only too glad to get groceries and clothing on any terms, and Miss Bertha's prices being no higher than those of the other shops, the work- men and their families kept faithfully to their written promises. There must have been some old trading blood in the Hoffmans, for Bertha developed a real shopkeeping genius in those busy days. She discovered as if by instinct where goods of the best quality could be bought cheapest, and in a short time many more important people than her workpeople were glad to be admitted among the number of her customers. And so the fine man- sion rose fair and stately out on the old Cool- gowan O'Kearney land, in the middle of the Hoffman's garden—a mansion even finer and more commodious than the one given up with such heartbreak by the luckless family. The townspeople speculated about its purpose, and the general opinion was that one or other of the spin- sters had a notion of marrying, and being, neither young nor handsome, deemed it necessary to add substantial and fetching attractions to offer with their "hand and heart."

" Terrible foolishness it was for a pair of mild cratures —the eldest of 'em with one leg in the grave, as you might say, to be thinkin' of world- liness and marriage—instead of sitting at aise an' reading their pious books an' preparing for their eternity." Some of this talk, no doubt, reached Bertha's ears, but she worked away busily and happily, finding in the progress of the building and the success of her shop enough of happiness to drown every ill-natured sting. One April evening when the snow of the cherry trees in the garden was floating in a breeze that was summer-like in its softness, Bertha stood at the porch door perfectly satisfied with her house. From attic to base- ment everything had been well planned and was well finished. Judgment and good taste, solid materials and skilful workmanship were every- where evident, and with a sigh of satisfaction she looked the door behind her and went home. Aunt Lizabeth, who was ailing a little, had taken but a faint interest in the house and shop, and yet to-night when Bertha brought out her carefully balanced accounts and showed that the expenses of the building were actually forty pounds less than the profits of the shop, she could not re- press an exclamation of surprise and admiration. That magnificent mass of masonry, those noble rooms, the possibilities for beautiful refined liv- ing all out of a 6 trifling shop '—it was wonder- ful! Just then it Uppened that the death of Colonel Patterson of Kilcullen House occasioned many changes in his family. The one that interested Bertha was the sale of the furniture of that com- fortable home. It was a forced matter—the family was impatient to have it over and to get away,—and everything went, as was said " for a song.' Bertha's surplus forty pounds procured the handsome furnishing of four or five rooms and the complete equipment of the kitchen. While the last touches were being given to the curtain-banging and other final arrangements, Bertha heard that the doctor had been going to the O'Kearney's lodgings for some days, and then it was known that one of the ladies was ill of fever. It was a light enough case of typhoid but the word 'fever' had untold terrors for Kilcullen, which in the pre-drainage times ten years ago used to have a visitation of typhus yearly. The alarmed neighbours, working on the fears of the chandler-landlord, made him insist on the removal of the patient from his premises to the only other available shelter—the work- house hospital—and this was about to be at- tempted when Bertha heard of it. The Union ambulance stood outside the door, around which a curious crowd was collected when Miss Hoffman arrived there. They were listen- ing to a storm of high words on the upper land- ing—the Miss O'Kearneys indignantly protesting against the intrusion 'of the ambulance people and relieving officer, and the firm refusal of the latter to leave without the patient. The health of the whole town was not to be put in danger by sick people who were unwilling to leave their in- sanitary quarters for a fine wholesome hospital. The doctor strove kindly to modify the apparent harshness of the proceeding, but the poor ladies could see nothing in the removal but disgrace,' and they would :la give up their patient. Bertha ca,." quietly forward, and laying her hand on tbz. mbling one of 31189 Rosina she said, " Dear Vim O'Kearney, there is no need whatever of th:. hospital. If you will only let your sister colb,. out to Coolgowan and accom- pany her yourselves, it will be pleasanter and better. You will find everything ready in the new house." The O'Kearneys were in that stage of acute distress when it seems the most natural thing in the world to have deliverance offered. _ _ _ .

'You are very good," Miss Rosina said sim- ply, and they hurried off to prepare themselves and the invalid for the journey. The O'Kearneys had some of the stoic in them, yet when, out of the blooming garden, they entered the rooms so exquisitely fresh and comfortable, uncontrollable tears filled their eyes. "It is heavenly —heavenly," murmured Miss nosina. "My God, whet a deliverance !" Even the inNalid rejoiced, and with Berthas nursing, was quickly on the road to recovery. When she was able to be up and about, however, by de- grees a sort of uneasiness stole into the manner of aer sisters. A great change had come over them with their change of abode. Their dress was carefully attended to, and their pretty surround- ings were kept in all the dainty order in which they had found them, though at what unearthly hour the latter work was done, no one could dis- cover. But that, Miss Rosina considered, was another advantage of living in the country; they could manage to do things unobserved. The re- newed feeling of well-being and satisfaction in them brought back the old keen sense of their own importance that resented any suspected or obvious pity or favour-bestowing. That these should be from an inferior ' was very bitter to them. _

One day Miss Rosina said to Bertha, who had been out in the garden with the convalescent, " I'm afraid, Miss Hoffman, you must have thought it very unbusiness-like of us not to have inquired before now the rent for these rooms. It may be beyond us, you know." Bertha detected something superior ' in the manner, and a desire to set her down. " My brother may be home any day now and it will be necessary of course to know the rent you will expect." " It will be time enough to 151 k of all that when he arrives," Bertha said cheerfully. " Oh, but, pardon me, that would never do. Tie is very proud—none of us can forget what is due to our family and name—and neither he not we would wish to incur a larger.debt than we can pay—to be under an obligation—to any one. Please let us know distinctly what your tams are." Bertha hesitated - She found it difficult in the
face of these grim, narrow, I.elf-sufficient iwings before her, to offer the house as a gift, us it had all. along been in her mind to do.

" But," she at length managed to say, " there must really be no question of rent at all—" " No question of rent ?" demanded the others haughtily. " I mean—l want to tell you about the house. Here it is on your own land, the natural home for you all. It has been built (and furnished to the extent you see) on the profits from the sale of goods to the workmen employed on it, and others. It has cost me absolutely nothing, so that in of- fering it to your family as a gift, there is no- thing really to thank me for." "As a gift ? Heavens above, are we sunk so low that the fruits of shopleeeping can be offered us in charity ?" cried Miss Rosina. "That a shopkeeper can insult the O'Kear- neys !" said Miss Selina. "It is insufferable. Thank God, our brother has been spared it." Miss Alison contented herself with rising and leaving the room, an example which the others made no delay in following. Unaccustomed waves of mortification succeeded each other hotly in Bertha's face as she too rose and left. She had not much leisure to think of it, however, for on reaching home 'she found her aunt seriously ill. When the Hoffmans ailed they made speedy work of getting ill or dying, and, alas, it was not getting well in the good aunt's case. A fortnight later she was lying in the Palatines' burying-ground, inland, and Ber- t. was trying to take up her old life and its duties with some of her old courage. It was hard to do so, for when her grief had by any chance a rest, there was sure to rise before her the remem- brance of that last scene with the O'Kearneys, leaving her humiliated and empty of every earth- ly interest. She was sitting in her black gown, one evening, at the window where she and her aunt used to spend a cheerful hour before tea, when she saw the O'Kearney coming up the street, genial and kindly looking as ever. She did not know that he wt at home, and a flush that prettily replaced her now usual pallor, mounted to her cheeks. He was coming to see her ! She had much ado to still the trembling that came over her, but there was, after all, no need for so much agitation. He passed on with- out stopping at the door. " They've told him," she groaned to herself, after the first gasp of disappointment, " they have told him of what I've done and he too is shocked at the insult.' "
It seemed too much, everything was wrong and heart-breaking, and with her face buried in her aunt's chair she wept the bitterest tears of her life.

" Miss Bertha ! Miss Bertha, dear. Whisht, achree ! The O'Kearney is coming up," whis- pered Peggy, the old servant, and a moment after the returned soldier was in the room. He went straight up to Bertha standing white and shak- ing, and with all the marks of tell-tale grief upon her that she had not had time to wipe away. Poor child, poor child," he said gently, draw- ing her to her old seat near the window, " poor little, lonely one, and this is how I find you." Between her sobs, for his tenderness had let loose her tears again, she told him all about her aunt's death.

"But you tell me nothing of all youhave done during my absence. Ali. little home-maker— noble one —I know what you have done and striven to do for me and mine. The sisters have had the grace to be ashamed of their reception of your generous offer, and I am here with their heartfelt apologies—they will be here with them, themselves, to-morrow. I liked you always, _

Bertha—l love you, now—but I would not tisk you to join your lot with mine only that I have recovered some means and standing at last. The law suit, so long pending, has been just decided in my favour, restoring to me enough of the old property to enable me to take my place in the county again. Will you honour me by sharing that place, by becoming my wife—my darling, little hues frau—my dearest ?'
