BERTHA'S HOUSE,
JULIA M. CROTTIE (Author " „Annals of a Dull 2'own," " toe Lost Land," 4c.)

The old weather-slated house at the corner o Kilcullen High Street, where it ended at Oat churchyard, was the most important residence in the town, and Miss Hoffman and her niece, Miss Bertha were looked up to by their neighbours, the shopkeepers, as very considerable people indeed. They dressed well, kept a housemaid and cook, attended the Presbyterian Church, had five hundred pounds a year in their joint right and showed many other signs and tokens of gentility. Among the latter was the fact of their descent from the Palatines, a colony that more than a century ago came over from Germany and settled in the interior of the county. The colonists long preserved the ways and habits of the home coun- try, and even now on the clear winter evening, when Miss Bertha stood looking dreamily out at the street there was a fragrance through the house that was not grateful to the sentimental mood which she was indulging. "Good gracious !" she cried impatiently, "sauer kraut again ! It is abominable that aunt will persist in having that wretched stuff. I never touch it and still, year after year, she will have those horrid cabbages cut up and barrelled and cooked." The odour was, in truth, over- powering, and only to be compared in disagree- ableness to that of the Limburger cheese which also, to Bertha's mind, made a too frequent ap- pearance on the Hoffmann table. But these vi- ands and the pancakes, and potato-and-herring salads, were part of the old times to which Miss Hoffmann clung with the same affection that she did to the old German Family Bible, the double feather beds, and the other ancestral housekeep- ing items. But Bertha's irritation was only momentary; there was a more anxious matter weighing on her. Mrs. Quirke, the doctor's wife, had called that afternoon, and among other bits of gossip had told them that The O'Kearuey was going off to Italy with the regiment of Papal Zouaves that he had raised in the county. "A man of fifty, my dear, think of that risking life and limb in a hopeless cause." It was worse than hopeless in Miss Bertha's Presbyterian eyes, but all the same, since it was he who was doing it, something gallant and generous seemed mingled with the rash " Papis- try " of it. They had known the O'Kearney since the time, six years ago when Bertha's father and aunt had fallen into a little fortune by the death of a relative in America, and had given up their farm and settled in the to am. Some of the money had been invested in a small freehold ' estate, the only remaining property of the O'Kearney whose people had once owned half the county. The negotiations consequent on the transfer of the piece of ground had brought the county gentleman into acquaintance with . the Palatine household, and something in the homely life there—the order and peace and calm of it— had been attractive to him. The women of the family were wonderfully German in their looks ; he was actually astonished, at first speech with them, to hear instead of the guttural Fatherland accents, the soft Kerry tongue. He had stormy times at home, a querulous old mother, sisters who sat in desolation because hunting and ball- going were no longer possible to them, and who were wearing into grim, hopeless, old maiden- hood, after the flightiest, gayest youth. The isolation from old friends, for he and his were toc proud to force themselves on those whose warmth had waned with the O'Kearney fortunes, the sullen gloom of the sour sisters broken by scenes of recrimination between themselves and the peevish mother—all gentle feeling seemed to have been annihilated in them by their troubles—, the poverty, the ill-ordered home in the lodgings over the chandlery shop, where no servant could be kept, and where nobody was willing or able to do a servant's work—all the sordid daily experi- ences and worries made the Hoffmann house a very haven of rest to him. At first, the old father had been there, with his shrewd, practical hard sense, and his clear-cut opinions on every subject. When he died three years ago the habit of going to the house seemed too strong to be broken. The O'Kearney had continued his visits, finding in the quiet domestic talk of Aunt Lizabeth and Miss Bertha, as they worked at their lace mal embroidery, something to soothe and in a man- ner, comfort him. Lately, however, for some inonths, he had been less with them. They knew that he was busy in the county recruiting the Zouaves, but it was a complete shock to Bertha to find that he meant to accompany and head these himself. And so she stood at the window, thinking with a pang that her soldier might never return. That he was " hers " she had no right to say, for beyond the most matter-of-fact ordin- ary friendship, of which her aunt, fifteen year. older, had as large a share as herself, he bad given no sign of feeling. But it is not what one receives but what one gives that counts in love sometimes. To Bertha, in her middle-class, commonplace, humdrum life, the broken-down RESULTS OF SATURDAY'S MATCHES. gentleman with his sad face, his ready, kindly smile and interest, the tragic melancholy of his YORKSHIRE v. CHESHIRE. lost fortune, his hopeless law suits, his unhappy At Sale,in miserable weather. Result :—Cheshire,five home all so patiently borne, was an element of goals. Going off even with that forlorn hope seems This match was played at Stockton Heath,and resulted better to him, perhaps, than eating his heart out in a win for Timperley by one goal to nil. jhere in his unhappy home. He will have an ac- tive life, and be out of sight, at any rate, of all that misery." "I often think I'd like to try and help the poor old mother and sisters of his. But how? They'd resent an approach of the kind—of any kind on our part." "Speak for yourself, Bertha. don't think I'm ever going to make any advances to them. They are eaten up with pride, and it isn't self-respect- ing pride, for if it were they'd net jr allow them- selves to become such shiftless untidy creatures. Look at those windows of theirs,don't they tell a story ?" "But ladies, Lizabeth—how, after all, could they be expected to clean windows, and to wash and scrub ?' She was of a later and more Irish generation than her aunt, and the pride that shrank from the performance of menial work' of any kind as from a defilement, was more comprehensible to her than to the older woman. "The disorder around them adds immeasurably to their unhappiness, I'm sure," she continued. " It would be easy to remedy things a little for them, if one might. But they'd never permit it." "They would not," agreed the aunt. "They're like many others, determined to work out their own destruction. Bertha, let its have a rest, dear, from these O'Kearneys. If you want to do good there are plenty of opportunities in the lanes and no obstacles to encounter there." But Bertha thad no special drawing towards the lane people and their wants. Those whom she desired to help were the women of the O'Kearney's household, and these simply that be might be happier, or more content. The going away of the Papal recruits was an occasion of much mreitement in the town. After they and their leader were gone, and the Vac° had fallen back into its usual stagnation, the dullness of it lay like lead on Bertha's soul. She used to sit for hours in her room, the swishing rain upon the window and out in the churchyard, deepening her feeling oE loneliness and loss. She could not keep her poor Soldier of Fortune out of her bead. Bye and bye news came. The chances of battle, like everything else in his life, were against him, as she knew they would be. He would be coming home, God sparing him, one of these days, but into what a home ? The sisters and mother were never seen now, and the win- dows had curtains of dust upon them that took away all need for outer blinds. Miss Resins, the one who had been the beauty of the family, had been heard to say that if she could only live out of " the horrid town," if they could live in the country, away from the prying eyes and prating tongues and "vulgarity " of this " inferno. things would not seem half RO bad.

THE LICENSING ACT.
Rules for its Administration at Warrington.

A meeting of the Warrington Bench of Magistrates was held in the magistrates' room at the Police Station on Tuesday afternoon, for the purpose of considering the provisions of the Licensing Act, 1901. Mr. John Fairclongh presided, and there were also present : Messrs. F. Monks, Charles White, R. W. Francomb, J. Geddes, H. Roberts, S. Wright, R. T. Fairclough, J. Smethurst, E. A. Fox, M.D., H. Thornton, A.Bennett,C. J. Holmes, L. W. Reynolds,William Roberts, D. Tinnion and J. Wilkinson.

At the request of themeeting, the Clerk shortly ex- plained the general provisions of the Act and the rules made by the Home Secretary. After a discussion it was decided to adopt the follow- ing rules :- 1. That at each meeting relating to licensing matters, tho senior magistrate present be the chairman thereof. 2. That Mr. E. A. White be appointed the deputy clerk of the Compensation Authority. 3. That the Warrington branch of the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Co., Limited, the treasurers for the compensation authority. 4. That Mr. Louis Adrian Voisey, chartered account- ant, be auditor to the compensation authority, subject to the approval of the secretary of state. 1,5. That the consideration of the salaries to be paid to the clerk and the auditor respectively be deferred for the present. 6. That the amount imposed under Section 3of the Act (the compensation clauses) for the year 1903 in respect to licences be at the maximum rate of charge under the Act. - -

7. That the fee to be paid to the clerk for copies of any reports of the renewal authority be at the rate of 4d. for every folio at 72 words. S. That all notices required to be published by the compensation authority shall be advertised in the three Warrington newspapers. 9. That the meeting to appoint the Licensing Com- mittee be fixed for Friday, 20th inst., at 3.30 p.m. With regard to Clause 6 of the above rules, it should be noted that the maximum rate of charge under the Act is a charge on the annual value of the public-houses as follows :—Under £l5, £1 ; £l5 and under £2O, £2 ; £2O and under £25, £3 ; £25 and under £3O, £4; £3O and under £4O, £6 ; £4O and under £5O, .£lO ; £5O and under £100; £l5; £lOO and under £2OO, £2O ; £2OO and under £3OO, £3O; £3OO and under £4OO, £4O ; £4OO and under £5OO, £5O; £5OO and under £6OO, £6O ; £6OO and under £7OO, £7O ; £7OO and under £BOO, £80; £BOO and under £9OO. £9O; £9OO and over, £lOO.

E•RLF.STOWN GIRLS AND A COUNTERFEIT COIN. At Wigan, on Monday, Glendora Matilda Calvert, of Earlestown, and Annie Barber, of Newton, were charged with uttering a counterfeit half-sovereign. Superinten- dent O'Hara stated that on Friday evening the defen- dants got into a car running to Ashton and tendered the coin as a half-sovereign. The conductor could not change it, but a gentleman in the car did so, and, dis- covering that it was a bad one, he demanded the return of his money. The coin was ultimately given to a con- fectioner at Brynn. Information was given to the police and the girl Calvert, hearing of this, returned the change which had been given to her. It was alleged by the girls that the coin was on the mantlepiece. and they did not know it was a bad one. A remand for a week was I granted.

div.head: ALL THE WORLD DANCING.
div.p: ALL THE WORLD DANCING.

"Everything seemed to dance before my eyes, in a strange, bewildering fashion ! " That sounds very blanch like one of the admiring phrases in which people are wont to describe some of the beauties of the pantomime at Drury-lane, or the brilliant dazzling effects of the ballet, at the Empire or the Alhambra. But it really was not any such outburst of admiration or of pleasure. It is a sentence from a letter dated September 6, 1904, at Hawarden, where one of England's cherished sons, "The Grand Old Man," as he is still affectionately spoken of, lived and died. The writer of it is a young woman, Miss Ellen Williams, who lives at" The Cottage," and is a native of Shrewsbury. In that sentence she described one phase of her feelings as they were three years ago ; when she was the victim of acute indigestion. She goes on to describe how she lost all desire for food, and became weak, pale, and thin, until she was 'little more than a shadow.' Other symptoms, she says, were' constant pain at the back, just between the shoulders and a tight oppressed feeling in the chest, as if a great weight were pressing on my heart. Then I suffered terribly from wind, and most violent and frequent headaches, so severe at times that I could not see. It was at this stage of the trouble that every thing seemed to dance before her. For months she tried many 1 so-called" remedies" aud used doctors' prescriptions without benefit. Then on a friend's advice she tried Mother Seigel's Syrup, and was " astonished " at the relief it gave her, even from the first doses. All her pains disappeared, her appetite returned, the dizziness passed away, and now she is " as well as ever she was in her life." No more illusions about " dancing "—any dancing she sees now is "the real thing."

Socrates called beauty a short-lived tyranny, Plato a privilege of nature, Theocritus, a delightful prejudice, Theophrastus a silent cheat, Carneades a solitary kingdom, Homer a glorious gift of nature, Ovid a favor of the gods. Aristotle affirmed that beauty was better than all the letters of rec- ommendation in the world, and yet none of these distinguished authorities has left us even a hint of how beauty Is to be perpetuated, or the ravages of age and disease defied. Time soon blends the lily and the rose into the pallor of age, disease dots the fair face with cutaneous disfigurations and crimsons the Roman nose with unsight- ly flushes, moth, if not rust, corrupts the glory of eyes, teeth, and lips yet beautiful by defacing the complexion, and fills the sensitive soul with agony. If such be the unhappy condition of one afflicted with slight skin blemishes, what must be the feelings of those in whom torturing humours have for years run riot, covering the skin with scales and sores and charging the blood with poisonous elements to be- come a part of the system until death? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S MR. CHAMBERLAIN speech at Preston on AT PRESTON. Wednesday night is

not likely to make Lancashire regret the verdict of Stalybridge. He did not fail to assure the representatives of the cotton industry that they were blind to their own interests. He asked his audience if they were satisfied with the position of cotton, and some of them answered "Yes," whereupon he retorted that if he were ',interested in that particular line of business, he should feel anxious. This is not exactly impressive. The obvious rejoinder is that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN knows very little about cotton, and that Lancashire knows a great deal. At the present moment the trade is flourishing. It hat had a period of depression, but every industry, even in the Protectionist countries Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is fond of citing, has its periods of depression. In the blessed land of America they are frequent. This is evidently not a good time to talk to Lancashire about the perils which are lying in wait for cotton in tie future.. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN felt this so strongly on Wednesday night that he shifted his ground to the general condition of trade, and repeated the familiar fallacies about the decline of exports. But exports have notoriously increased, and the extremely lively figures for 1903 are very inconvenient for Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S case His friends are busy with laboured arguments to show that, although exports have increased by ten millions,w6 are really no better off. The prosperity of our foreign trade refuses to be explained away. There were signs at Preston that Mr. CRAM. ezitearn is falling back on Mr. BALFOUR'S formula. The advanced guard of Tariff Re. form feels himself beaten,and with unwonted weak- ness is taking refuge in the policy of retaliation which his two violent followers have served up as a makeshift. "My object," said Mr. Casiummx- Lam, " is to comp' foreign countries to lower their tariffs. Unless we meet them on their own ground they will send us more and more of their manufactured goods,while we export less and leas of ours." Then he drew the usual pictures of"dumping" which is to end by dumping the British work- man out of his employment. Nobody knows better than Mr. CHAMBERLAIN that the electorate does not believe all this, and in the light of that knowledge his recent message to Australia is much more to the purpose than the oratory at Preston. The Unionist party, he says, is to be invigorated by a short period of opposition, and it will then return to office to reap the fruit of the inevitable triumph. It is not upon economic facts and economic argument that he founds his hopes, but upon the mistakes which his opponents aro to oolige him by making when they are in power. Cotton may be flourishing, and the Board of Trade returns may continue to be highly favourable for a country which is supposed to be heading towards bank- ruptcy. But that will not matter to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN if he can make out that a Liberal , Ministry has mismanaged everything,and persuade the country to sigh for another spell of the sort of , administration we have had for ten years. We I are quite as eager as he is to put it to the test without delay.

Most of the Unionist AFTER STALYBRIDGE. journals accept the disaster at Staly- bridge with resignation, and even with fatalism. It lathe conventional thing to say that no Govern- ment which has held office for ten years can expect to retain its hold upon the electorate. There were sure to be blunders in ten years. Even excel- lent measures like the Educstion Act and the Licensing Act, says the " Standard" have offen- ded a great many people. A 5 for the Fiscal question, it was no; presented to the Staly- bridge electors with that convincing force which belongs to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S policy. In a sentence fifteen lines long—really too long to quote, and bearing signs of the most conscientious effort—the " Times " assures us that Mr. TRAVIS. CLEGG "would have made things easier for his supporters if he could have brought himself to make a bold pronouncement on the Fiscal question which would have been the issue clear between himself and Mr. CHEETHAM." The Unionist cham- pion was by no means bold. He treated the Fiscal

question as if it were an extraneous nuisance,foisted upon the constituency by the disingenuous acts of his adversary. Nevertheless the issue was clear enough to the electors. They saw that Mr. TRAVIS-CLEGG was a BALFOUR candidate, an advo- cate of the blessed formula which would make our commercial policy Protectionist in fact though not in name. The Tariff Reformers worked hard for him, despite his abstinence from any "bold pro • nouncement." He was !just as soundly beaten on the main issue as he would have been if he had declared himself for Mr.CHAmaaararx through thick and thin. The chief value of the Stalybridge election is that it demonstrates the total failure of Mr. BALrourt's tactics in the country. They have I had a considerable measure of success in the Unionist party itself, as the aberrations of Sir I MicEAEL Hrexs-BEAcrr and Lord GEORGE HAMILTON have borne witness. Mr. BALFOUR can I preserve his majority in the House of Commons by the:blessed formula of Retaliation. But when it is submitted to the electorate, even in a con- stituency which has been Conservative for twenty years,it gets the sort of reception which the people of this country are in the habit of giving to hollow devices.

A comic explanation of the defeat is furnished by the "Daily Telegraph." Mr. TRAvis-CLEoc was the political foster-father of Mr. 'WINSTON CHuRcuiLL. He was instrumental in securing Mr. CHURCHILL'S election for Oldham. Since Lord RANDOLPH'S son became a resolute opponent of the Ministry, all the odium of his defection has fallen on the man who helped him into Parliamentary life. We are asked to believe that Lancashire resents Mr. TRAVIS- CLEGG'S association with Mr. CHURCHILL so deeply that she will not have him as a representa- tive of any division iu the county. "Mr. TRAVIS CLEGG, with splendid if mistaken devotion, stuck to his protege to the last, and even beyond the last. The more robust Toryism of Lancashire revolted against this more than human loyalty, and Mr. TRATIS-CLEGG paid at Stalybridge the penalty—if we may compare small things with great—which so many adherents of the Pretender in Scotland paid for their magnificent but most vain constancy to a quite undeserving personality," Mr. BALFOUR will be more than human if be find consolation in this beautiful mixture of ancient history and moonshine. If we may com- pare small things with great, we would suggest I that we have still among us a Scottish Pretender, I whose adherents at Stalybridge and:elsewhere have been rewarded for their most vain constancy to his charmin gpersonality but quite undeserving policy. The'moral of Stalybridge is that the blessed formula will not do. By an admirable coincidence the good sense of the Stalybridge electors is inforced by the Trade Returns for 1901, which proves to have been a "record year for British exports— those exports which, according to Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, are going to rack and ruin.

There is a political resemblance between War- rington and Stalybridge, in addition to both being to all intents and purposes Lancashire boroughs. They have both been Conservative for t wenty years —and they have both changed their political com- plexion this year, we were going to say, but it does not do to anticipate joyful events. Stalybridge has at any rate, shown her determina- tion to have nothing to do with either Protection or Retaliation, and her voice is unmis- takably, we believe' the voice of Lancashire on thel fiscal question. Warrington may have an oppor- tunity ere long of testifying her faith in Free Trade, and we doubt not that that testimony will be unhesitatingly given. The issue is not in the least obscured. Mr. R. Pierpoint has long ago committed himself entirely to Mr. Chamberlain's chimerical views, and as , a whole-hogger he affords a ready target for the Free Trade artillery. In the 1900 election he obtained an inflated and unreliable majority of over a thousand. Just as there were special cir- cumstances contributing to his triumph then,there will be special circumstances and weighty reasons ' tending towards his overthrow in the coming struggle.

We are not surprised to learn that the local L.R.C. is, (to •quote the report of the Secretary, "yet far from being wholly representative of the trade unionist and reform societies of Warring- ton." It has long appeared to us that the L.R.C. was like a very little man with a very big voice,and our supposition has apparently been correct. Now, the members of the Independent Labour Party have retired from the L.R.C., as they find that the trade unionist members are out of sympathy with them. The Com- mittee must be getting smaller by degrees and beautifully less. As it has so far been constituted it has been too much like a house divided against itself to stand very long, and we should imagine ' that the time has almost arrived when it might be disbanded and the question of labour represen- tation reconsidered in a new light. With the aim of labour representation we have always been in sympathy. There is ample room for it, and the condition of the masses demands that they should have men from their own ranks qualified to raise the voice of labour in the halls of authority. But the attainment of labour representation has proved itself to be a problem of con- siderable magnitude beset by many difficulties. The L.R.C. wishes to drive a straight road through or over all existing wiles to the House of Commons. This is an unwise and well nigh hopeless course. Labour must seek to raise its head to a respectable legislative level by the aid of the existing powers and parties, and not by attempting to ride rough-shod over them. Labour men are usually wide-awake to the advantages of co-operation, and they are being misled when they try to cut a path of their own. We should like tv see the local L.R.C. reconstituted so as to admit a wider membership of men whose desire it is to re- adjust the social order and uplift the masses, At present such a body as the Social Service League, which is whole-hearted in its aims is denied association with the L.R.C. The latter is, not- withstanding the secretary's denial, committing suicide, and we advocate a broader policy if the situation is to be saved and Labour benefited.

"Warrington as a port" may sound much like a dream, but its fulfilment largely rests within the power of the people, and more especially of the manufacturing concerns, of this town. It is a atanding reproach that a great waterway like the Manchester Ship Canal should be lapping our shores, carrying past us a tremendous volume of traffic, and yet without the slightest appreciable advantage to Warrington. If thme great vessels could make Warrington a regular calling place for the shipment and discharge of cargoes for our many manufacturers and traders, the possibilities of the development of the town into a busy shipping centre would net be so remote as many people imagine. The apathy which has led us into a state of quiet contentment with an anomalous position which we imagine, few places similarly situated would toler- ate, is indeed surprising. Traders have continued the system of barging or training their goods to Manchester and Liverpool for shipment, and have received imports by the same roundabout means. Every handling means an additional cost and there is the extra carriage to and from the ports to be paid. To firms possessing a fleet of barges the advantage of direct shipment and importation irom and to Warrington would perhaps not be great, but as we have before pointed out, there are numerous concerns less favourably placed which could hardly fail to profit by the altered condi- tions.

The Ship Canal Company provided Warrington with a lay-by equipped with transporter near the Stag Bridge at Walton— with what result ? The facilities have been almost entirely ignored and the stoppage of a vessel at the lay-by is something quite unique. We are glad that the Chamber of Commerce is making a determined effort to arouse interest in so important a matter. Of course, before there could be a regular shipping service, storing accommodation would be necessary, and the company have already been approached with the view to the erection of a suitable building. They have plainly intimated that they cannot see the wisdom of undertaking an additional outlay without the prospect of an adequate return in the shape of traffic, but there is little doubt that if hearty public co-operation 'is forthcoming the structure will be readily provided It may not be generally known that about two hundred vessels traverse the canal weekly. There are regular sailings both along the coast and to colitinental and other foreign ports which should meet the needs of the traders to the fullest extent. As far as the shipping firms are concerned they de- cline to stop at Warrington for small cargoes which are really more trouble than recompense,but many have intimated that they would be only too'pleased to call for considerable quantities. It is clear that what is needed to make the Canal a source of benefit to Warrington's commerce is local co-opera- tion. The injunction to " Wake up I " might well be taken to heart in this instance, so that in future it cannot be said that Warrington neglected great opportunities to the lasting detriment of her commerce.

Angling may not always be an exhilarating sport, in fact some people regard it more as a supreme test of patience than an amusement. Nevertheless,it undoubtedly has attractions which its devotees would not on any account forego, and in Warrington the disciples of Izaak Walton present a formidable array. For the good feeling which happily prevails among our local anglers a great deal is due to their most representative organization, the Warrington Anglers' Association. Year by year the mem- bership increases steadily, and the officers are hopeful that soon it will be counted by four figures. The past season with its beautiful weather has been no exception to the general run of suc- cessful seasons, and the report presented at the. annual meeting onThursday was a highly interest- ing resume of outings and competitions which have left the most pleasurable recollections. May the present year be one of good-fellowship,. innumerable " bites" and record catches !

An interesting discussion was raised at the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday by the chairman, Mr. A. R. Norman, who moved a resolution aimed at one of those concrete instances of state patronage of the Church of England which are constantly zropping up in con- nection with religious instruction. Most people are probably unaware that only Church of England clergymen approved by the Bishops are appointed chaplains of workhouses, or that the duties of the chaplain include the administration of the Sacraments according to the rites of the Church of England. If a Board deEired to appoint a Nonconformist or Catholic chaplain it would be met with insuperable difficulties, and te bring matters more into line with principles of equality and equity Mr. Norman's resolution was intro- duced. The members of the Runcorn Board are, however, very conservative and they were almost fearful of discussing the question lest religious strife should be aroused. There was no doubt as to their private views, neverthe- less. They were strongly adverse to any change in the existing order cf things. Mr Hallows, of Stockton Heath was quite pathetic He thought :it hard: to see " the ruthless hand sweeping away the old landmarks which were dear to them." Local Government and a good many other things would go on much better but for Mr. Hallows' " landmarks." Usually they are obstruc- tions, as in the case under notice, and Mr. Norman is to be congratulated on his idetermined stand for principle. We have no doubt that some day an enlightened public opinion will put an end to the anomaly which was the subject of his motion.

"Love your Enemies," is policy, but difficult. Japan is in these days giving a world exhibition of the quality, as she has latterly (though "Pagon ") given a series of:demonstrations in efficiency, prud- ence, courage, restraint, and other virtues. Japan has been magnanimity itself to her captives. She has taken care to be the first and most generous of their admirers. In Russia the Japanese have been held for barbarians—Russia's calamity has been the small charity which could think so—and now a large deputation from Russia,vrho would not other- wise have had the chance, is meeting the Japanese at home as nominally an unwilling but really a supremely contented guest. Russia is getting a new view of Japan, in peace as in war. That Japan should deal well with her piisoners in the Isle of the Chrysanthetunm and theßising Sun will cover her with a new glory better than any feat of arms. She is, too, willy-nilly, acting as the missionary of Christianity. General Booth and the Salvation Army have lamented that they could get no foot- ing in Russia ; here says the General, joyously,is their opportunity. Japan has welcomed them, and they will go from Japan to the heart of the Czar's dominions in the wake of the returning prisoners. It is the true prophetic outlook.

Cairo-street Literary and Debating Society. On Tuesday evening the members of the above society were favoured with a visit from the Rev. R. P. Farley, BA., of St. Helens, who gave an interesting lecture on "Some social points in the history of ancient Ireland." The Rev. C. Harvey Cook occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance of ladies and gentlemen. In the course of his lecture, Mr. Farley showed the inhabitants of ancient Ireland to be an advanced and civilized race of people, who, at an early period of English history,bad a strong influence for good upon the people of this country. He also spoke of their musical and literary tastes, and com- mended many of their social and legal customs. A hearty Tote of thanks was accorded Mr. Farley for his kindness in attending.

2. Women's Chat and Fashions. Science Notes. Motor Notes. "The Winning of Fricla." 3. Football, Hockey, &c. The Licensing Act in Warrington. " Bertha's House," by Julia M. Crottie. 6. Mr. Thomas Massey, for eleven years licensee the Waggon and Horses Inn, Battermarket-street passed away in his sixtieth year on Saturday morn- ing. The cause of death was paralysis, from which the deceased gentleman had suffered for about six weeks. He was a member of the Licensed Victuallers' Association, and was,also identified with the Ancient Order of Shepherds. He leaves a widow, five sons, and one daughter. The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Wednesday afternoon. Progressive Labour League. The weekly meeting of this league was held at the Liberal Club on Monday evening, Mr. Joseph Elwell presiding over a good attendance. Mr. J. Cotterell introduced a discussion on " Chinese labour " and the various speakers were strong in their condemna- tion of the ordinance in force in South Africa. Another meeting will be held next Monday when a debate on "The effects of the late Boer War ' will be- opened by Mr. J. Heywood. PustacißENEFiT. UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Warrington Tobacconist's Claim. Albert Stanway, tobacconist, of Warrington, sued Messrs. Goodbody, of Liverpool, at St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, for damages for trespass and illegal distraint. Stanway said he bought a tobacco business in Duke-street, St. Helens, from a person named Lomax, and Goodbodys distrainecl for a debt due from Lomax. The defendants questioned the genuineness of the sale, but Judge S hand held that it was a valid transaction, though defendants might have been deceived. He gave judgment for £1 damages and costs. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt. Death of an Old Congregationalist. Wycliffe Church has lost a respected member by the death of Mr. Henry Watkin, 38, Winwick-road, at the age of eighty-five years. The deceased, who was a widower, was a native oj Stourbridge. He came to Warrington sixteen years ago, and during the whole of the time he had lived here he had attended Wycliffe Church. He had also acted as a teacher in tine Sunday school. The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Thurs day, the Rev. Harry Wall officiating. The bearers were Mr. Geo. Wallington, Mr. Robert Lewis, Mr. Wm. Beswick, Mr. Atkinson and Mr. Charles H. Mills. There were also present Mrs. Wilkinson and Mrs. Ince. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC iS the KING OF TONICS.-63, SANKEY ST., WARRINGTON.—Advt. The Late Mr. R. W. Murray. The following appears in the current issue of "The Wycliffe Church Record " :—" On Saturday, Decem- ber 24th, at his residence at Newcastle, County Down, Ireland, somewhat unexpectedly, there passed away Mr. Robert Wallace Murray J.P.. who, when the pastor entered upon his ministry at Wycliffe, was a valued member and deacon of the church. He was also the devoted and industrious superintendent of the Sunday school.He was possessed of fine and handsome appear- ance of manly and courteous demeanour, of warm and sympathetic heart. Regular at public worship, week- day as well as Sunday; equally punctual at Sunday school, never permitting trifles or moods to hinder his presence, beset an example, which along with that o Air. Samuel Rigby, had vastly to do with the church behaviour of everyone else. In these 'good old days ' when the leaders were always foremost in fidelity to worship and work, all others were faithful in follow- ing their lead. Perhaps in nothing was this so Mani- fest as in Thursday services. Attendances of 80 to 100, or even 130, were not exceptional, and the memory of them creates regret and sorrow in these days when to find 20 at suck a service is a pleasant surprise! Mr. Murray endeared himself to both church and school, and his removal was felt to be a very serious sorrow and loss. Our respectful sympathy will go forth to his bereaved wife in her distress, and we pray that the God of All Comfort • may be her 'Refuge and Strength.' " FOR GLASS AND CHINA Of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Manchester and Liverpool District Banking 'Company, Limited. In their report to be presented at an ordinary meeting of shareholders to be held at the head office, Spring Gardens, Manchester, on Wednesday next, the directors of the above bank state that the gross profit for the half-year ending December 31st last, after providing for all bad and doubtful debts, is £228,159 os. 10d., to which has to be added the amount brought forward from 30th June last, namely, ;£34,452 Os. 4d., making a total of £202,611 Os. 2d. From this sum the following deductions have to be made : Total expenses at the head office, London office. and branches including salaries, stationery, taxes, &c., £80,952 3s. 3d. ; half-year's provision for income tax, £4,879 Bs. ; total, £85,831 us. 3d.; leaving a, net profit of £176,779 14s. lid. The directors recommend the declaration of a dividend of 21s. per share, which will take 1-,131,250, leaving a balance of £45,529 14s. 11d. Of this it is proposed to carry to the reserve fund £lO,OOO, and £35,529 14s. Ild, to next account. The reserve fund, with the above addition, will then amount to £1,805,000. The term of office of the following directors will expire on the 18th inst. : Xressrs. George Barbour, Andrew Bennie, Edward Tuotal Broadhurst, Edward Donner, and Sir William Mather, and all are eligible and recommended for re-election. The term of office of Mr. James Halliday as a director will also expire on the 18th inst., but, owinc, to advanced age, he does Lot seek re-election. The directors desire to record their high appreciation of the valuable services rendered to the bank by Mr. Halliday for a period of nearly thirty years. They believe that in this expres- sion of appreciation their fellow shareholders and the members of the, staff will cordially concur. ASK for CIINNECGFIA.M'S HIGH-CLASS lAINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Trades and Labour Council Mr. J. Podrnore presided at the monthly meeting of this Council which was held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Schools on Tuesday evening. lathe absence of the Secretary (Councillor Stott) the minutes ' were recorded by Mr. 0. Buckley.—The report of the proceedings at the annual meeting of the War- rington Labour Representation Committee was sub- mitted: byMr. Buckley. A letter, he said, was received from the Independent Labour Party tendering their resignation from the Committee and giving as their reason that they thought their presence had been resented for sometime by some trade uni:mists. As ,they seemed to stand in the way of other societies , Joining,they took it as a gracious act on their part that they should retire and make way for a trade unionist. • They hoped the course they were taking would not result in any injury to the Committee, as they wishtd 'it every success. The Committee passed a resolution -expressing regret at the secession of the Independent • Labour Party—At the same meeting Councillor Wright • presented a report on his work in the Town Council, particularly dealing with the question of the purchase -of land for new schools at Latchford. The high price which had to be paid was, he contended, another • evidence of the necessity for taxation of land values or the nationalisation of the land. The Committee's '-financial statement showed a balance in hand of I£l Os. sd. The following officers were elected President, Mr. E. Horrocks ; vice-president, Mr. W. ' York; treasurer, Mr. J. Kendrick ; secretary, Mr. 0. • Buckley ; executive committee, Messrs. J. Podmore ; W. Backhouse, and T. Howliston.—The principal ;lousiness under the consideration of the Council was •• the agenda of the conference of the National Labour Representation Committee at Liverpool, Mr. 0 Buckley, who will represent the Council, being instruc- ted as to his voting. A number of resolutions and amendments dealing with the Committee's . constitution will be submitted, and it was the wish of the Council that Mr. Buckley should *vote in such a way as would not endanger the Principle of the independence of the organization. Councillor Stott will be the Council's representative at a special conference on the questions of the un- • employed and free meals for school children, to be held at Liympool in connection with the Labour Representation Committee meetings. The principal , resolution will be one declaring the unemployed problem to be due to the existence of monopoly and the burdens which the non-producing section impose • -upon the industrious classes together with the lack of such organization of industry as will prevent alternate periods of ovetwork and unemployment.

div.p: Accident to Judge Bowan Rowlands. His Honour Judge W. Bowen Rowlands, K.C., was unable to take his seat at Leigh County Court yesterday, Mr. Cuthbert Smith, Barrister of Liverpool, acting in his stead. It transpired that Judge Bowen Rowlands, whose circuit includes Birkenhead, North- wich, Warrington, and Leigh, had sustained an accident to his knee through slipping on the footpath. Black Bear Angling Society. The first monthly meeting of the year in connection with the above was held on Monday evening last at the Club house, there being a good attendance. Six new members were enrolled. The election of officers 3ulted as follows: President, Mr. 11. T. Bridge;Com- mittee, Messrs. F. J. Emson, B. Hampson, J. Cook, J. Brown, W. Dakin and G. Taylor ; Secretary, Mr. G. Smith, 5, Slater street ; Assistant Secretary, Mr. S. G-rindley ; Treasurer, Mr. Thomas Nixon. A hand- some pipe and case was presented to Mr. Grindley as some slight acknowledgment of the services he had rendered to the club during the season of 1901. The I Secretary with each of the committee in turn were appointed as regular delegates to the Protection Society's meetings. Application for membership ' should be made at once to Mr. T. Nixon as there are a I few vacancies.

Girls' Friendly Society. On Monday a united meeting of the members and associates of the three Warrington branches of this organization was held in St. Paul's Schools, Kendrick- street, representatives being present from St. Elphin's, Holy Trinity, and St. Paul's Churches. Interesting addresses were given by Miss Rich, St. Helens, the head of the literature department, and Miss Kate Rimmer, formerly of Warrington. The Rev. W. Bracecamp, vicar of St. Paul's expressed the hope that, as the result of the gathering, the associates and members would be more united and work together most heartily for the cause they had all so much at heart. He believed tho Girls' Friendly Society was calculated to cl 3 a great deal of good, and he had no doubt that, if the members would carry out its teach- ing, they would be better themselves, and more help- ful to all around them. The usual votes of thanks were passed. P.S.A. Anniversary. A large gathering assembled in the Co-operative Hall on Sunday when the 12th anniversary of the Warrington P.S.A. Society was celebrated. Mr. R. Nelson (vice-president) occupied the chair. A special feature of the service was a visit of the Silver-street Prize Juvenile Choir (under the conductorship of Mr. B. Wadsworth) who gained premier honours in their section at the recent Eisteddfod. The children rendered the test piece " ton't forget the old folks," in a maener which called forth hearty plaudits. Master Cox sang the solo " The Holy City," in a praiseworthy manner, the choir joining in the chorus. Mr. T. Brough was the accompanist. The President of the society (Mr. E. W. Jones) gave an address on the motto for the year, " Quit you like men ; be ' strong." He pleaded for strong Christian men and women, strong spiritually, physically, and mentally, who were not afraid of the taunts in every day life, and who lived for others as well as self. A collection was taken in aid of the funds of the society and realized £1 Os. 10,14. Volunteer Sergeants' Ball. The new quarters at the Drill Hall which had been brilliantly decorated, were on Monday evening the scene of a most successful function in the shape of the sergeants' third annual ball. The attendance numbered about',2oo.Mr. knderton's band supplied:excellent music, and dancing was kept up with zest from eight to two o'clock. The catering was in the capable hands of the Winmarleigh Cafe Company. The following officers attended :—Colonel Edelsten, Major J. Fairclough, Major B. 'iFairclough, Major * Appleton, Captain and Adjutant Bundock, Captains G. R. Crosfield, Avery, R. Smith, A. F. Cr. Potter, and Gordon Roberts ; Lieutenants R. McMinnies Roberts, Owen and Ridg- way; and the chaplain, the Rev. W. Bracecamp. Mrs. Edelsten and the wives of several of the officers were also present as well as a number of sergeants from the Barracks. The ball committee consisted of Colour-Sergeant Russell (president), Sergeant Bugler Plinston, Sergeant Richardson, Sergeant Fern, Ser- geant Dagnall, the hon. secretaries being Quarter- master-Sergeant J. T. Bennion, and Quartermaster Sergeant J. Willcock. The duties of M.C's. were discharged by Sergeants T. Richardson and G. Fern. BASSINETTES AND MAIL C.iRTS in latest art shades.—J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt.

Warrington and Knutsford Light Railway. At a meeting of the Runcorn District Council on Tuesday, Mr. J. Mounfield said the Parliamentary Committee had met that morning and Igone through many of the details of the Warrington and Knutsford Light Railway scheme, which were very much more satisfactory and favourable than the details of the proposed Northwich light railway. There was one respect in w'aich the Committee thuught a very great improvement could be made, and by a deviation which they suggested the line would miss their road altogether,: be of no greater length, and prove a very much greater convenience to the public generally. The Committee decided to oppose the Bill on the understanding that if the promotors agreed to their proposals they would support the scheme. The Council approved this course—The exact wording of the committee's resolu- tion, which was proposed by Mr. Whitley and seconded be Mr. Woodward, was as follows: That this District Council in order to safeguard and protect their interests oppose the Knutsford and Warrington Light Railway, owing to the very acute angle near the Ship Canal at Latchford, but in all other respects we approve the scheme. Death of Mrs. John Burgess. We regret to announce that Mrs. John Burgess, widow of the late Alderman Burgess, a magistrate of the Borough and Mayor in 1800-1-2, passed away at her residence, Vine Cottage, Wilderepool, on Friday evening. The deceased lady who was 80 years of age and had lived in comparative retiremeat since the death of her husband in November, 1898, had been in a delicate state of health for some time. She was a Churchwoman and when her health permitted wor- shipped at St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath. Her end was both sudden and peaceful. The interment took place in Overton Churchyard (where the remains of her husband werelaid to rest) on Tuesday afternoon the funeral service being conducted by the Rev. Mr. Pugh, curate. The mourners were Messrs. William Fletcher (son-in-law), W. Y. Dawbarn, J. Dawbarn and J. S. Burgess ' (grandsons), W. J. Burgess, C. S. Burgess, John Burgess, Samuel C. Burgess, H. E. Burgess and Alfred Burgess (nephews). Mrs. Pick- mere and Mrs. Fletcher sent private carriages. The following is a list of the ladies and gentlemen who had forwarded floral tributes :—" Her loving' children," Esther, Mary, Lucy, Edith, Willie, John, Fred and Hubert, "her affectionate grandchildren " (Bootle and Waterloo), Mrs. Kendrick (Altrincha.m), Mrs. George E. Burgess and family (Liscard), Mr. and Mrs. W. J. Burgess, Mr. and Mrs. C. Sawkins Burgess, Mr. John Burgess, Mrs. Pickmere, Miss Garner (Kingswinford) Mr. and Mrs. T. Longdin, Mrs. Wallace and family, and Mr. and Mrs. Stubbs. " Three Thousand Miles Through Russia." This was the subject of an illustrated lecture given by Mr. W. Barnes Steveni at a meeting of the Literary and Philosophical Society held at the Masonic Hall on Monday, under the presidency of Mr. F. G. Ruddock. —Railway travelling in Russia, said Mr. Steveni, was not very expensive. Indeed, one could travel 1,000 miles third class for about a guinea—and com- fortable travelling at that. That was because the railways were in the hands of the Crown, and one result of it was that the farmer there could send his grain to London and our big towns at far lower rates than our wretchedly neglected and unfortunate farmers could convey goods over here. Travelling through the Russian territory one could not I but be struck with the enormousness of her resources, Besides her grain growing, she had vast forests of timber and mineral wealth, which could still astonish I the world. Many parts abounded with coal and ore while her great petroleum output was well known. The Russians were very religious and extremely supersti- tious, and the country possessed numberless beautiful' churches and monasteries. The peasants, and there were 120 millions of them, were ignorant but loyal to the Emperor, the saints, and the Church. It was only the educated classes that were against the Govern- ment, and perhaps that was to some extent why the peasants were kept so ignorant. They had a great capacity for suffering and self-sacrifice. On every hand, almost, one saw how the country could be opened out, and he thought that when the war was over that would be done, because the Japs had taught the Russians a lesson they sorely needed. He really thought that after this war they would be another people, the influence would be so strong. Of the Czar himself he could say that he was a man of good princi- pals, well intentioned, and kind-hearted. (Applause). —On the motion of Mr: W. H. J. Jenkins, Mr. Steveni was cordially thanked for his most interesting lecture.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, January 14, 1905.
Coming Events. The annual interchange of pulpits and united Communion service in connection with the Free

'j Evangelical Churches of Warrington will be held to-morrow, and fall particulars appear, in our ! advertising columns. The Communion service will be ; held at Beivsey-road Wesleyan Church. I " Christianity and the problem of poverty" will be , the subject of the Rev. H. Dunnico at Parr Hall. I In connection with the Knutsford Division Liberal Association a public meeting will be held in the IChurch Institute, Moore, on Monday evening under the presidency of Mr. Josiah Longland. The speakers I will include Mr. Alfred J. King, vice president of the j Association and prospective candidate. I The 45th annual meeting of the Warrington j Co-operative Society will be held on Monday evening, when an important resolution will be submitted as to the best means of recognizing the forty years' services of Hr. A. H. Rathbone as manager and secretary. ';` I The annual Christmas treat to poor children will be given in the Parr Hall on Tuesday evening. The entertainment, to which the public will be admitted !at a nominal charge, will include items by scholars of People's College. j Vice-Chancellor Hopkinson, K..C., M.A. L.L.D (Victoria University, Manchester), will distribute the prizes and certificates gained by students at the School of Art, Secondary School and Pupil Teachers' Classes and the Technical Institute at the Parr Hall on Thursday evening. Mr. F. Honks, J.P., will preside. The first of a series of University Extension lectures on "Social Questions of the present time" will be delivered in the Co-operative Hall on Friday evening by Mr. S. J. Chapman, MA. (Victoria University, Manchester.) His subject will be "Social questions, their nature and development." The annual ball in connection with the Butcher's Association will be held in the Parr Hall on Thurs- day, January 26th. The annual general meeting of Parr's Bank Limited, will be held at the Cannon-street Hotel, London E.C., on Thursday, January 26th. FIRE GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, & 55, Bridge- street, Warrington.—Advt. Personal, Mr. F. M. Darby, Mug. Bac. Oxon., organist and choirmaster of the Parish Church has just passed the examination for the Diploma of Fellow of the Royal College of Organists. The judges in the Hackney section at the forthcom- ing Hackney Horse Society's show inchtde Sir Gilbert Greenall, Walton Hall. Mr. D. Lloyd-George, M.P., got back to London on Tuesday, after a holiday at Naples and (as the guest of Lord Rendel) at the Chateau de Thorenc, near Cannes. , Mr. Lloyd-George will plunge at once into a heavy programme of political meetings and confer maces in Wales, Scotland and the North of England Till Parliament opens almost every hour of his time is mortgaged. As our readers are aware Mr: Lloyd-George has prom'sed to address a mass meeting at Warrington on Friday evening, February 3rd. Last week we were wrongly informed that a number of seats would he reserved at a charge of one shilling. All seats will be free. The chair will be taken by Mr. Frank A. Roberts, an old Warrington Liberal. Canon Willink, vicar of Great Yarmouth, formerly of St. Helens, has been offered, but has declined, the rectorship of Birmingham in succession to Archdeacon Diggle. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER TILE CLOCK FOR•BEST
BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. The _Hens and the Crops.

Before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowland; K.C., at the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, John Rimmer, farmer, Burtonwood, sued Martha Jones also of Burtonwood, for damage done to his crops by defendant's hens. Mr. C. H. Unsworth represented the plaintiff and said his client had repeatedly asked the defendant, who lived near to his farm, to keep her fowls out of his field, hut she refused to do any- thing. The amount of damage done to his crops was at least 30s. Defendant said she looked after her fowls, and the damage was done by children and other people's hens. Defendant undertook to get rid of the hens, and the case was adjourned for a month. A Father's Sad Discovery. A. wire-drawer named William Barker, of 19, Brook-street, made a sad discbveryon. Sunday morn- ing. His five year old son went out to play on Saturday afternoon and as he had not returned when darkness set in, a search was made in the neighbour- hood, but without avail. Tbe following morning the distressed parent was looking round a clay pit about 1300 yards from the house when he found the boy lying drowned in the water.—At the inquest which was conducted at the Police Station on Monday by Mr. F. A. Jones, it was stated that the pit was a great resort of boys, being known as the "jacky pi t."—The Deputy-Coroner suggested that it might be given a less inviting name.—The jury returned a verdict of "Found Drowned," the foreman (Mr. Whittle) remarking, that it would be well if the pit were filled up. SUGAR IS ADVANCING.—Advt. Fatal Result of Playlnd with Fire. "Playing with fire" has resulted in another sad fatality at Warrington' the circumstances being dis- closed at an inquest held at the Police Station on Monday by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, on the body of Patrick IPCormack, two years and nine months old, 25, Bewsey-street. The mother of the child said that she and her husband were the care- takers of the League of the Cross rooms, which were situate next door. On Friday morning she Iv-nt into the rooms for the purpose of dusting, leaving deceased and two other children, aged seven and five years, in the kitchen. Shortly afterwards she heard screams, and on going into the house found the child with his nightdress on fire. She extinguished the flames, and took deceased to the Infirmary, but he died a few hours later. Her little girl told witness that the deceased was playing with a piece of wood at the fire when his nightdress, which was composed of a kind of cotton material, became ignited. Deceased was wearing a flannelette shirt under his nightdress. There was no fireguard. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." Mr. Chamberlain at Warrington. - • - -

A number of local Conservatl7es assembled on the platform at Bank Quay Station on Wednesday after- noon to see Mr. and Mrs. Chamberlain as they passed through on their way to Preston. The train arrived from Birmingham at 4.40 and xvi 6 in Bank Quay station for about seven minutes. A rush was immedi- ately made to the first saloon in which Mr. and Mrs. Chamberlain had been observed. For some time the right hon. gentleman maintained a marked indiffer- ence to his admirers on the platform, in fact he persistently looked through the opposite window. Eventually, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, who along with Mrs. Pierpoint was attend- ing the Preston demonstration, entered the compartment and was very warnaly received by the distinguished travellers. Evidently he intimated that the gentlemen who had gathered on the platform were Conservatives who desired to show their respect for Mr. Chamberlain, for immediately afterwards the right hon. gentleman left the saloon by a side door and came to the entrance of the luggage compartment. He was wearing a cap and had, of course, the inevitable monocle and orchid. A cheer was raised, and souatone shouted "Good luck," Mr. Chamberla;a responding with " Thank you." There was also a cry of "Speech," but by a significant shrug of the shoulders and shake of the head Mr. Chamber- lain clearly intimated that he had no desire for oratory at that juncture. As the train left the station, c beers were given for Mr. and Mrs. Chamberlain and were smilingly acknowledged. In addition to Mr. and Mrs. Pierpoint, Mr. and Mrs. W. P. Rylands also went on to Preston to attend the meeting. The Late Mr. Joseph Bennett. The following reference to the "inspiring example" of the life of the late Mr. Bennett appears in " The Warrington Circuit Wesleyan Methodist Church Record" :—Mr. Bennett was deeply attached to Padgate Methodism and he served the Church of his choice in many ways until illness compelled him to retire. The department of Church work which appealed to him most was the service of praise. He took a great interest in devotional music, and for many years he was organist and choirmaster, and he invariably paid all the choir expenses. To him the Padgate Wesleyans are chiefly indebted for their I beautiful organ. He found the greater part of the money for it, and took great pains to make himself master of the instrument he loved. Joseph Bennett was a Bible student, not only reading the various books through consecutively, as he did many times, but also studying systematically the different Biblical characters. He lield strong views on the importance of method in Bible study, and urged his friends to adopt some such method as his. For 20 long years Joserir Bennett was face to face with the problem of suffering, and his faith in the wisdom and goodness of God was put to a severe test. But he stood the test well. Suffering was patiently borne, and he has eft an example of the way in which the trials of life Ii ould be met.

Old-Age Pensions at Port Sunlight. Messrs. Lever Brothers have decided to establish an old-age ponsion scheme for the employes at Port Sunlight. The firm will hand over to trustees about £5,000 per annum, or such sum as may be required Ito keep the fund in a sound financial position. No contributions will be required from employes.

div.head: SCJGAR IS DEARER.—Advt.
div.p: SCJGAR IS DEARER.—Advt.

! Warrington Women's Liberal Association Meeting. The second social of the season took place at the Liberal Club last week. Miss Crosfigld spoke very ably, on behalf of the National Service League. An earnest expression of the views of the members was followed by an animated disc ussio a. Light refreshments were provided. A vote of sympathy with Mrs. Armi- tage on the loss sustained by the death of her father, Ur. Henry Lee, was passed, and forwarded to her. The exceptionally stoimy weather militated against a good attendance. The next meeting is convened for February 16th. N.S.P.C.C. Work. The Warrington and District Branch of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, (Local Office, 49, Bewsey-street, Warrington), has during the quarter ended .31st. December, 1904, inquired into 66 complaints of neglect, ill-treatment, and other wrongs of childhood, of which 64 were dealt with. Of these all were found to be true and 197 children were affected. There were 93 offenders; of these 3 were prosecuted, 53 were warned, and 5 were dealt with in other ways. The penalties inflicted were 5 months of imprisonment and 19s. in fines; 3 of the children died. The Society's Inspector made 485 visits of supervision. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good Boars.—Advt. Dance at the Workhouse.

There was a happy gathering at the Workhouse , Infirmary on Thursday evening when the second ' annual dance promoted by the officers of the Warring- ton Union was held. The rooms had been beautifully decorated with red poppies made by the nurses and drapery which had been tastefully arranged by Miss Biggin, superintendent nurse. Dancing was indulged ,in with zest, the master (Hr. f. F. Awbery) acting as 1' H.C. Miss Biggin supplied the music. The Guar- dians present were Hr. A. J. Jolley, Mrs. Wilkinson, and Mrs. Clay, and the company included Mr. George Clay, Mr. Walter Clay, Miss Willkinson, Mr. S.Hassall, Hr. Brown, Mr. E. J. Sutton, Mr. B. Shearer, and Mr. Banks. During the interval refreshments were served, the catering being undertaken by the matron and Miss Biggin. At the close cheers were given for the master and matron.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL & THE NON-TRADERS' REPORT.
div.p: THE TOWN COUNCIL & THE NON-TRADERS' REPORT.
SEVERE CENSURE BY THREE COMMISSIONERS.
The Printing Bill Paid.
The following letter has been addressed to the Mayor by the three Non-Trading Commissioners, Messrs. Horrocks, Pemberton and Williams :
[TO 'HIS WORiIIIP THE MAYOR OF WARRINGTON.] TRADING INQUIRY. • -

Dear Sir,—We have read with surprise and regret the report of the proceedings of your Council at its last meeting at which it refused to pay the bill for the printing of our Report. The end has come at last and thoroughly discreditable it is to your Council. The Trading Inquiry was for the whole town and not merely for your Council, which is but a small section of it. We three represented the burgesses, as you are aware; we represented therefore, the most important portion of the ratepayers. Your Council resisted the Inquiry for many months, and only agreed to it at last owing to the overwhelming weight of public opinion in its favour and the public demand which was too strong for your Council to any longer resist. Your Council have from the beginning, as we con- tend, held a mistaken view of the Inquiry. They have , looked upon it as a Council affair, and some of your officials seem to have regarded themselves,as of right, officials of the Inquiry. This is a wrong view, as we believe. The report of the six commissioners was to 'be presented to your Council and through the Non. Trading Association to the burgesses. The three commissioners appointed by your Council resolved, when only half the evidence was heard, to sit no longer. They prepared a report, had it printed, and issued it broadcast. Their three colleagues who sign this letter, heard further evidence. Having been throughout the Inquiry entirely independent of ' our Council colleagues, and being required to report to the Non-Traders' Association (which our colleagues had failed to do), we ordered our Report to be printed nod circulated, precisely as that of our colleagues had been. Great pressure was brought to bear upon us by the Council to com- plete our reFort, and b:t working day and night, we finished it. We had fully intended to ourselves pay for the printing of it. We had no other thought until your Deputy-Town Clerk interposed. And now your Council, which from the first resisted the inquiry, but which printed without demur or comment the report of its three Commissioners, refuses to pay our printing bill ! This is a, paltry affair. It is a piece of calculated meanness, as it , seems tit us, and is worthy of a body which has played so ignominious a part for the past three years, and has earned the contempt of the public for the way in ' which it has defended and winked at the members of its own body who have beea directly and indirectly trading with your Corporation for a long period. We are certainly not wishful to enter upon the undignified course of haggling about the pay- ment of this £22 printing bill with a body which has already, without demur, wended many hundreds of pounds upon the Inquiry. In order to make an end of the matter, we have, therefore, ourselves paid the bill, and we desire, as Commissioners, to wash our hands of any further transactions with your dis- credited Council. We are, Dear Sir, Yours respectfully, ADAM HORROCKS, JOHN PENEDERTON, S. NORBURY WILLIAMS. Warrington, 13th January, 1905.

div.head: LABOUR REPRESENTATION.
div.p: LABOUR REPRESENTATION.
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE WARRINGTON COMMITTEE. The Question of a Parliamentary
Candidate.

The second annual report of the Warrington Labour Representation Committee has just been issued, and from it we cull the following extracts : Fellow Workers: In presenting to you the second annual report, we must congratulate you on the progress made for Labour Representation in Warrington. During this last year several more socipties have joined the local Committee, and our membephip has increased considerably. We are also pleased to report a respect- able financial balance to our credit. Weans yet far from being wholly representative of the trade unionist and reform societies of Warrington, but we trust during the coming year to see a greater influx of new members. The attendance of delegates during the last year leaves great room for improvement, and we would press upon our members the necessity of seeing to the appointment of delegates who will look well to their duty. Darin:: the last year the Committee has seen fit to revise slightly its rules as regards the ordinary working but nothing that will affect or interfere with the objects and constitution ; your Committee has strictly adhered to the principle of independence that was laid down at the formation. We had occasion to clearly demonstrate this fact on the receipt of a

LETTER FROM THE LIBERAL EXECUTIVE asking us to meet them in conference to discuss the bringing out of a joint candidate at the next Parlia- mentary election. The Committee, after some con- sideration, passed the following resolution : " Inasmuch that the Rules and Constitution of this Committee strictly forbid any compromise or alliance with either of the two political parties, and recognising that our object is to form the Labour forces in War- rington into one united party; and also considering that our members hitherto have either been allied to or voted for the Conservative or Liberal Parties, we con- sider it would not be permissable or wise for us to take any steps which would alienate any of our members from our Committee, which Committee is represent- ative of the necessity and rapidly growing intention of Labour to be directly represented in Parliament by a distinct and independent party, whose central policy shall be the rights of labour." This was sent as a , reply to the Liberal Executive and also to the Press. It was not the intention of the Committee to hide themselves behind a rule, but to make it quite clear that our policy is a policy of independence, and to show that we have sound reasons for remaining so, as it is only by an independent action on the part of the workers that we can hope to achieve our objects. We have been much criticised by one of our local organs, and also by some individuals, as to what they choose to term our foolish and suicidal policy. We can only answer to these critics, that they do not understand oar position or our movement; it is not we who are com- mitting suicide, but they who would have us do so. - An attempt is being 'made, both locally and nation- ally, to try and get rid of the toform or Socialist Societies. This will not serve any good purpose, and will only tend to cause disruption in the ranks of Labour, and cannot affect the policy of the Committee. Very early in the year your Committee commenced to consider the municipal elections, but not till later on were any definite steps taken, when the affiliated socie- ties were circularised, asking if they wished the Com- mittee to contest municipal elections, and how many wards should be contested, and would they nominate a candidate for municipal election. A majority voted in favour of one ward being contested, and Mr. Thomas Wright, the nominee of the Independent Labour Party, was the selected candidate by a unanimous vote of the meeting, The bye-election in Bewsey Ward was the chosen contest. This election proved to be a remarkable one. At one period three candidates were in the field, but just prior to the election one candalate withdrew, ' and the other, not .wishing to tight against Labour, retired, but too late to prevent a poll. We were obliged to go to some expense in the election, but having no serious opposition to face, it did not necessitate any great eff.rt on the part of Labour, and we are pleased to record the return of Councillor Wright as a second Labour member on our Town Council. To cover the cost of this election we were obliged to ask the socie- ties to levy themselves, and in a very short space of time every society had paid its proportionate share of the cost. A municipal programme had been drawn up during the year, and during the election in Bewsey Ward this was placed before the electors. This will be amen- ded as required as time goes on, and all candidates, both present and future, will be expected to use their efforts in carrying out this programme. You are aware that at the close of the previous year we had invited Mr. Alexander Wilkie, of the Ship- wrights Society to

BECOME THE LABOUR CANDIDATE for this Borough. It was rather disappointing that directly after entering upon our second year we should receive a communication from the Shipwrights Society stating that they were unable to advise Mr. Alexander Wilkie to contest Warrington at the next election. Your committee accepted their disappointment with a good grace, and at once took steps to procure another candidate by applying to the National Labour Repre- sentation Committee to recommend us a suitable candidate, and Mr. Macdonald, secretary of that body, recommended to us Councillor A. W. Raynor of Battersea, who was the nominee of the General Union Carpenters and Joiners. We invited Councillor Raynor to visit Warrington and address the local committee. Our invitation wis accepted, and Councillor Raynor addressed us on general labour topics. A vote of con- , fldeitie was passel in his favour, and it was generally I considered that he was a most suitable candidate for our borough. We at once got into bomsnunication with the Executive Committee of the General Union, and negotiations were carried on with that body for some time with a view to Councillor Raynor's adoption as a I Labour candidate for us. Unfortunately we were unable to come to terms, and negotiations were ended. Your local committee is still without a candidate for the next election, though seve-al names have bean subjected. The matter is not entirely anded,and a great number of trade unionists are very anxious that we should contest this borough with a Labour candidate, but whether we shall do so it is diacult to sly. In the meantime, our most important work lies in fortifying our present position and increasing our forces, and to do that we must agitate, educate, and co-operate. With all best wishes for a successful future.—l remain, fraternally yours, 0. BUCKLEY, Secretary.

div.head: PANATE WESLEYAN CHURCH.
div.p: PANATE WESLEYAN CHURCH.
The Work of the Sunday School.

The annual congregational tea and entertainment in Iconnection with Padgate Wesleyan Church were held in I the schoolroom on Thursday evening and proved highly successful. About ninety sat down to tea, ladies of the congregation presiding at the tables. At the sub- sequent entertainment, Alderman Bennett presided and referred to the past history and progress of the Sunday school. The Rev. Joseph Manning addressed the gather- ing on the value of Sunday school work. The annual report in connection with the Sunday school was presented by Mr. John Jackson who said there were 225 scholars, an increase of six on last year. Ninety-four scholars had gained prizes for punctual and regular attendance. The school was very well supplied with teal-hers, and there was a good young men's class sith an average attendance of fifteen. During the year 54 members of the Savings Club had paid in £l.OB 14s. 6d., which was a decrease of ViG on the previous year, but it was largely accounted for by the bad state of trade in the town, lie was sorry the library had almost fallen into disuse from the lack lof interesting books, but it would shortly be replenished. The Treasurer commenced the year with a balance in hand of £2 2s. 4d. The receipts had amounted to £34 13s 9d., and the expenditure to .£35 17s. 101 d., leaving a credit balance of 18s. 21d. The °facers appointed for the present year were :—:Superin- tendents, Mr. El. Ward and Mr. V. Wright ; treasurer, James Gandy ; auditor, Mr. Percy H. Bennett ; secretaries, Mr. U. H. White and Mr. John Jackson; savings club treasurer, Mr. Leonard Bennett ; librarian, Mr. H. Brough. Theschool was becoming very crowded on the Sunday afternoons and before long they would have again to appeal for an enlargement. An interesting programme was submitted, one of the most pleasing items being a song cycle entitled" The Sun bonnet " by Miss Wilson, Mrs. Cotterill, Mr. Levi Richardson, and Mr. Walter Clay. Miss Millard effectively sang "Land of hope and glory," and Mr. Clay gave " Till death" and "Long shoreman Billy" in spirited style. Mrs. Cotterill and Mr. Levi Richardson sang "Home sweet home" very sweetly. A recitation "The stowa- way" was contributed by Miss Ada Egerton, and there were two excellent musical dialogues by the school children. Miss C. J. Bennett and Miss L. Ward acted as accompanists. _ _ _
A vote of thanks was accorded to all who had taken part in the concert, on the proposition of Mr. F. WRIGHT seconded by Dr. BENNETT.

div.head: Sankey Harriers.
div.p: Sankey Harriers.

Th . Sankey Club met the combined teams of Latchford and Bewsey-road Y.M.A. Harriers on Saturday, starting from the Filecutters' Arms, the residence of an old captain of the club(Mr.E.Eastwood In spite of the fact that the Sankey team were all novices, they managed to win by three points, the figures being :—Sankey, 26 points: Latchford and Bewsey-road Y.M.A., 29 points. Mr. Eastwood pre- sented a medal for the first Sankey novice home, and it was won in fine style by L. Beckett.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.

I There appears to be an increasing force of opinion in I Warrington in favour of the general utilization of the lay-by on the Ship Canal at Walton for the facilitating lof local traffic. Our readers will remember that at a I recent meeting of the Chamber of Commerce an influential sub-committee was appointed to go into the matter and it has already held two meetings. At the first meeting it NM decided to seed out a circular, of which the following is a copy, to leading local firms:— "Market-gate Chambers Warrington. Dear Sir,— You will doubtless have observed that we are making= effort to utilize the Warrington lay-by. A special committee has been appointed to go into the matter, and the Manchester Ship Canal Company have expressed their willingness to improve the means of access and to [ provide the necessary accommodation if we can guarantee them a reasonable amount of local traffic. It is proposed to make an experiment, in the first instance, with the London, Glasgow and Belfast steamers, which, we have reason to believe, may be induced to call at Warrington. In order to assist us in our negotiations, we shall be glad to know whether, in case we could show you a saving in cost, you would be willing to make use of all or any of these steamers, ' and what would be your probable tonnage per annum. We should also welcome any other suggestions you may have to
The Proposed Utilization of the Walton Lay-By.

make in reference to the canal, as we are strongly o opinion that Warrington is not at present deriving from it the benefit which was anticipated, and which could probably be secured by co-operative effort.—Faithfully yours, ARTHUR BENNETT, hon. secretary." At the second meeting, on Monday, the Hon Secretary reported that he had received many replies to the circular, and that these were almost uniformly favourable to the idea, it being generally felt that the lay-by might be used with advantage, assuming that proper facilities were provided, and that the rates were satisfactory. It was, after some discussion, decided to invite any local firm which had not already communi- cated with the Chamber to forward its views in order that this might be communicated to the Ship Canal Company, along with the letters already received. The Canal Company it is understood, is anxious to facilitate the new movement, and is willing to make the necessary arrangements if anything like a reasonable return in the shape of local traffic can be assured. The committee will be greatly obliged if all local firms who have not already done so will accede to the request embodied in the circular above quoted. On; Tuesday next, the " Watchful," one of Niessrs. F. H. Powell and Co.'s steamers will call at the lay-by to take up a local cargo for BristoL
