div.head: WARRINGTON ANGLERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON ANGLERS.
Successful Season's Sport Reviewed.

Enthusiasm runs high among local pliers of the rod and line, and theta was a large attendance at the annual meeting of the Warrington Anglers' Association which was heti at the Norton Arms hotel on Thursday evening. In the absence of Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, the chair was taken by Mr. W. A. Proud.

Havitig expressed regret at the absence of Mr. Whittle, the CHAIRMAN remarked that both numerically and financially the Association had made progress during the year. They had lost one water which he considered had the makings of a very excellent water, but he hoped they would be able to offer the members something as good during the present year. (Applause) AN INTERESTING REPORT.

Mr. P. KNIGHT, in presenting the fourteenth annual report, said he had great pleasure in recording the great progress the Association had made during the past year both numerically and financially. At the end of 1903, they had 658 members, including 115 ladies and juveniles, sad they had now reached a total of 861, which with 11 who had paid no part of their subscriptions, made a total of 902, an increase of 243. They had in addition supplied travelling cards only to 50 members of four angling clubs in the borough, making a grand total of 952. In dealing with their private waters, they would remember that in the report for 1903, the wretched season of that year was strongly com- mented upon, but the Past season had beea an improved one. Taking the waters separately, the Bridgewater Canal did not continue the form showed in 1903, owing to the drought. The Bailin had suffered somewhat frdm the same cause. The old river, Lymm, had not maintained its good reputation and it was with great regret that they had to re tlize that that very popular fishery was lost to them for all time. The Old Quay canal had done somewhat better than last year,but was not yet up to its required form. Other waters were much on a par with last year. Stocking operations engaged their attention. During the past year, 2,500 roach were obtained from Mr. Ford, of Caister, and were divided proportionately between the Old Quay Canal and Acker's pit. In addition,about 1,500 lgood mixed fish were obtained through the kindness of Mr. J. C. Parr, which were transferrefl to the Bridgewater Canal. Also Later in the season about 10,000 young rainbow trout, the gift of Mr. J. Lyon While, were placed in that water, making a total of about 14,000 stock fish dealt with during the season. They were about to place another order for stock fish of a mixed quality, and which no doubt would find a home in the Bridgewater Canal. As to the acquidition of nee, waters, most of the members were aware that the negotiations for fishing at Llangollen were successful and had been a source of benefit to many of their members, both financially and from an angling point of view. This would be continued during the ensiling year, but under better conditions. In addition to this, they had secured the right to fish en the off side of the North Stafford- shire Canal at Acton Bridge, between bridges No. 207 and 209. They were also in treaty to obtain the fishing in the Gowy at Mickle Trafford—(applause) —the water which was formerly held by them, and hoped toarrive at a satisfactory conclusion in the coarse of a few days. As the occasion arose, further waters would be secured. The angling contests of 1904 had been the most successful ever yet held and reflected greater credit on the Association for the fact: that they were conducted on a sound, self-supporting principle, and dispensed with the obnoxious practice of begging prizes. (Hear, hear). The amount realized by entrance fees and the grants from the Association represented the aggregate of £66 13s. distributed among 144 prize winners averaging over Ss. per prize. (Applause). The shield competition createda record, twenty-seven teams competing for the honour of holding the shield for another year, and the two sets of handsome medals offered for the winners and run- ners-up. The event was brought off at Moore in fine weather, and very keen indeed was the competition. The result was in doubt to the final, honours being won by Victoria team, Mr. W. Hamblett, the captain,being the ~.ero of the match, his catch alone exceeding that of his five colleagues combined It had been decided to abandon the Benevolent Fund competition as the I funds at the dis- posal of the Committee were insufficient to arrange a satisfactory prize list. Their specimen list was some- what in advance of last year, the number of fish weighed being as follows :—Roach 18, perch is, dace 15, bream 10, pike 9, gudgeon, 24, trout 10, grayling 7, chub 15, rudd 6. The aggregate weight was 1541 lbs, the prize fish weighiag 671 Ib4. Tmant six prize fish had been caught in Association waters— Bollin 9, Bridgewater Canal 6, Old river, Lymm, 5, Old Quay canal, one. Twenty prize fish were secured from foreign waters. The income had increased in proportion to their membership and in addition to the ordinary expenditure they would note that expenditure had been accounted for in the extra watching of the Bridge- water canal, stocking and prizes and rents, which absorbed the whole of the £4B increase. The issue of travelling cards would be on the same lines as last year. It was their desire that every class of angler should be catered for, and the workingman angler at a fee well within the reach of his means. They wished to draw attention to the numerous reported instances of poach- ing in the Bridgewater Canal and to request that mem- bers would assist the committee and watchers in preventing this. The new member's card would contain a spacial authority for. every member to challenge a person fishing or committing any breach of rules. Mr. E. PICKAVANCE moved the adoption of the report and observed that, like good wine, Sir. Knight's reports improved each year. The club was in a very strong position, and he hoped that during the year the membership would reach four figures. The proposition was unanimously agreed to. A BALANCE IN HAND.

_ The finAncial report showed that the income for the past year had been £232 and there was a balance to carry forward of £5 10s. skl. The statement was adoptea on the pi °position of Mr. A. COOK, who remarked that the Committee did not deal with the money rashly, and while they did not aim at saving a great deal, the funds were expended judiciously.

div.head: BENEVOLENT FUND.
div.p: THE BENEVOLENT FUND.
Mr. RANGE reported that the income to this fund showed an increase on the previous year of £1 6s. sd. There was a balance of £ll3 16s. ld. to be carried forward.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
-- --- Bold-street Wesleyan Church.

, The Rev. James Dunk, of Liverpool, preached special sermons at this church on Sunday, the offertories being on behalf of the funds of the Wesley Guild. On Mon- day evening the rev, gentleman delivered a lecture in the schoolroom on "Belles and their ringers." In the absence of Mr. John E. Richardson, the chair was occupied by Mr. William Hickman, who said he was sorry at Mr. Richardson could not preside, especially as it was owing to illness. Mr. Dunk, in the course of a humorous and instructive lecture, said there were many women who never had a fair chance to become beautiful as they lived and worked in large manufactur- ing towns. Men should take care not to fall in love because a woman was handsome. (Laughter.) The attest thing was character, and before a man selected a partner for life he should be sure to have a supreme affection for her, always be generous to her, and she would be kind to hirn,and build un the home which was the grandest thing in English citizenshin. Let them love one another, weigh everything in religious scales, look at things in a religious light and that would enable them to steer clear of the bad. A vote of thanks was passed at the close to the lecturer and to the chairman. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. There was a good attendance at the meeting on Sunday. Mr. G. Smiley presided, and spoke upon "Thou renderest to every man according to his deeds." They ought, he said, to be careful in their sowing. Whatever seed was sown would come forth, whether thistles or wheat. J. B. Gough once said "if he could only undo some sins he had committed he would sacri- fice anything." Mr. R. W. Davidson, of Manchester, was the speaker, his subject being "The burdens the Bible speaks about." They had, he said, to bear their own burdens, and also help to bear the burdens of others. Man was the author of his own destiny. What he did to-day was preparing him for to-morrow. He formed a unit in the world, a link in the chain. Each had his own part to play, and that part could not be filled by another. Let them use their charity to others, be blind to their faults, and quick to see the good in others. The Secretary welcomed four now members,the total being 575, the largest number for four years. He also referred to an old brother just passing away aged 85. Miss Lena Duckworth sang sweetly "The children's home." The Secretary, on behalf of the brethren, con- gratulated Miss Duckworth on winning First Prize recently at the Eisteddfod. Mr. Payton, Mus. Bac., presided at the organ. Mr Alit and Mr. J. Bailey also took part in the meeting.

div.head: SOCIAL SERVICE LEAGUE. " Success Already Assured."
div.p: SOCIAL SERVICE LEAGUE. " Success Already Assured."

A social gathering in connection with the above league was held in the Baptist schoolroom, Go'borne- street, on Thursday evening. About ninety persons were present. The §,choolroom, which had been speci- ally decorated and set out in drawing-room style, pre- sented a very pleasing appearance. Amongst those present were the Rev. H. Dunnico, Messrs. J. Morton, E. Osborne, E. Lloyd-Jones, J. Heywood, T. Trow, N. Cook, Joseph Elwell, Mesdames Dunnico, Osborne, Trow, Jones, Walker, and many others. Refreshments were served by members of the Committee, and during the evening Miss Turner's mandoline band gave several selections. Songs were rendered by Mrs. Osborne and Messrs. N. Cook and Joseph Cotterill. Mr. Bratt gave several pieces on the gramaphone. The PRESIDENT (Rev. H. Dunnico) in the course of a short address said that the success of the Social Ser- vice League was already assured, and they were now in a position to undertake effective work. He invited the Indies who were present for the first time that evening to become members of the league. Certain phases of social work could be undertaken by women more effectively and more efficiently than by men, and such work was for the most part neglected at the present time. _

Mr. MORTON, as secretary, announced that the weekly debates would be resumed next Friday. Mr. E. OSBORNE in proposing a vote of thanks to the caterers referred to the recent address of Sa-ah Grand on.". Mere man." According to the lecture it was tin* opinion of Sarah Grand that man was growing out of his moral obliquities into the sphere of his better self. The Social Service League was to play no unimportant part in this process of evolution. If they required any proof of this they had it in that gathering. Mr. JOSEPH ELWELL in seconding strongly resented being termed a "mere man" but if any one still doubted the improvement of man after what they had seen and heard that evening they mast be very sceptical indeed. It had been stated that the way to win a man was to "feed the brute" and at an election time such a mode of attack usually • succeeded. The Social Service League, however, existed to demonstrate that the final test of "mere man" was his moral worth and courage. The resolution was unanimously carried, the chair- man remarking that important though "mere man" might be it remained for the ladies to put that finishing touch upon his work and such assistance was of infinite value to mere man in his fight for a higher civilization.

Jessie Coifingliam, aged fifteen, was told by the Hay- wards Heath magistrates on Wednesday that she deserved a medal. She risked her life in rescuing a young woman who attempted suicide in a lake. Miss Cottingham, who had to break away the ice which covered the water, is a strong swimmer.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

Two MONTHS ?Olt WIFE ASSAULT. At the Borough Police Court yesterday,John Pownall, 39, Lord Nelson-street, was summoned for assaulting his wife Catherine on January llth.—Complainant stated that defendant came into the house and commenced to quarrel with her. He used filthy language and she told him to go out, whereupon he thrashed her severely. Complainant alleged that she had been continually ill-used during the past five years, and she did not know what a night's rest was." Defendant said his wife aggravated him.—He had previously beei* before the magistrates for assaulting his wife, and he was now sentenced to two months' hard labour.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court. ---- Minor Cases.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court. ---- Minor Cases.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (presiding), Alderman Smethurst, Messrs. J. W. Hayward, S. Wright, H. Thornton, W. Roberts, and G. Pilling. SUNDAY FOOTBALL.—George Cooper, 181, Wellfield- street ; William Bates, jun.. 177, ; Thomas Jefferson, 35, Liverpool-road; and Richard Jefferson, 35, Liverpool-road; were charged with play- ing football in Holland-street on New Year's day to the annoyance of passengers.—Detective Clough said in consequence of a letter having been received at the Police Station, he proceeded to Holland-street and saw the defendants kicking a football. They were very disorderly.—The Chief Constable said numerous com- plaints of this kind of conduct had been received. Defendants, who pleaded guilty, were fined in the costs (3s. 6d.) each. TUESDAY.—Before Dr. Fox (presiding), Messrs. W. Richardson and C. Jackson Holmes. Firry CONVICTIONS.—Margaret M'Loughlin, of no settled abode, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Cloth Hall-yard on Monday night, and also with stealing a pictorial postcard album, from the shop of Sarah Ann Dickenson, Scotland-road. —The evidence showed that prisoner went to the shop for a newspaper and appropriated the album. Later Sergeant Barnett found her in a drunken state, and she struck him in the face.—The prisoner had fifty previous convictions. and the magistrates committed her to gaol for three months.

A COWARDLY BLOW.—Peter Lee, a pauper, was charged with assaulting another pauper named Patrick Lowery, at the Warrington Workhouse, on Monday.— Lowery, an old man, stated that he was sitting on a form waiting for his dinner, when Lee came into the TOODI and struck him a heavy blow on the nose.-11 Mr. J. F. Awbery, workhouse master, stated that prisoner was subject to fits of bad temper, and on Meaday morning he had wilfully broken a form, and complainant told witness about it. He supposed that Lee had struck Lowery for spite. It was a most cowardly blow, and the prisoner was an able-bodied man.—Lee was sent to goal for a month with hard labour.

div.head: Daresbury Petty Sessions.
div.p: Daresbury Petty Sessions.

TERiDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Charlton Parr (presiding) John White, and William Long. ABORTIVE INLAND REVENUE PROSECCTION.—James Percival, Reed House, Antrobus, was summoned for having pursued and killed a pheasant at Antrobus, with- out having the proper licence or certificate.—Defend- ant, who was represented by Mr. Browne, pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Edward D. Lowry (supervisor of Inland Revenue, Chester) prosecuted, and stated that on _ .

November 16th, the 'defendant Was seen on a field next to one in the occupation of his father by a gamekeeper named George Tomkinson. It was a !foggy morning, but Tomkinson could see defendant distinctly as he knew him personally. He saw him raise a covey of pheasants and shoot twice, bringing two down. Tomkinson afterwards went up to him and told him he would report the matter. He saw pheasants' feathers sticking from under defend- ant's coat.—Tomkinson corroborated this.—Replying 11, Mr. Browne, witness said there was no enmity between he and defendant. He (witness) had to trespass on two fields to follow defendant. He had not told anyone he was in a hut at the time of the occurrence.— Mr. Browne said the case was a most extraordinary one. Defendant's father and family had been at the farm for over 73 years, and this prosecution was the first that had ever taken place, and they felt it very keenly. Defendant never shot any pheasants whatever but only a wood. pigeon. As it was a foggy morning, it was impossible for the gamekeeper to have seen him shoot at the distance he admitted he was away. He thought the Bench would agree that the evidence was not such as they could convict upon.—The magistrates retired, and on their return, the Chairman said the case would be dismissed.

div.head: Alleged Game Trespass on the hold Estate.
div.p: Alleged Game Trespass on the hold Estate.

Thomas Garner and Josiah Bowden, colliers of datton, St. Helens, were summoned at St. Helens on Tuesday for unlawfully using a net for the purpose of taking game on December 31st. Mr. E. W. Swift prosecuted for Messrs. Bromilow and Warren, who hold the shooting rights over the Bold Hall estate. The two men were caught redhanded by Gamekeeper Shepley, of Abbot's Farm, who saw the men draw a net across a field and catch a hare. He went into the field and spoke to them, taking possession of the hare Bowden was the only one who appeared, and on oath swore that he was not with Garner, but Garner after- wards told him that he had been caught with a mate nd they had given Bowden's name to deceive the keeper. Bowden said this was the third time they had tried to prove him guilty wrongfully. The magis- trates adjourned the case for 1, fortnight, and issued a warrant for the arrest of Garner, so that the whole story °quid be investigated.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, January 14, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, January 14, 1905.

iiibit, how great is the reward ! To call /iseased mind out of its self-built dungeon :to :low like a clean wind through the dust an' oorbidity of the four-walled life lived by mos thhappy humans; such is the mission of tin. .heelful, the gay of heart, more glorious by far ,lian to go about preaching and teaching, and though they may have their ONIM wry moments (where the light is brightest, the shadow is deep- est) they are Using up their ' ounce of cheerful- uess " with which to serve God royally. tip not we all more or less hypnotise each other, impress our own moods on those near to us. elevating or depressing their spirits, mu: forcing them to look through our own specta- cles, rose-coloured or blue as.the case may be I' May not we even narrow mid vulgarise their mental vision., even as we have power to inspire them with that larger litauaaity which throws its u eight into the scale of pity, not condemnation of its fellow-men ' BE CONPUBBBACE.

• We can make them sea the strong under-cur- rent of fun that runs through life; the gleams of pathos and humour that illumine the most sor- did and unlikely subjects; in a word, each one of us is a maker of sunshine, or a producer of gloom in himself and others, and loved or dis- liked according to which role he elects to play. To be "merry and wise " is not given to all, but to cultivate the bright side of things, to get a laugh out of unpromising material is open to everyone, and it is astonishing how the habit of laughter, once indulged in, grows on us, till at last we come to recognise it as one of the great sweeteners and purifiers of life, while from a physical point of view, its value is untold. The veriest grumbler and misanthrope alive, might be improved by a laughter treatment, supplement- ed by plenty of fresh air, for in addition to brooding far too much over imaginary troubles, we are all too much indoors for our spiritual and bodily health—The Gentle Art of Fooling does not permit stagnation of men's mind, but rather makes it quick-moving, keen to ob- serve the humours of the crowd, of Nature, and lastly, of oneself, for not to be able to smile at our own peculiarities and foibles, is to be en- tirely bereft of that sense of the ridiculous which encroaches so nearly on humour, and is so price- less a belonging to its possessor, keeping him armoured against all the minor misfortunes and accidents of life.

BE APPRECIATIVE. It is a good world, a beautiful world, it is man himself who makes most of the trouble, by indulging in purely fictitious desires and sor- rows. Turning his back on all the glories of the universe, he fights tooth and nail for the one bit of coloured glass that has caught his fancy, only to discover its worthlessness when seized; mean- while he is blind to all most worth having in life, for are not his the sky, the earth, the sea, his also the parks, the treasures of picture gal- lery and museums, such as the richest men alive cannot bring together It might do some of us good if we deliberate- ly set ourselves to count up the amount of plea- sures we can take for nothing, it would not hurt us indeed to be vain-glorious, and strut about, vaunting the joys so freely provided for us, Wf might even in time come to patronise the multi- millionaire who has not a tittle more right in a superb sunset, a rosy dawn, and the recrudes- cence of spring, than we have. _

If we come to measuring our personal happi- ness with his, he might be the loser by the com- parison, but in any case it is a fine thing to stand up to wealth, not be cowed by it, to say, "A man's a man for a' that —and a' that—" and when we are able to do this, we are far on the road to a serenity of spirit that begets the desire to fool discreetly at a fitting opportunity. "There's always a little something—she can't abide the mon," said one old farmer to an- other, when bragging about his daughter's mar- ried happiness, and while not unduly rejoicing over those whom the world envies, it may con- sole poor folks to reflect that there is always " a little something" to discount the happiness ol fortunate people, who, if we only knew it, deep- ly envy us, the obscure and happy.
AND BE HAPPY.

They may have all the desire to fool that we have, feel impulses as eager to take life rather as a picnic than a solemn feast, but they can- not escape from their surroundings, or rather from the circumstances that make them famous or remarkable, let us then, more happy, learn to fool gently, fool wisely, and laugh while we fool, encouraging others to a like pursuit, only taking care that such „fooling do not degenerate into sheer folly, or worse—but to the honest and pure of heart, to whom I especially address my- self, the practice is more likely to tend to their ennobling, than to their deterioration.
• HELEN MATHERS.
Next Week: " THE DETERIORATION OF BRITISH HEALTH AND PHYSIQUE." BY THE EARL OF MEATH.

A SPOILED CEMENT CARGO. Claim for Alleged Defective Warehousing. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday the Peerless Patents Company, Warrington, sued the Man- chester and Liverpool Transport Company Limited for 48 ss. 4d. in respect of damage alleged to have been done to 142 bags of cement while they were stored at Bishop's Wharf, Warrington--Mr. E. A. White appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Greer, barrister, represented the defendant company. The case as stated by Mr. White was that in April or May, 1903, bags of cement, including the 142 in question I were sent by a man named Joseph Parr, of Liverpool', , consigned to the plaintiffs, by the Manchester and I Liverpool Transport Company Limited, who acknow- ledged their receipt. On May 9th the goods were delivered at Bishop's Wharf and the defendants notified the plaintiff company by an advice note bearing the intimation that the cement was now held by the company not as common carriers but as warehousemen, at owner's risk. On the back of the note were sundry conditions which, he continned, were not applicable to warehousing but merely to carrying,no reference to them appearing on the face of the note Although the " owner's risk" condition was inserted, the defendants were bound to exercise reasonable care in the warehousing of the goods as the conditions only freed them from their liability as carriers. The cement was placed in the warehouse at Bishop's Wharf, but having regard to the nature of the material, it was not properly stored. If kept dry, cement would last for an indefinite time, but:if damp it lost all its virtue and became solid pieces of stone, valueless for any purpose whatever. Cement should be stored from 12 to 18 inches above the floor, in order that it might not come into contact with any dampness coming through the floor, and that sufficient air might pass underneath, which had a tendency to keep the cement dry. In the present case, the warehouse floor had placed upon it three inch planks, the spaces between them being filled with rubbish which was exceedingly damp. The cement was stored on the lowest pa rt of the floor. In addition, the warehouse roof of galvanised iron was not water- tight. The dampness of the floor in itself was sufficient to have caused the damage. If the cement had been properly stored, raised from the floor, and in a proper water-tight and dry place, the damage would have been little or none. As it was, the whole of the cement was completely spoiled. Arthur Knight,a traveller in the employ of Mr. Joseph Parr, corroborated Mr. White's statement as to the way in which the cement was stored. The material was hard and unlit for use, a portion of it being stone and worthless. _

Samuel Booth, who trades as the plaintiff company, also gave evidence, and in reply to Mr. Greer said he noticed some printed matter at the back of the advice note, but he did not read it. Mr. Greer read one of the conditions printed at the back of the advice note which was to the effect that the goods were warehoused at owner's risk, and that the company would not be liable for damage done in any way. Witness, continuing, said it was not a fact that the cement now was worth half its original value. Thomas Johnson, builder and contractor, said he had a practical knowledge of cement. He examined the con- signment in question on Monday and it was useless. Mr. Greer submitted that the conditions on the back of the advice note were part of the contract and even if I plaintiff had omitted to read them they exempted the company from liability. There was a further document which defendant received, and this gave it to be under- stood that there was no undertaking on the part of the Company to store for any period, and they could put an end to the storage whenever they liked. Mr. White argued that the conditions on the back of the advice note applied only to transport. His Honour gave judgment for the defendants without costs, remarking that he considered it a very ungracious defence,
Mr. Greer remarked that no warehouseman who had not premises specially built for the purpose would accept liability for the storing of cement.

At the conclusion of the meeting of the Royal Agri- cultural Society, in London, on Wednesday, Lord .liddleton announced that it bad been decided to hold the annual show at Park Royal on June 27, 28, 29,and 30. The death took place on Wednesday of Mrs. Sarah Bambridge, of the Almshouses, Little Bardfield, Essex. The deceased, who was in her 105th yew, had a cheerful disposition, and until her last illness had suffered from no particular ailment.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD_OF GUARDIANS , tAm. Moms Rznayse4 THE GENTLE ART OF The Rev, J, Lowe and Mr. W. Houghton. FOOLING,
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD_OF GUARDIANS , tAm. Moms Rznayse4 THE GENTLE ART OF The Rev, J, Lowe and Mr. W. Houghton. FOOLING,

This Board met at the Warrington Workhouse on Wednesday. Mr. A. Brooks presiding. There were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson, Rev. D. Mercer, Rev. T. R. Matthews, Dr. Patterson, Messrs. W. Houghton, A. J. Jolley, S. Davies, J. Payton, J. Billinge, G. Mather, J. 1,17'. Knowles, G. Thompson, W. Flannagan, M. W. Seton, J. Turton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (superin- tendent of Padgate schools.) THE RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION AT PAIDGATE SCHOOLS. The Padgate Schools Comruitteo recommended that the Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool be requested to submit the name of a person to be appointed as religious instructor to the Romon Catholic children in the homes on the terms set forth in the minute of November 29th, 1934 and subject to the approval of the Local Government Board. On the motion of Mr. MATHER seconded by Mrs. CLAY the minutes were approved. HOUSE COMMITTEE'S BUSINESS.

—,...._,—, „,.._. ... At a meeting of the House Committee it was reported that probationer nurse McEwen having completed her three years agreement resigned her post, to take effect on January 25th. There being two vacancies it was decided to advertise for probationers upon the usual terms and conditions. Since Christmas the following gifts had been sent :—Mrs. Owen, Newholme, Latch- ford, oranges and buns; Junior Conservative Club, toys. At a subsequent meeting it was resolved to appoint Louisa Haley, of 116, Hood-lane, Sankey, as probationer nurse in place of Louisa Wagstaffe, resigned. 1 These minutes were also approved without comment. THE WORKHOUSE EXTENSION. The CLERK said he had forwarded for the Local Government Board's approval plans of the proposed infirm block at the Workhouse. Up to the present he had only recei fed a formal acknowledgment. THE REV. J. LOWE AND R. W. HOUGHTON. THE LATE MR. JOHN HOUGHTON. I The CLERK reported the receipt of the following letter from the Rev. J. Lowe:—" St. Peter's, Wooston, , December 28th, 1904.—Dear Mr. Sutton,—l have found it necessary to write to the Guardians after the publica- tion of what passed at the meeting of the Board of ; Guardians on December 17th. Please read same and I inform me if anything has been said in your presence affecting me personally, and oblige, yours faithfully, REV. J. LOWE. ' The CLERK said he replied informing the Rev. Father Lowe that nothing at any time had been said in his ; presence to the rev, gentleman's prejudice. In another letter the rev, gentleman, in reply to Mr. Sutton. said :—I beg to thank you for your kind- ness. Your letter is all I could desire. Allow me to i thank you at the same time for the unfailing courtesy which, as Cltrk to the Guardians, I have always received at your hanas. Mr. THOMPSON said that when he read the Rev. .1. Love's letter in the Warrington papers he felt fearfully indignant, because he had such respect for their esteemed friend, Mr. Houghton, the oldest member of the Board, and he could hardly contain himself until that meeting. After the conversation he had had with one of the mem- bers he concluded that it was perhaps better for him not to say what he had intended saying, because he thought the public generally knew Mr. Houghton so well that he did not need defending by anyone. During the last few days Mr. Houghton had lost his brother, who was an old member of the Board, and he (Mr. Thompson) thought the Board ought to express their ,condolence with the widow in her affliction, and convey to Mr. Houghton their sense of his loss. Mr. BILLINGE seconded and endorsed all that Mr. Thompson had said. It was his joy and privilege in his earlier days to meet the late Mr. John Houghton both at Board and Assessment Committee meetings. The deceased gentleman took a deep interest in the work he performed for the ratepayers. The CHAIRMAN said that as far as the vote of condo- lence was concerned they were all at one with what Mr. Thompson and Mr. Billing° had said. Personally he Idid not know the late Mr. Houghton but he knew of his reputation. His services on the board had come down as tradition.

The CLERK said the name of Houghton h•td been con- nected with that Board and Union business over since the formation of the Board in 1838. He served person- ally with a brother of Mr. William Houghton—Mr. Joseph Houghton—as a guardian for many years Afterwards Mr. John Houghton was connected with the authority during the early part of his (Mr. Sutton's) clerkship and since then they had had Mr. William Houghton so that the name had really been represented in the interests of that part of the Union in connection with Poor Law administration from 1838.

The vote of condolence was unanimously agreed to. Mr. HOUGHTON thanked the Board and said it would afford him a melancholy satisfaction to convey their expression of condolence to the members of the family. With regard to the first part of Mr. Thompson's remarks he felt very pleased nt the compliment the speaker had chosen to pay him. With regard to the Rev. Father Lowe and himself, he assured the Board and the rev. gentleman that he had not the least personal feeling or animosity in any sense of the word, and kad not had. His feelings were more of sorrow than of anything else.

div.head: POLICEMAN CHARGED WITH PILFERING.
div.p: POLICEMAN CHARGED WITH PILFERING.
All the Cases Dismissed.

On Thursday, Police-constable James Dugdale, stationed at Collins Green, Earlestown, was charged at the Newton-le-Willows Police Court with having on the 18th October last, stolen half-a-pint of oil, value 2d., from the Collins Green collieries ; of having on Decem- ber Ist stolen a sack of potatoes, value 25., belonging to Harry Bridge, farmer, Vulcan Village, Earlestown ; and with having on the 7th July attempted to obtain Bs. by false pretences from George Taylor, of Collins Green. The evidence in the first case was that the constable was seen by a colliery weighrnan helping himself to the oil in the lamp-shop, the witness asking if he was "pinching." In cross-examination witness denied being the instigator of the prosecution because defendant had been concerned in obtaining a conviction against a woman for keeping a betting-house.

Mr. ThorapsOn,° manager'at the colliery, said that defendant explained his action by saying that it would save him a walk of a mile and a half to get a fresh supply. Defendant had no right to take the oil, but after the defendant's explanation he decided to take no further action.

Mr. Browne, for the defence, said it was a Lancashire custom for constables connected with collieries to get the oil from the premises. After other evidence the case was dismissed. The alleged false pretenc, case was based by the prosecution on the contention that Taylor's father attempted to commit suicide, and that defendant bor- rowed the Collins Green Colliery ambulance, which, though not charged for, defendant represented there was h charge of Bs. The defence called for the production of defendant's report to his inspector, and as it was not forthcoming, the Bench dismissed the case. The third case was that Bridge's man lost a load of potatoes en route for St. Helens, and that three days later the constable asked Bridge if he had lost anything and he replied a sack of potatoes. The constable said he had found them, and Bridge said he might as well keep them. The case was withdrawn. Superintendent Cocker said the cases had come to the notice of the Chief Constable, who felt they ought to be properly investigated.

To fool properly, I take it, in a purely physi- cal sense, requires two persons, young, slim, long-limbed, and light of heels and heart, not necessarily of opposite sexes, as:zwo girls, or two youths can fool together with equal felicity, sometimes even better than when love interferes to make too serious their frolics, and end them. Yet, to watch two graceful young lovers in the initial stages of courtship, is a pretty sight, the swallow-like character of their advances, flights and retreats, the half-averted way in which they glean hints of each other's charac- ters and predilectiom, till gradually the circle narrows, and by imperceptible degrees they draw nearer to en, o ,•• I!cr. the sport over, the fooling done, they sit hand in hand, dull human fashion, and. w e know that unless one of them is wise, and keeps the game up after mar- huge, their happiest days are over. For the gentle art of fdoling does not com- prise fooling another person—it means that you yourself have a great capacity for playing the fool, and with wise discrimination admit another person to share your pleasure—it means that you have a gift for seeing the light side of Nature, and human nature, instead of the dark; the hu- morous instead of the tragic ; and this is less a gift than an art that can be acquired, if you resolutely set lout to learn it.
BE CHEERFUL.

And primarily, I say that none of us fool suf- ficiently, but grizzle far too much; that if for only one hour of the day, we tied up memory, and our worldly and domestic worries in a bag, and dropped them somewhere out of sight, then did afething that without hurting anyone else, most particularly pleased us, our tempers would improve vastly, and t we should male much hrighter companions to those wifh whom Fate, or circumstance, has jailed Us. The heart of youth is light, because pure, and fooling' follows inevitably, but as years advance, it inevitably gathers weight, feels that it cannot rise, and this is where art should come in, to teach us that it we will throw overboard the useless lumber we have piled on it, that heart will spring light as air to meet the thousand joys of life, aye, and enjoy them consciously, as in careless youth it did not.

I have seen qsome exquisite . fooling between quite old people when they thought themselves unobserved, persons in whom an innate gaiety of heart, and a happy knack of seeing the bright side of things has outlived all the pain and disillusionment of life, and I have been fain to ask them the secert of this art—for is it not an Art to retain in middle and old age, a privi- lege peculiar to youth? They must have ana- lysed this precious quality, have tracked it to its. source, finding out what qualities of heart and brain go to its making, or is it that they have emptied their wallets of all grievances, throwing overtoard Malice, Selfishness, Acctuisi- tiveness—above all—Fear?
BE BRAVE.

It is the bogie man Fear who extinguishes in us that joy of living, which is the very es- sence, the raison d'être of our presence here, fear of the future, fear of the past, fear of death, fear of losing what we love, what we have amassed, though since we know clearly the con- ditions on which we hold existence—that we are as torches lit only to be sooner or later extin- guished—why fear? De athmust come—well, ,et us meet it with decent dignity, loss of what we love must come—that too is in the bond. Being human, we must more or less often, ac- cording to the strength of our humanity (it is not the strength of our will, but the feebleness of our desires that most often gives us the vic- tory over them) do things that make us regret the past—but the future? Acaunt Fear ! We mean to do our best with it—if we fail, we shall ilI have tried—fear makes our defeat a fore- g ale conclusion—we will have none of him.

Loss of worldly goods? If —tile- brains and will to work are there, these may be replaced. Ilie only real calamity to be dreaded, is loss of health, and that very state of things is oftener :him not, brought about by the fear of it. Fear is an artificial condition of mind that nature knows nothing of in its chronic state—her chil- dren only experience it in momenta of acute physical danger, when their racial enemies are near, and if we also reserved our energies fox meeting the inevitable bad moments of :mr life, instead of anticipating them, we sh mld have considerably more time ,left over for enjoyment in a word, we should fool more, and grizzle less.

BE JtiDICIOrSLY FQRGETErL. Just as our houses contain numbers of per. fectly taselesP,lthings, so do we insensibly allow minds to become receptacles for disagree- able, tedious, unprofitable thoughts, regrets and desires, that wander aimlessly to and fro like ghosts, and like them, vanish into mist. If we resolutely set ourselves to enjoy, moment by mo- ment, the much that life has to offer, facing our misfortunes with equal courage, and forgetbar, hem, would we not add enormously to our Own, and others' store of happiness? How few of us dare to say, " I am happy," yet the reasons tire purely artificial that prevent our being so, and when we realise this, when we climb up, and look over the paling that man has raised to fence us off from God and His works, we are ingrates indeed, if we do not take of the feast so bounti- fully set before us. . _

All Ict-itUr:e- rejoices in its own way, and at proper seasons, all but man, who even when neither hunger, thirst, nor sickness :threaten him, looks about for trouble, and stores it in his mind as a bee, with more wisdom, stores honey in the hive.

He is always expecting something to go wrong, he completely misses the i moment of en- joyment in fearing, or expecting t will be -.natched from him—surely if, as a recent brilli- ant writer suggested, a school for Happiness -liould be founded, a School for Cheerfulness is even more necessary, with teachers who would diligently point out to us our blessings and oc- casions for rejoicing, insteaclAif reviling. By comparing what we might have been, with what we are, physically, mentally, commercially; by counting up the misfortunes we have just missed; the occasions when luck or circumstance has saved us from ruin of one kind or another; by forcing ourselves to measure our paltry grievances with those of the really afflicted and heart- broken, how many of us would not then sit down to reflect soberly on our advantages, feeling ashamed of our perpetual grumblings ?

HE ACTIVE. Over much reading, especially of society papers, with their idle tattle of rich folk's do- ings. is responsible for a good deal of mind- vapouring, especially among women, iwhose minds are confused by a variety of matters not in the least essential to their comfort or happi- ness. But let them fix their attention rather on the wants of those beneath, than the extrava- gance of those above them in the social scale, and they will end by hugging themselves rather on what they have, than desiring what would probably make them no hoppier than that does which they now possess. It may be taken for granted that those hav- ing great possessions cannot fool light-hearted- ly, for even as the soldier with the lightest knap- sack steps out quickest, so are the rich weighed down to earth by the gold taken out of it, or rather the overwhelming responsibilities at- tached to their position. They may be the cause, and often are, 01 others' light-heartedness, but seldom of then own ; it is the moderates who inherit the earth, those who have known neither starvation, nor a plethora of the good things of life, and it D. among them that we must look for the " merry ' men and women who take the sunshine with them wherever they go, and who, whatever ma be their faults, are loved accordingly. To turn always a bright face to the world may at first be difficult, but how quickly it become

"After many years of effort, I am able to say I can make him do any- thing he wants to." " Cnoss with him? Why he wrote a lovely poem to her." "Yes, but she never read it. When she saw the title of it she tore the whole thing up in a fit of anger. You see, he called it, Lines on Mabel's face.'" "I do not doubt you, my dear ; but every time I know to a certainty that you have deceived me I will cut a notch in the piano." "No, you won't, Edwin Jorgles ! Do you suppose I want that instrument ruined?" THRRE is a story hailing from the siege of Paris of a lady who was compelled with great reluctance to eat her favourite pet dog. When she had finished him she swept the bones to the side of her plate with a pathetic gesture, and murmured, "How poor Fido would have enjoyed them !" "I'LL know better next time," said Mrs. Fer- guson, speaking of it afterward. "I told George', uncle to consider himself at h.& in our house." " Well ?" "Well, it wasn't Oh minutes after- wards that he began to grumble about the :cook- ing," UP-TO-DATE. —" I want to tell yo', my dear brethren," said Deacon Johnaing to his flock at prayer-meeting, " dat in dese days of chain. less bikes, hossless kerrid,ges an' skin, dat what we need fo' the glorification of de oullud folkees am chickenless coops, mazer-less pahties, melon- less patches, and scrapless games. Does yo' follow me ?' "I WANT to stop in front of this window," said Mr. Blykins. "Why, it's full of millinery ! " exclaimed his wife. ' I didn't know you admired such things." "I not only admire—l marvel. I take off my hat to genius ; and the people who can get the money they ask for a lot of bunches of odds and ends like those are qualified to give lessons to a Napoleon of finance." A MAN lost a small opal out of his ring, and went to the jeweller to have it replaced. Return- ing home, he found the old one, and, putting it in his mouth for safe keeping, hurried back to the jeweller's to have that set used instead of the new opal. Rushing into the shop, he said "Say, rye found the old set, so don't use the new one.' He attempted to remove the stone from his mouth, gave a gulp, looked sheepish, and said: "I think you'll have to use the new stone." Pr is told of a certain Bishop that, while dining at the house of one of his friends, he was pleased to observe that he was the object of marked attention from the son of his host, whose eyes were firmly riveted upon him. After dinner the Bishop approached the boy, and asked, "Well, my young friend, you seem to be interested in me. Do you find that I am all right?" "Yes, sir," said. the boy with a glance at the Bishop's- knee-breeches. You're all right; only "—hesitatingly—" won't, won't your mother let you wear trousers yet ?'" WASN'T SO POOR. —A coaching party was sing through a bleak stretch of country on the war to a famous pleasure resort. The coach halted et a watering-trough opposite a dilapidated old house, and the tourists indulged freely in comments on the dreariness of the spot. "I pity the people who live here !" said one young woman, in a tone unwisely clear. "They must be as w r as poverty. Look at that pasture full of . aders and that discouraged meadow !" "Well, now, ma'am," came a voice from the doorway, in which suddenly appeared a lank man in corduroys and a bright red shirt. "I'm not so poor as you think. I don't own this land. I'm only tenant! Dye see?" " This," said the artist, "is a battle scene— time, say, the year 2000 A. 1). The defending foroe is on the extreme right of the canvas—" "I can't see them," observed the friend. " Certainly not; they are strongly entrenched " "Can't see any entrenchments." "Of course you can't. The entrenchments are skilfully concealed from view." "I should think you'd show some big guns or something." " Nonsense ! The guns are disappearing guns, and they have disappeared." Well, how about the attacking force?" "Oyer here on the left—all under cover. You can't ex- pect them to expose themselves to the spectator any more than to the enemy." "Well, your pic- ture is a mere landscape." " Yes ; but I take it that's how a battle will look in the year 2000 _

div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
IMPRISONM-RNT. FOR POACHING,

For poaching on the Aston estate and Sir Richard Brook's estate on the 31th ult. Charles Stubbs was sent to gaol for two months' hard labour at Runcorn on Monday. His brother, William Stubbs, who kept watch, was allotted one month's hard labour. CHARGE OF SETTING A WIFE ON FIRE. _ .

At Runcorn on Tuesday, a farm labourer named John M'Mahon, of Aston, was charged with doing grievous bodily harm to his wife, Ellen. It was alleged that the prisoner, on Christmas Day, quarrelled with his wife, thrashed her, and then set fire to her underclothing. She was shockingly burnt about the legs, and since has been unable to leave the house. On the application of Superintendent Eianion, the prisoner was remanded for a week. WIDNES SCHOOLM ISTRESS ASSAULTED. At Widnes. on Thursday, IFrances Taylor, Frederick street, was charged with assaulting Teresa Burke,school- mistress, at St. Bede's Roman Catholic School, on December 21. Mr. Poole represented plaintiff, and said that on the day in question the defendant came to the school in a very excited state' and after asking for a certain teacher, saw Mrs. Burke near the stairs. Defendant exclaimed that she was the one she was looking for. She rushed at her, struck her twice on the face with her closed fist, and beat her about the head with her straw hat.—Mrs. Taylor, for the defence, said that on the 21st her daughter came home crying and said she was ordered to sit on the pipes, which were hot and blistered her. The Bench were of the opinion that an assault had been committed, and a line of 10s. and costs or fourteen days in default vhs imposed.

div.head: DIAGRAM 4,9.
div.p: DIAGRAM 4,9.

A cannon from the D. Position A shows the wrong way of playing the stroke. and Position B the rignt way of playing it. Red ball 12i inches from the baulk line and 14 inches from the side cushion, object white 21 inches from the baulk line and 12i inches from the side cushion.

Diagram 48 shows a position (either side ot the table) that commonly occurs. The player is in hand and the only stroke to play is a cannon. Figure A shows the wrong way and Figure B the right way of playing the stroke, the object balls being as regards the stroke, in exactly the same position on either side of the table. The player who seldom makes more than a twenty break always plays the cannon as shown at A. That is to say he spots his ball for a half-ball cannon. Played in this way the balls must be separated, and should the cannon be made full or nearly full on to the second object ball the cue ball will remain between the object balls. In any case the first object ball which in the diagram is the red will alwaFs be left behind (as shown by the intersected line in Fig. A) and it may easily happen that nothing may be left for the next stroke except a pot into the centre pocket, and when this means potting the white it only emphasises bow wretched a stroke the hall-ball cannon is in such a position. Sometimes, too, the second object ball will be driven past the centre pocket so that even should it be the red ball, position catnot be recovered by the agency of this pocket. The correct way of playing the cannon is shown at B. The cue ball is spotted so as to make the cannon a partial run-through. In this way the first object ball, owing to its being taken fuller is kept in front of the cue ball instead of being left behind. The degree of fulness with which the first object ball must be struck will, of course, vary with variations of the positions of the object balls, sometimes it will 3nly be necessary to strike the object ball slightly fuller than half-ball, at other times it must be strufk quite three-quarter ball. The idea of the stroke is to bring the first object ball off ihe side cushion in such a manner that it will come to rest near the second object ball, the cannon being played with such strength that the cue hall in cannoning on. to the second ball moves it very little. As, however, the first ball has to be hit fuller than half-ball the contact takes most et the pace out of the cue ball so that, generally speaking, a stroke which is just the right strength to bring the first object ball to the second- one will ensure the cue ball cannoning gently on to the second ball, thus leaving all the balls together. DIAG'

A cannon from the D. Position A shows the right Way of playing the stroke, and Position B the wrong way of playing it. Red ball 13i inches from the side cushion and 11i inches from the baulk line. Object white 17 inches from the side cushion and 25i inches from the baulk line.

Diagram 49 shows another cannon trom too D, and also the right and wrong way of playing it. In positions similar to this, the balls cannot so easily be brought together as in the position shown on-diagram 48. If, howevec:the cannon be played by means of a half-ball stroke, the red, which is here the first object ball, will be !eft behind, and in all probability nothing easy will be left for the next stroke. By spott;ng the cue ball for a partial run-through instead of a half ball cannon, the red ball will be kept in front of the cue ball, and rebounding from the side cushion will leave position for a pot or an in-off into the centre pocket if the strength has been at all good. Position Aon the diagram shows the cannon correctly played, and position B the way the stroke is played by inferior Players, who never take the trouble to think out a stroke. Note how the half ball stroke ves the red behind.

1 Diagram 50 shows another position that con- stantly creurs. The red is on the spot, and the striker is in hand. The easiest way of getting the cannon is by spotting for and playing a half trill stroke, but eueh a stroke would not bring tle, white up to the top of the table, so that whether any position or not were left would depend to a very great extent upon the red being left in a favourable position. If, instead, the white ball be taken somewhat fuller than half ball it can be driven to the top of the table, and thus, with both balls there, not only wilt the probability of position being left for the next stroke be greatly increased, but alga the position will most likely be one from which a good break may be made. Of course to the ordinary player the cannon played this way will Olot be quite so easy au the elementary keill ball stroke, but no player will ever make decent breaks if he play every stroke in the easiest way. In order to leave favourable position for the next stroke some departure from the simplest way of making a stroke is generally necessary. In the shot under discussion the object white has not to be struck very much fuller than half ball, and played in this way the cue ball takes very nearly the same course as it would were the object ball struck half ball, for the throw-off angle in medium-pace strokes varies very little whether the object ball be taken a true half ball or a shade fuller or thinner than half ball, but a slight differotee in contact materially alters the path of the object ball. In playing this camnon some little allowance for the fuller than half-ball contact should nevertheless be made, and per- haps the best way to do this is to spot exactly the same as for a half-ball stroke, and to use a little running side (right hand side in the diagram) to compensate for the fuller than half- ball contact. The thick intersected line shows a path the white ball may take when the stroke is played as a partial run-through, and the thin intersected line shows how it may be left behind when the cannon is made by a half-ball Or (as may easily happen when playing a half-ball stroke) a somewhat thinner than half-ball stroke.

div.head: WORKHOUSE CHAPLAINCY.
div.p: WORKHOUSE CHAPLAINCY.
The Instruction to Roman Catholics and Nonconformists at Dutton. "A QUESTION OF EQUALITY AND EQUITY."

The most important business under consideration at the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday related to the religious instruction given to the inmates of the house. Mr. A. R. Norman presided and there were also present :—Rev. Father Donlevy, Messrs. C. litoylance, H. Eyes, P. Mounfleld, J. Stokes, J. Whitlow, A. Broome, T. Baxter, H. M. Davies, C. E. Linaker, J. H. Davies, T. Wright, S. Woodward, W. Harrison, G. Pilling, J. L. Jones,E. Bretherton,C. Horton,J. Sprnoe, S. Taylor, J. Douglas, J. Rutter, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, R. Billington, C. E. Linaker, jun., J. Mounfleld, A. G. Guest, T. Cook, T. Riley, and W. R. dePrez (relieving officer), G. F. Ashton (clerk) and W. E. Hough (deputy clerk). The Rev. A. L. Temple, writing from the Paddock, Chatham, said he would have pleasure in accepting the chaplaincy of Dutton Workhouse at a salary of £3O per annum and he would write to the Bishop for his sanction forthwith._ _

there was any necessity for an alteration. He did not object to a Nonconformist minister or a Roman Catholic priest visiting the House. Mr. Woodward seconded the Chairman's proposition. It was just as right for a Nonconformist minister to administer the sacrament to the members of the Church of England as it was for a Church of England clergy- man to administer them to Nonconformists. He was strongly with Mr. Norman in the matter. Any disabili- ties which attached themselves to public bodies and the administration of public affairs should be removed. The Chairman said that while he quite agreed with Mr. Wright that an Anglican clergyman should admin- ister the sacraments to the Church of England inmates, he claimed the same right for Nonconformists. Mr. Hallows said it was hard to see " the ruthless hand sweeping away the old land marks which were dear to them. The Chairman said he had no wish to exclude the Church of England clergymen. He simply claimed equality. Mr. Stokes asked what would be the outcome of the resolution. What was at the bottom of it? Why had they reduced the salary of the chaplain from £4O ? He considered that if anything the chaplain was underpaid. The Chairman said the committee were unanimous in their action and the Board approved it. The only thing that was at the bottom of the resolution was equality for all. Mr. Stokes said he was the oldest ramber of the Board and for many years they had complimented them- selves that the question of religious strife or political animosity had never cropped up. He hoped the same spirit would continue. The Chairman : I disavow all sectarian feeling in the matter at all. I hope everything will go on as smoothly as it has done in the past. Mr. Linaker said the question was a very delicate one. He had every sympathy with Nonconformists and Roman Catholics in their work but he hardly thought the resolution FRS in the right direction. He did not think it was a matter for the Local Government Board, but a question of law. It was a pity the motion had been brought forward, because he feared it would stir up a bit of religious feeling. He did not think it would do any good, and it would be far better to with- draw it. The Chairman declined to withdraw the motion. The Clerk told him the Board would be moving on the right lines by approaching the Local Government Board. Mr. Baxter asked if there might not be strife as to whether a Church of England chaplain or a Noncon- formist should be appointed,if the change were brought about.
One vote being taken, the resolution was defeated 8 voting for it and 17 against.

Messrs. Gamon, Farmer, and Co., solicitors, Chester, forwarded the Bishop's formal consent to the appoint- ment. Mr. Thomas 'Ferran, of Preston Brook, wrote accept- ing the appointment of religious visitor to the Non- conformist inmates of the Workhouse., Be "prayed that Heaven's blessing might rest upon the appoint- ment." _ _ _

The Rev. Hugh Donlevy, St. Edward's, Runcorn wrote : I have to thank your Board for their thought- fulness in offering me some remuneration for my services at Dutton Workhouse. On the other hand, I must say that the offer locks rather paltry and that I have difficulty in making up my mind to accept it, especially as to do so will involve the resignation of my present position as Guardian. I have hopes, how- ever, that the same considerateness which has led the Board to offer me the sum of £5 will, on a reconsidera- tion of the question, induce them to suggest an amount more worthy of my acceptance. In such a contingency it will be a pleasure to me to bow to the decision of my colleagues and to return my sincere thanks for this expression of their sense of justice and goodwill. Mr. Roylance moved that Father Donlevy and Mr. Tarran be paid £lO each per annum, instead of the £5 agreed upon at the last meeting. It was pointed out that such a course could not be taken at that meeting, and Mr. Roylance ',rave notice that he would move the increase a fortLighthence. The Chairman pointed out that in fixing the amount the committee had no idea of putting a value on the re- cipients' services. Father Donlevy had been doing the duties in the past that he would be expected to do in the future,and the Nonconformist inmates had also been attended to. When the vacancy for the chaplaincy arose, the Board thought it right that they should try and re- arrange matters so that some consideration could be given to those who had been working willingly and voluntarily for sometime. It was with that idea that a nominal amount was fixed.

Mr. Linaker thought that as the matter was entirely a new departure its reconsideration might be deferred for a year. It would be well to see how the arrange- ment worked before the Board committed themselves to any further expenditure on salaries. Mr. Jones said he understood Father Donlevy would have to resign from the Board if he received a salary. Mr. Hallows said it was a question of principle and right—whether Father Donlevy thought mote of his £5 than his position on the Board. If he thought of his Catholic friends he would look after them. Mr. Jones: He has done.

Mr: Hallows: And would do in the future. I objec t to giving any more money. Mr. Woodward said the committee had no idea of the amount as a full and sufficient recognition of the services rendered. It was merely an official recognition of the gentlemen named, as visitors to the house. Eventually Mr. Roylance agreed to withdraw the question on the understanding that it was considored twelve months hence.

The Chairman remarked that if Father Donlevy felt he could not accept the position, the Board would be willing to consider his nomination of another instructor to save the necessity of his resigning. The iChairman, in accordance with notice given, moved :—" That the Local Government Board be petitioned to remove the restriction that only Church of England clergymen approved by the Bishops be appointed chaplains o f workhouses and to empower Boards of Guardians to appoint RS chaplains ministers of any denomination. Mr. Norman remarked that he considered the Board ought to have power to appoint anyone whom they considered fit and proper to a chap- laincy. It was perfectly right that the Anglicans should have a paid clergyman, but the Roman Catholics and Nonconformists were entitled to equal consideration. It was simply a matter of justice and equity, for at present instructors like Father Donlevy were only recognized as Workhouse visitors. Mr. Woodward asked if the Board were correct in assuming that they could only appoint a clergyman of the Church of England as chaplain. He believed there was nothing in the Local Government orders to that effect. The only stipulation was that the Bishop of the diocese should give his approval. The Clerk said that while the order did not use the words' Church of England clergyman" the duties of the chaplain were defined, and they included the administration of the Sacraments according to the rites of the Church of England. It stood to reason that a Bishop could only approve the appointment of a mem- ber of his own church.

The Chaiernan : We can only appoint onechaplain. Mr. Wright said he as under the impression that a lonconformist minister could not very well administer le Sacraments in the House.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL

The fortnightly meeting of this Council was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. S. Woodward pre- siding. There were also present :—Messrs. G. Pilling, J. Stokes, J. L. Jones, A. G. Guest, T. Wright, C. E. Linaker, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, C. E. Linaker, jun., J. Mountield, R. Billington, .J. Spruce, T. Baxter, W. Harrison, H. M. Davies, J. H. Davies, J. Rutter, A. G Guest, C. Roylance, H. Eyes, P. Mounfield, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (deputy clerk), J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances), J. Swinton and W. Diggle (surveyors), and Dr. Adams (medical officer of health.) THE SURVEYOR'S EXTRA WORK AT STOCKTON HEATH. The Stockton Heath Parochial Committee submitted a recommendation that Mr. J. Swinton be paid £l5 15s. for extra services in acting as surveyor to the Council in connection with the making of Dundonald Avenue and Kimberley Drive under the provision of the Private Street Works Act.

Mr. Swinton expressed himself disappointed with the grant and hoped it would-receive reconsideration. Mr. Hallows said there had been some misunderstand- ing and on his proposition the matter was referred back to the committee.

HEAVY MOTOR TRAFFIC. The Clerk submitted a copy from the Local Govern- ment Board of the Heavy Motor Car Order of 1904. Accompanying it was a circular letter stating that the recommendations upon which the Order was based aimed at giving effect to the objects of the section by facilitating the development of motor traffic of a heavier character than that allowed by law but subject to the observance of suitable conditions for the protection of the roads against damage and the avoidance of incon- venience to other users of the highway. It was pointed out that whilst only the Councils of Counties and County Boroughs had any duties in regard to the registration of heavy motor cars other Councils were concerned in the provisions of the Order respecting the uses of such cars on highways and bridges. The Clerk said the question affected the Council as the Order gave local authorities power to decide upon what bridges should be used by cars of certain weight. The question was referred to the Parliamentary Com- mittee, the surveyors being instructed to report as to the strength of the various bridges.

div.head: ISOLATION HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE ISOLATION HOSPITAL.

The Chairman reported that the Committee found the building of this hospital was proceeding fairly satisfac- torily. At the last Council meeting the Clerk was instructed to inform the contractors that the date named in the contract had expired, but Messrs. Marshall had pointed out that the Council or their agents had been defaulters, as certain materials and fittings had not been forthcoming when they were required. Mr. Baxter: May I suggest that we get the King to open the hospital? The Chairman: lam sure it will be the Council's pleasure that Mr. Baxter should undertake the duty of asking the King to come. (Laughter and loud "Hear, bears.")

div.head: FINANCIAL.
div.p: FINANCIAL.
_ Mr. Wright presented the financial statement which showed a credit balance of .£1,465 17s. Bd. The pay- ments included several totalling £4lO in connection with the new isolation hospital.

HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. Dr. Adams reported five cases of scarlet fever at Grappenhall. The outbreak of the disease at Weston Point had been followed by four additional cases. He had investigated several chicken pox cases reported from various townships and had satisfied himself that they were not small-pox. No further cases of the latter disease had been reported. One patient bad been dig - charged from the hospital and the only remaining one was ready for discharge.

FAILURES IN ENGL %ND AND WALES.—According to "Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of failures in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, January 6th, was; 165, viz.:—New bankruptcy proceedings published in the London Gazette,lo3; deeds of arrangement registered, 62. The lespective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were: bank- ruptcies, 75 ; deeds of arrangement, 59—total 134 ; being an increase of 31.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENT.

div.head: Welsh Revival.
div.p: The Welsh Revival.

Sir,—Tn your issue of the " Examiner " for December Slat T find on page 17 under the heading "The Free Churches," two paragraphs dealing with the Welsh Revival. In the second paragraph on the subject you draw some attention to the doubtful attitude of the English temperament towards the revival as distin- guished from the more emotional nature of the Celt. Well, sir, I want to say here that English and Welsh are equally impressed. There is absolutely no question of nationality in the wonderful working of the Holy Spirit, many foreigners in the ports of Cardiff having come under its influence equally with the Saxon and Celt. We all know, in these districts, that the Press has been, and is nowa wonderful medium in the spread- ing of the Revival influence. Whole communities have been stirred to their very depths by the reports of meetings in the columns of the local newspapers, and much good has been done. Publichouses are having a very bad time, and in many places the administrators of the law have little or nothing to do. I am a Warrington man, so it may be no matter of surprise that I take much interest in what is going on at "home" as when livingithere. The daily papers here are giving as many as two and three columns to the reports, special correspondents are sent to the different places, and one paper has begun the issue of a Revival edition. We are sure that it will spread all over the country, and I am convinced that it is in your power to bring a great deal of good to the dear old town and other places.—Yours truly,

div.head: E. SPRUCE.
div.p: E. SPRUCE.

Newport, Mon. January Sth 1905. In a further note, Mr. Spruce adds :—" I should say that the presence of the missioners is not at fall neces- sary in the services. The minister or pastor opens the service in the orthodox way and calls on the congrega- tion for prayer. The people are full of the spirit and spontaneous prayer and singing follow, with results the most impressive. The same thing could take place in every place of worship in Warrington as well as here, when the people earnestly wish for the spirit and courageously testify to His loving kindness."

div.head: Mr. Chamberlain and the Rebate on Leather, &c.
div.p: Mr. Chamberlain and the Rebate on Leather, &c.

Sir,—A question was put to Mr. Chamberlain by some Preston manufacturers as to how the following articles which enter into the cost of cotton manufacture would be treated under his proposed scheme—leather, oil, cement, steel, bleach, die stuffs, window glass, and sawn timber. Being interested in the manufacture of one of these articles I looked forward to his answer with a good deal of interest. Mr. Chamberlain left the question to his Tariff Com- mission, but explained that such goods would either be treated as raw material, in which case there would be no tax, so that the manufacturers of these goods, although they had to suffer the disadvantage of the rise in price on the protected articles they used, would get no advantage for their manufacture; if on the other hand they were treated as manufactured articles pro- tected by a duty, he would advocate their being dealt with by a "rebate "as is sometimes the case in foreign countries.

.. _ The rehat,, in foreign conntrres is given when import- ed goods upon which duty has been paid are incorpor- ated in manufactures that are exported, and a rebate is given equivalent to the duty paid upon the goods so incorporated and exported. When this is done the home trade making tile goods in question gets no advan- tage for the manufacturer of the composite article, say cotton and is placed at no disadvantage by buying the foreign products. But the things named, leather, oil, cement, steel, bleach, dye stuffs, window glass, and timber, are not (with the possible exception of dye stuffs) exported with the cotton, but simply go to aid the manufacture. For example cotton manufacturers are the tanner's best customers for leather driving belts and roller covers, but these are not exported. I wish that some of the supporters of Mr. Chamber- lain's scheme could tell us upon what system this rebate could be arranged, and where would we tanners get our share of 6e general plunder, and how would we be recouped for the increased cost in our manufacture consequent upon what I may call the back lash from the protected industries. CHARLES E. PARKER, Penketh, January 13th, 1905.

div.head: BY-ELECTIONS.
div.p: BY-ELECTIONS.

Big Free Trade Victory in Stalybridge. The result of the poll at Stalybridge was declared shortly after ten o'clock on Saturday night as follows : Mr. J. F. Cheetbam (L) 4,029 Mr. Travis Clegg (C) 3,078
„ Majority 951 The results at the three preceding elections were :- 1900. M. White Ridley (C) J. F. Cheethatn (L)

Conservative majority Bl 1895. 1892. Sidebottom (C) Wright (L) -- Con. majority ... 632 Con. majority 337 The result of the poll at Stalybridge as set forth above was declared on Saturday night, and proved more satisfactory to the Liberal Party than they had ventured to hope. From the commencement of hostilities the supporters of the Free Trade candidate were confident of being able to convert the minority of 81 in 1900 into a majority for Mr. Cheetham, but the most sanguine of them, recognising the forces arrayed against them, and the fact that the seat had been held by the Conser- vatives for such a long period, never ventured to pre- dict a majority of close upon a thousand. Despite all attempts to obscure the issue, the victory is one for Free Trade. In the words of the successful candidate, a death-blow has been administered by the electors of Stalybridge to Protection. Mlle End Result—Unionist Majority Largely Reduced.

The poll was declared in the Mile End election on Thursday evening, the figures being The Hon. Harry Lawson (C) 2,138 Mr. B. Straus (L) 2,060 -- Conservative Majority Such was the verdict of the electors in the Mlle End dietrict of London in the election of a Parliamentary representative to fill the vacancy caused by the death of ' Mr. Charrington, Conservative. Great interest was manifested in the contest, in which the Aliens Bill has played no inconsiderable part, the district being largely populated by foreigners princi- pally of the Hebrew persuasion. Voting opened very slowly, but became lively as the day wore on, and the fact that the votes recorded numbered 4,254 out of a total electorate of 5,380 shows how keen has been the canvass.
The following are the figures at the previous elec- tions :- 1900. 1895. Charrington (C) Clark (14 Majority 1892. 1896. Charrington (C) Haysraan (L) Majority

THE IRON TRADE. Birmingham Quarterly Meeting The quarterly meeting of the Midland iron trade was held at Birmingham on Thursday, and brought I together an unusually large attendance of traders from all parts of the country. London and South Wales were especially well represented. The tone of the market was more buoyant than for a long time past, and the prospects for the coming year were regarded with cheer- fulness. Ever where there was apparent an optimism which has not been a very conspicuous feature of recent quarterly meetings, though whether some of the rather extravagant anticipations which were indulged in were justified is open to question. For the moment, at any rate, there is more doing, and prices have an upward tendency. div.head: INFIRMARY BALL.
div.p: THE INFIRMARY BALL.
BRILLIANT FUNCTION.

brilliant function, and one which fully merited the success attending it, was the annual ball in aid of the funds of the Warrington Infirmary and Dispensary which was held at the Lion Hotel on Thursday even- ing. The beautifully decorated assembly room, filled with a fashionable gathering, presented a scene of charming colour and animation, and there probably never was a more enjoyable ball in the course of the long series which has been organized on behalf of the worthy institution. No fewer than ninety Infirmary and Dispensary Balls have, we are told, been held at , the Lion Hotel, and with such an enthusiastic band of workers there does not appear to be the remotest possibility of the effort dying out. This year the arrangements had largely devolved upon the following ladies' committee, under the presidency of Mrs. Pick- mere :—The Mayoress(Hrs. Bolton), Miss Massy, Lady Greenall, Mrs. Monks, Mrs. Airey, Mrs. Monro, Mrs. Armitage, Mrs. J. Charlton Parr, Mrs. George Dakin, Mrs. H. V. Pigot, Mrs. John Fairclough, Mrs. W. P. Rylands. Mrs, Fox, Mrs. John White, Mrs. Henry Greenall, Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Long. The Ball Com- mittee was fortunate in having the help of such an admirable hon. secretary as Mr. W. Peter Rylands who worked indefatigably to ensure the success of the function. To Mr. J. H. J. Hampson, secretary of the Infirmary, credit is alse due for valuable and willing assistance.

The artistic decorations were much admired, flowers and evergreens, flags and drapery of various materials having been pleasingly utilized. Mr. Ralph Johnson was responsible for the work, the following ladies assisting with the floral embellishment :—Mrs. Rylands, Mrs. Hartley, and Mrs. Henry Greenall. Flowers and plants were sent by the Mayor, Lady Greenall, Mrs. Parr, Mrs. Henry G-reenall, and Mrs. Long. Mr. Vetter's well-known band had been engaged and discoursed an excellent selection „f music, the programme including twenty-two dances. The guests numbered about 150, and dancing con- tinned with zost from nine to two o'clock. The following gentlemen had been appointed to act as stewards, and most of them were present and discharged the duties efficiently :—Lieutenant Colonel J. D. Buskton, Lieutenant Colonel J. A. Edelsten, Major R. L. Hartley, the King's (Liverpool Regiment). Major J. D. Fairclough, Captain G. R. Crosfield, Mr. John Coxon, Mr. Henry Greenall, Mr. James Hepherd, Mr. Roger C. Parr, Dr. Reginald Smith, and Mr. W. Peter Rylands. Ths catering was in the capable hands of Mr.J. Lee, the really artistic arrangement of the supper tables being quite a feature.
