div.head: Examiner, Saturday, January 14, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, January 14, 1905.
LOCAL EVENING SCHOOLS.
DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES.

During the week opprtunity has been taken to present the prizes gained by students at the local evening Continuation Schools during the session 19034. On Monday evening the students in attend- ance at the Fairfield and Hamilton-street schools received their awards at the hands of Mr. John Upson, but, owing no doubt to the bitterly cold and showery weather, there was but a small representa- tion of the Education Committee. Mr. A. J. Jolley visited Heathside and Wycliffe schools on Tuesday evening and distributed the prizes in the presence of a large gathering. The distribution at Warrington British school was made on Wednesday evening by the Rev. N. Wilson. The pleasing functions and the interest and enthusiasm displayed served to show ' that the schools are in a healthy state, and that the facilities for continuing the education received in the Iprimary schools are fully appreciated.

- . FAIRFIELD SCHOOL. The opening distribution took place on Sunday evenidg at this school the superintendent of which is Mrs. S. I. Price. The Rev. N. Wilson presided, and there were present in addition, to the students, Mr, John Upson Mr. J. Moore, Murray(director of education), and Mr. E. Haigh Mr. UPSON said it afforded him very great pleasure on behalf of the committee to distribute the prizes to those who had earned them during the past session. He , was somewhat sorry that the number of prizes was not greater and he could only hope that the present session would produce a very ranch larger number of those who were entitled to awards. He would remind the students that they did not come there for the purpose of winning prizes. None of them, he supposed, lived their lives for the sake of the prizes that were to be had. They heard a great deal nowadays about virtue being its own reward. So far as the Education Committee and the scholars of that school were concerted, they were not content to let virtue be its own reward. They attended those classes to fit themselves for the life that lay before them. The primary object of all of them was to improve their minds, to educate the powers which had been given to them, so that they might be enabled to do the work which lay before them better than they otherwise would do. That being so, the committee desired to reward those who, by their industry and attendance at the classes, had made marked progress, and it was with that intention that the prises had been given. He sincerely hoped that those who were now in attendance at the classes would attend so regularly and do their work so well that the , committee would have the happy privilege of distribut- ing every much larger number of prizes at the end of the session. (Applause.) The prizes and certificates were then distributed to the following pupils:-- Annie Ball,4certificates,domestic economy and needle- work; Elizabeth Bridge, 1 certificate in needlework; Lily Brown 1 certificate in domestic economy; Fanny Clarke, 1 certificate in needlework; Gertrude Clayton, 1 certificate in needlework; Alice Coupe, 1 certificate in needlework; Margaret Fearnehough, 1 certificate in domestic economy; Mary Ann Fearnehough, 1 certifi- cate in needlework; Mary Griffiths, 1 certificate in domestic economy; Elizabeth Molyneaux, 1 certificate in needlework; Margaret Newton, 1 certificate in needle- work; Ada Smith, 1 certificate in domestic economy ; Alice A. Wilkinson, 1 certificate in needlework; Lizzie Ball, scholarship certificate and certificate in needle- work: Emily Jones' scholarship certificate and certifi- cates in needlework and domestic economy; Gertrude Jones, scholarship certificate and certificate in needle- work ; Maggie Kelly. scholarship certificate ; Nellie Mellor, scholarship certificate and certificate in domestic economy ; Amy Profitt, scholarship certificate ; Jane Sankey, scholarship certificate and certificate in needlework ; Clara Sanson, scholarship certificate : Nellie Shaw, scholarship certificate and certificate in domestic economy; Margaret Malone, certificate in needlework' and three books; Gertrude Burgess,2 books: Nellie Clarke, 2 books ; Bertha Hackwell, 2 books ; Amy Proffitt, 2 books. The Rev. FATHER WiLsox' on behalf of the scholars and committee, thanked Mr. Upson for distributing the awards, expressing regret that more members of the committee had not attended the function. HAMILTON STREET.

This school was visited on Monday evening, and occasion was also taken to distribute the prizes gained by the students of the Warrington Parochial Evening School which was discontinued at the end of thei last session. Mr. F. H. Longshaw is the superintendent of Hamilton-street school while Mr. Charles Hale discharges similar duties at the National school. The gathering was again presided over by the Rev. N. Wilson and Mr. J. Upson presented the prizes and certificates. The visitors examined with considerabie interest specimens of recreative drawing which had been done by the students during the session and reflected great credit upon them and upon thls staff. In the course of an interesting address, Mr. UPSON congratulated Mr. Longshaw and his staff upon the success which had attended the work of the session,the flourishing condition of the school as shown by its numbers, and the work which had been done by the students as evidenced by the results of the examinations. He noticed that a fair proportion of the students had gained certificates entitling them to entrance at the Technical School or certifying that they had passed the examination of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Institutes. Prizes also were awarded to the students for the work they had done and for the regularity of their attendance. Ifelwould like to impress upon his hearers the value of education as such; first of all to themselves, and then to the community of which they formed a part. If there was one thing certain to-day above all other things, it was that education was the one thing that paid. They saw in their daily lives that there were men hanging about our street corners unemployed or irregularly employed, and there were men in works who never made any progress, who were workmen at the bezinning and workmen at the end, simply because they had not trained their mental powers. They might have manual dexterity but the absence of training of the mincilkept them in the same position all their lives. By attending evening classes the lads showed that they had an ambition and the very laudable desire to get on in the world. They must remember that continuation school work was but a step in their educa- tion. They completed their primary education at the elementary school and they came to the evening classes to continue their instruction. Unfortunately he was afraid there were many students who had to go back and learn again what they had for- gotten in the interval which had elapsed between leav- ing the primary school and going to the continuation classes. The object of the evening schools was to enable them so to progress in knowledge that finally they might enter the technical school where the training was of a higher nature. The students at Hamilton-street had done splendid work in the past. They were doing good work now. They must not be satisfied, but on the contrary, be discontented with their own attainments, and be determined that they would educate and train the faculties of their minds to their very furthest extent. They must hear in mind that no one lived to himself but formed one of a great community which was bene- fitted or suffered according to the ability, knowledge and power of the individuals who formed it. That being so, there was a social obligation resting upon every student of those schools. He ought to consider that it was his bounden duty to train his faculties not only for himself, but for his fellows, and for the benefit of society. Professor Sadler told them some months ago in Warrington, that the object of all secondary and higher training was that the students who were par- ticipating in that training should become better able to render social service. In conclusion Mr. Upson asked the students so to train themselves that they would be able to discharge satisfactorily to themselves and to the other members of society the work which fell to them. (Applause). The following is a list of those who received prizes and certificates :

HAMILTON STREET :—Lewis Barton, Simeon Barton John Bennett, Harry Boscow, James Darbyshire, Alfred Evans, Percy Gardner, James Garnett, William Grundy , (of Brick street), Charles Logan,Stanley Morris,George Rushton. James Wilson, scholarship certificates ; Joseph Carey, 2 books ; William Delooze, 1 book ; John Grundy,l book; William Grundy, (of Lairs Street), 2 books ; John Heesom,.2 books; Btanley Houghton, 1 book; Philip Jones,l book; Joseph Mc Govran,l. book; William Bothwell, 1 book ; Thomas Swindells, 1 book ; John Willett, I book. WARRINGTON PAROCHIAL :—George Dutton Taker, and John Taylor, certificates in elementary arithmetic ; Charles H. Baldry, scholarship certificate and certificate in commercial correspondence and handwriting, William Hilson, scholarship certificate ; Harold Richardson, scholarship certificate, and certificate in elementary arithmetic ; John Robinson, scholarship certificate ; William H. Bate, 1 book ; John Gibbs, 1 book ; Stanley Gleave, 1 book ; James Heywood, 1 book ; Albert Richardson, 1 book ; Tom E. Taker, 2 books : William Warburton, 1 book ; Mozart Wilcock, 1 book.

div.head: HEATHSIDE.
div.p: HEATHSIDE.

Great enthusiasm characterised the proceedings at the prize distribution to the students at this school on Tuesday evening. The Rev. W. Bracecamp presided and was supported by the Rev. Father Wilson. Coun- cillor J. Fulton Smith, Messrs. A. J. Jolley (who pre- sented the prizes and certificates) Thomas May, James H. Smethurst, J. Moore Murray (director of education), Ernest Haigh (education office), and the following members of the evening school staff :—Messrs. T. Edden (Principal), Fred J. Emson, G. Newburn, J. Holt. C. George. ad A. Malcolm. The Rev. NV. Bracecrimp said the school had always been noted as a successful one,long before the Education Committee was thought about. The managers had tried to encourage boys to attend it, and he was glad to see that the education authority were interesting themselves I in evening schools because it was of the utmost impor- tance that their young friends should be enabled to keep up their education. After they left school there was a great danger of neglecting it and if they did they would

be left in the background. It was the lad who educated himself or allowed himself to be educated, who would make his mark in the world. (Applause). Mr. JOLLEY, in the course of an interesting address, said Mr. Bracecamp had spoken very fittingly about the necessity for every one of them striving to complete his own education. That was absolutely true and a vital matter for all of them if they took it in its right sense—meaning by education, not merely grinding away at bread and butter subjects but in a much fuller sense than that. Some at least of them knew and realized fairly that education only ceased with life for anyone worthy of the name of a man. A fellow who thought his education was finished was only a fool, however old he might be, or however clever he might think he was. The younger scholars there had a magnificent opportunity of im- proving their position from a money point of view and a still better opportunity of widening their intelligence increasing their knowledge, and enabling them to live lives happier for themselves and more useful to their fellows. Many of them knew from what little history they might have learnt in the day schools that in many ways during the last century we in England had made very great progress in civilization and in the general comfort of the people. They hadheard a great deal about bad trade. There were many people feeling the pinch very acutely, and throughout the country there was no doubt a great deal of misery, suffering and distress. But they also knew, if their resoling of history had been of use to them, that considerable progress had been made, and that the proportion of poverty and distress was less than it was before, and there were better houses for the people to live in, better clothes to wear, better food to .at, and that there had been an improvement in the standard of living. (Applause.) But what they parti- cularly wanted to see was not merely the raising of the standard of living but of the standard of life. Money was a very good thing in its way, but it was neither the chief nor the best thing It was not money, however much some of them,might get, that made life worth living altogether. In conclu- sion Mr. Jolley said the evening classes in that building were carried on formerly by the voluntary school managers, but last winter and this winter they had been carried on by the town authorities, and he hoped that the change of responsibility would lead to further successes. (Applause.) Because the management had changed no one who attended the school must lose sight of the spirit of connection with Heathside School that had existed with them, and in many cases with their fathers. Let everyone present feel a pride that he had received a portion of his training in the day or evening school in that building. As some of the greatest men in the country felt a pride in looking back at their old schools or universities, let those going through that school feel a pride in it, and do their best, not only immediately,but in after years, to help along its success. (Applause.) Mr. Jolley then distributed the awards. The following won certificates as stated :—John Battersby, scholarship and arithmetic; Hubert Bloor, scholarship and shorthand ; Charles Bradshaw, scholar- ship'; Joseph Bradshaw, shorthand; Henry Cheney scholarshin, commercial correspondence and hand-, writing; Stanley Ice, scholarship; Sydney rhomas Ince, commercial correspondence and handwriting ; Harry James, scholarship: John Johnson, scholarship ; Arthur Jolley, scholarship; James E. Marshall, , scholarship and arithmetic ; Charles McDonald, arithmetic ; James Oxley, scholarship; Arthur S. Percival, scholarship, commercial correspondence and handwriting; Thomas Smith, scholarship; Christopher Vose, scholarship; Sydney Wood, scholarship; and , Henry W. B. Wright, scholarship, commercial corres- pondence and handwriting. Books--Winners of two : Arthur Drinkwater, Joseph Glover, James Corean, James Gleave, Wm. A. Hopkinson, Thomas Hardman, Harry Head, Samuel Holt, John Johnson, Herbert uightfoot, Ed. Lloyd, A. W. Long, A. Martin, Chas. Marklove, James Mather, Win. Morgan, John W. Riley, W. Robinson, H. Shaw, Joseph Smith, John Wood, Wm. Ashbrook, Fred Brobbin, Joseph Chatterton and Thomas Cookson. Winners of one book: Geo. Edwardes, John W. Holden, Benjamin James, James Seacombe, Horace Smith, John Tolberg, Walter Wilkes, Arthur E. Bellian and Harry Broadhurst. The CHAIRMAN eulogised the services of the super- intendent and staff which contributed so largely to the success of the classes. Mr. EDDEN proposed a cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Jolley for distributing the prizes. Mr. 3 olley, he said, was always ready. to do what he could for Heath Side and they might in a way look upon him as being the property of Heath Side. (Applause). The Rev. Father WILSON seconded the motion, and said he was very glad to hear Mr. Jolley remind them that they must not look altogether upon education from the pecuniary point of view, but also look to the moral and ethical side. There had been a great rage for education and it was looked upon largely with the view of its monetary value in life, but that point of view might be somewhat overworked. Students should be reminded that that was not the chief and most import- ant side of education. Its power to improve moral conditions and the development of character should be emphasised. (Applause). Mr. SMETHURST seconded the motion. The number of prizes they had seen distributed that night showed that Heath Side school was able to give teaching equal to that of any other school or institute in the town, and as one of the managers of the school he earnestly hoped that the classes would go on and flourish. (Applause). Mr. MAY observed that nobody was more interested in education in Warrington than Mr. Jolley, and he was pleased to have an opportunity of according some thanks to him.

The motion was then carried with acclamation. In reply Mr. JOLLEY said he had been pleased to per- form his duty that night. He had noticed with pleasure also, the class of books which many of the prize winners had selected, some of the volumes being the best in the English language. He hoped,they would cultivate a taste for good literature, as they wbuld find that it not only gave them great pleasure in after years, but would in an unconscious sort of way influence their lives for good and help them to develop their minds and characters instead of working simply from the £s. d. point of view. (Applause). The CHAIRMAN was thanked on the proposition of Councillor Fulton Smith seconded by Mr. May. The students also gave cheers for Mr. Murray.

div.head: WYCLIFFE SCHOOL.
div.p: WYCLIFFE SCHOOL.

The scholars at Wycliffe (girls) school, Bewsey- street, also received their prizes on Tuesday evening. The Rev. John Yonge presided, and there were also present, the Rev. Father Whittle, Councillog. Fulton Smith, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, T. 31 IT, J. KJ Murray, Miss Clay,and Miss James (superintendent and assistant superintendent). The CHAIRMAN said they were met that evening, so ' far as Wycliff. , was concerned, for a new function, that was to distribute scholarship certificates and prizes to those who had attended the continuation school there. Mr. Yonge then proceeded humorously to criticise some of the presents chosen by the young ladies, and thought that they had shown very good taste in their selec- tions. He afterwards called upon Mr. A. J. Jolley to make the presentations. Mr. JoutEY said the Education Committee desired that all the classes in the various schools of the town should be successful and success would depend very largely upon the scholars who attended the schools. The committee also desired that there should be thoroughly established, a school spirit, each scholar taking a pride in the school which he or she attended. If that spirit were developed, they would see even greater success. He hoped they would also do their utmost to attend regularly. He was sure they would be materially helping their chief teacher, Miss Clay, and benefitting themselves if they did so. He would have been glad if some of the students had chosen books for their prizes. There was a lot of money wasted at the present time in cheap and useless books, and if the money spent in ffseless serials and such ways were spent on good works, they would soon have a respectable library of thoroughly good books. The aim of the evening classes was not merely to teach them to set more remunerative employment in after years, but It was to help them to make their lives fuller and better and to raise the standard of life all round. For half a century they had been raising the standard of living, and the material comfort of people had been increased. There was now less poverty, disease aid suffering than there was formerly. They now wanted to raise the standard of life. He hoped next year a number present would receive good books which they would treasure not merely for their money value but for tke value of their contents and the influence they would exert on themselves, and indirectly on others. The prizes were then distributed as follows :—Lucy Bennett, Martha Irons, Ethel Long, Mary E. Smith, Catherine Whitfield, scholarship certificates ; Nellie Houghton, case of scissors; Cissie Jones. work-box with fittings, needles, cotton, etc. ; Frances E. Kendrick, work-box (wood) silk-lined, Sarah A. Leicester and Sarah Wright, umbrellas. Father WiLso.N proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Mr. Jolley, and said Mr. Jolley had made some very helpful remarks, and he would like to endorse what he had said with reference to the value of good books. They could get almost a library of classics at the present time at a very moderate sum. Councillor FULTON Sminf'seconded and remarked that I with all deference to Mr. Jolley he rather approved of the form the prizes had taken that night. In fact he thought that if boys were taught something of knitting and darning it would get them out of many difficulties in after life. (Laughter.) He was sure dm teachers must be gratified that so many of the students had gained prizes, as it was the best reward they could get to see that their efforts had been appreciated and suc- cessful. It WM no easy task to teach all day and resume the work in the evening. His sympathies went out towards the teacher, whose profession was a very arduous one. (Hear, hear, and applause). The motion was heartily carried, and the CHAIRMAN and Mr. JOLLY returned thanks, Mr. Yonge remarking that the choice of prizes by the students had struck him as being very practical and womanly'.

WARRINGTON BRITISH. Evidence of the good work done by this school during last session was afforded by the large number of prizes and certificates distributed to the students by the Rev. Father Wilson on Wednesday evening. There was a larze attendance, Mr. A. .1. Jolley presiding. in addition to the Rev. Father Wilson there were present, the Rev. John Yonge, Mr. J. Upson, Mr. .J. Moore Murray, Mr. E. Haigh, and the following members of
the stall—Mr. S. W. Jeffery (superintendent), Mr. A. Knowles, Mr. W. H. Cragg, Miss Pickavance, Miss Cook, and Miss E. Arnold.

Addressing the students, the Rev. Father WILSON said there was a great virtue in the word continuation in connection with those schools. The work done by them should not be mere treadmill work and a repetition of what had already been taught in the elementary school,but it should be a continuation, leading on to further and higher stages of education. He was pleased to notice that the attend- ance during last session was most satisfactory and he hoped the present students would emulate that example, as he understood there had been a slight falling off in the present session. He would ask them to back up the devoted efforts of their superintendent and staff, for he was sure they deserved at least that much on the students' part. The rev, gentleman proceeded to speak of the advantages of education not from the commercial , or pecuniary point of view, but as a means of con- tributing to each one's happiness and pleasure in life, a means of making labour instead of a curse and penalty a blessing andan advantage. There were some people who had no mental or intelligent interest in life at all, and we were usually told that that was because they were so bowed-down with toil and worn out. There life, of course, was a life, more properly speaking, of drudgery. Others had a proportion of mental and intelligent interest, but often-times it was divorced from their daily labour. In his opinion their mental interest should not be separated and divorced, but rather wedded to their daily employment. Cer- tainly it should not be confined to that, but it should chiefly centre upon their avocation. Some people simply used the interest to which he had referred as a recreation, a respite from labour and a solace ; but it ought really to be brought to bea on their ordinary work. That, he took it, was the aim and object of the continued education offered to them at that 'school, as a stepping stone to the technical classes where the instruction was more praztical and final. Education ought to enable them to bring mind and muscle together. People asked why it was that work was so often soul-destroying, and fatal to mental energy. and seemed to act as a drug and poison on the minds of many. He did not think the reason was because it was work, or even hard work or hardship, but it was accoun- ted for by the absence of a mental and intelligent interest which made the difference between labour, properly so-called, and drudgery. Despite modern invention's and machinery, there was very little work that was not capable of being invested with some really intelligent interest, and he would urge his hearers to look upon it in that light. The awards were then distributed as follows:—Blanche Ashbrooke: certificate in cookery; Margaret Astley, certificate in arithmetic; Elizabeth Cartwrigh t,certificate in cookery ; Sarah Cox, certificate in cookery ; William Dennett, certificate in arithmetic ; Ruth Greenwood certificate incookery ; Arthur Milne, John Paterson, John Peers,William H. Rench,Alfred Rogers, and Harold Sisson,certificates in arithmetic; Lily]Spink, certificate in cookery ; Albert Turton, certificate in arithmetic ; Ada Gertrude Williams, certificate in cookery; William Banks, Stanley Bingham, Edward Bowers' Joseph Cragg, Alfred E. Downing, Maggie Fo3ter, Kate Grounds, Albert C. Hodgson, and Annie Holden' scholarship cer- tificate and certificate in arithmetic ; Albert Corradine. scholarship certificate ; Annie llnnstone 2 certificates in arithmetic and cookery ; Ada Monks, 3 certificates in cookery, principles of cookery, and arithmetic • Ethel Platt, scholarship certificate ; Edith Reddish', certificates in arithmetic and dressmaking; Harry Warburton, John Warburton, William Webb and Joseph Welding, scholarship certificate and certificate in arithmetic; Winifred Wood and Eva Woolley, 2 certificates in shorthand and arithmetic; Alfred R. Baines, and Harriett Barnett, certificate in arithmetic and 1 book; Lily Barton, 3 certificates in cookery, principles of cookery and arithmetic. also 1 book; Eva Bowcock, 1 book; Elizabeth A. Dodd, certificate in cookery, and I book; Margaret Gatley, 1 book; Ann Gleave, and Hetty Gleave, certificate in cookery, and 1 book; Lily Griffiths, 1 book; Donald J. Jackson, 2 books; Francis H. Jinks, certificate in arithmetic, and 1 book; Amelia Johnson' certificate in cookery, and 2 books; Arthur Jones (Mill-lane), 1 book; Catherine Kilgallon, certificate in cookery, and 2 books; Elizabeth Lee, 1 book; Clara Mason, 1 book; Margaret Moran, certifi- cate in cookery. and 1 book; Elsie Pepper 1 book; Harry Pitchford, and Fred Platt, certificate in arithmetic, and 1 book; James Sudell, 1 book; Alice Taylor, 2 books; Elsie Throssell, 2 books; George Wakefield, 1 book; Maggie Warburton, certificate in cookery and 2 books: John Waywell, certificate in arithmetic and 1 book; Joseph Whitmore, 1 book; Fred Clare, 1 book. . .

Book prizes were given by the Superintendent to Harold Brandwood, Nellie Thomasson, Ada Williams, and Elizabeth Cartwright. In proposing a vote of thanks to Father Wilson, Mr. JEFFRRY said he hoped the rev, gentleman's remarks would find a resting place in the minds of the students. They could not hope to put old heads on young shoulders—were it possible it would not, perhaps, be desirable—but he hoped all would remember that there was a to-morrow as well as a to-day, and that when the days of youth werelput aside they had something much more earnest and realistic to think of. The fact that this year the prizes had not been granted for attendance alone, stamped the recipients with a certain hall mark of efficiency. Mr.l.TesoN seconded and said Father Wilson had taken an intense interest in the work of the continuation schools. The vote was accorded with enthusiasm.

On the motion of the Rev. JOHN YONOE, seconded by the Rev. FATHER WILSON, Mr. Jolley was thanked for presiding. In acknowledging the compliment, Mr. JOLLEY asked the students to take to heart the words of Father Wilson, as coming from one who had taken an honour- able and active part in public life. Mr. LONOSITANY expressed the gratitude of the students to the representatives of the Education Com- mittee for attending. lie sincerely hoped Mr. Upson's excellent advice would be acted upon. He spoke from experience as a headmaster of a day school, and knew the advantages obtained by those who continued their education immediately on leaving the day school. The Rev. Father WILSON briefly acknowledged the compliment.

div.head: ALLEGED NEGLIGENT MOTORING. £5O Damages Claimed at Warrington.
div.p: ALLEGED NEGLIGENT MOTORING. £5O Damages Claimed at Warrington.

A case of interest to motorists was commenced at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C. James Shephard, a well-known horse dealer, of Lymm, sued Norman Holinger, Moss Sidefor damages in respect of injuries alleged to have been done to himself, his pony and trap in consequent of the negligent driving of a motor cycle by the defendant at Lymm on September 4th—Mr. A. Browne, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. F. Cuthbert Smith, barristor, (instructed by Messrs. W. D. Jeans and Son) defended. Plaintiff, said Mr. Browne, alleged that he was driv- ing slowly along Higher-lane, Lymm, when without any warning defendant passed on his motor cycle before the pony's head, causing the animal to plunge wildly. Plaintiff was thrown to the ground, the trap was smashed, and 'the pony was injured. Defendant, it was further alleged, drove on for 150 yards before he was stopped by some boys who shouted that they thought Mr. Shephard was killed. Plaintiff had been practically helpless, said Mr. Browne, ever since the accident and the consequent loss in business had been very serious. Originally Mr. Shephard did not claim any personal damages, but said he would be satisfied if defendant would pay him for the injury to the horse, trap and harness and the loss of his time resulting from the accident. Defendant would not agree to that. The amount now sued for was £5O which did not adequately represent the damages to which plaintiff contended he was entitled, but in a case I, of that kind his Honour was precluded from adjudicat- ing on a claim above £5O. Plaintiff, in his evidence, said he had no warning whatever of the motor cycle's approach. Defendant caught the pony's head with his elbow as he passed. The pony made a jump and got one of its legs over the shaft. He tried to pull the animal up but it went head over heels, and throw witness four or five yards forward on the road. After the accident he asked defendant why he didn't give an alarm and defendant said "I must own to the truth. I didn't."

Dr. De Jong said he examined the plaintiff a few days after the accident, when he complained of pains in the head and hip, and dizziness. Witness was still attend- ing him, and had recommended rest and quietness. He was suffering from a shock to the nervous system. At this stage the hearing was adjourned.

div.head: Farm Fire Near Warrington.
div.p: The Farm Fire Near Warrington.

It was not until 2.30 on Saturday morning that the Warrington Fire Brigade returned to town after a trying experience during the severe gale which raged throughout the night. The fire to which they were summoned at 7.30 on Friday ovening was at the farm of Mr. Joseph Wilkinson, Newton-by-Daresbury, about five miles from Warrington. The men turned out with the engine "Major," Deputy-Superintendent Turner being in charge, and on reaching the farm found that a Dutch barn filled with produce, clover, hay, baled straw, and implements was ablaze. The structure was of wood with a tarred-felt roof which I had already fallen in. Fanned by the strong wind the flames spread with great rapidity, and so far were the ember carried that at one time fears were enter- tained for an adjoining farm. Two powerful jets were got to work from a pit and in a few hours the fire was under control. The barn and its contents were destroyed, the damage which 'is covered by insurance, being estimated at £350. The farm is the property of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. The North- wich. Fire Brigade turned out and rendered assistance in subduing the outbreak.

To-day Stockton Heath will play Latchford Ist and 2nd, when the following teams will represent Stockton Heath :—First (at Grappeuhall-road.) R. G. Pierpoint,. goal; E. Pierpoint and E. E. Woods, backs; L. Fair- dough, Eric Fairclough and J. Richardson. halves; R. Fairclough, W. Richardson, R. Pierpoint, S. Baxter, and C. H. B^nd. Bully-off 2.30. Referee, N. W. Bellamy, Esq.—lt will be noticed that Eric Fairclough again takes up his position at centre-half, after being absent from the team for a month.

Warrington have a wonderful opportunity from now to the end of the season, and if they played up man- fully the League Championship would by no means be out of reach. There are only two out of the remaining fifteen matches which Warrington ought not to be confident of winning. These are Bradford and Wigan away, and neither is hopeless. The balk of the other matches are at Wilderspool, where success should always be assured, and the away fixtures are with clubs considerably below Warrington in the League table. Of course, to expect Warrington to win prac- tically all the matches in the second half of the season is a very tall order, and not for one moment do I imagine that they will accomplish the feat. Still the fact remains that if the available players set themselves out to do so they are capable of it. At the very least they ought to make such headway during the next 11 four months as will land them in the first flight.

Second (at Latchford). P. G. Kertlan'd, goal ; P. B. Hawtin and J. Oliffe, backs ; A. Hodgkinson, captain ; H. Smith and J. Oliffe, hales; D. Skelton. W. Linnet, Longdin, C. R. Hartley and A. Ferguson, forwards. Bully-off 2.30.
The first eleven is composed of the same players, who beat Latchford 3-0 earlier in the season, so that on form Stockton Heath ought to add another to their long list of victories.
The second will be minus three of their regular eleven and may find Latchford second string too good for them.

Warrington's superiority at Halifax was some wha remarkable, and if all the chances had been taken the total would easily have been 20 points instead of 10 points. Isherwood did not reach the ground until 25 minutes after the commencement of the game,but during the whole of that time Warrington were masters of the situation. In fact they got poasession of the ball oftener when a man short than before: Halifax had Ithe same forwards who won the cup, and yet War. rrington beat them with ridiculous ease. The rain, which was pretty persistent, spoiled the open play somewhat, but the Warrington backs likewise rendered a good account of themselves. Kenyon again showed improved form, and once ran right round the posts, only to be recalled for stepping in touch, while his tackling was most effective. The best man on the side was, as usual. Hockenhall, who played fine football throughout, Di Davies giving him excellent support. Brooks and Isherwood also did well, but Short seemed to lack the required physique for his position.

The Latchford first team will be : Goal, J. Wilkin- son ; backs, J. Conway, R. Hallows ; half-backs, H. Rathbone, ,T. B. Wilkinson, W. Knight ; forwards. A. Al b inson. E. Cliffe, W. H. Banks, J. Pearson, W. Spensley; referee, Mr. T. Wicks. . _ _

Latchford 2ndl team: Goal ;W. Unsworth ; full- backs, C. Hale, T. Young; half-backs, J. Rathbone, W. B. Cobb, T. Dixon; forwards, J. Callon, R. Jones, D. Knight, W. B. Smith and E. Pickles. Referee, Mr. J. Unsworth. Bully off 2-45.

Some'of last week's matches, played on ground of first named in all cases. Latchford 4, Bankfleld 3. Timperley 1, Stockton Heath 1. South Manchester 2, Sale 0. Cheshire 5 Yorkshire 0. Chester 2, New Brighton Won:ln—.,l. Stockton Heath 2nd 0, .laki 1.

There were no important changes in the position of the leading clubs as the result of Saturday's matches. Oldham and Bradford each had fairly easy games and won comfortably, while Broughton Rangers improved their position at the expense of Swinton. Bradford simply made 'rings round Widnes, Dechan running in no less than six tries. This is, I believe, a record for the Northern Union and has only been equalled by Bevan of Swinton who once crossed the 'Morecambe line six times in a League match. Another notable feat on Saturday was Runcorn's decisive win over Batley. The latter are hopelessly at the bottom, and gallantly as the Linnets are struggling with fate I can hardly imagine them getting out of the mire. Wakefield, however, are in a very tight corner and there is a chance that Runcoin may just beat them on the post.

Warrington are still in difficulties owing to the number of men incapacitated. Dickenson and Harris are both crocked at the knee and are not expected to be of much use for some time. Fish still has his nose plastered, but is fit for play. What he requires is a permit, and it is to be hoped the League Com- mittee will be in a more lenient frame of mind this week than, last. Bob Bate's broken finger is almost sound again, and another week should see him on the list once more.

Warrington have a popular annual fixture down for to-day. The Hull men always play good football and are cordially welcomed at Wilderspool. Just now they are playing strongly, as witness the crush- ing defeat of Salford at the third port last Saturday. Warrington, especially if Fish's permit is again refused, will have to strain every nerve to win, but they ought to manage all right. Considerable interest is felt in the first appearanc. at Warrington of Freear, Hull's Irish International three-quarter, who has already made a reputation fer himself in Northern Union football. Good judges say he is the only wing man in the Union who approaches Fish's style and ability.

The Warrington team is selected as follows: —Hallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Brooks and Kenyon, threequarters; Hockenhall and D. Dav,ies, half-hacks; Boardman, Preston, Shugars, Thomas, Belton, Jolley, Harmer, and VT. Swift, forwards.

Hull will probably clay: —Taylor, back; Freear, Goodfellow, Cook and Jenkins, threequarter-backs ; Hall and Salt, half-backs; Ritson, Harrison, Langhorn, Wade, Hutton, G-. Lewis, J. Lewis, and Carroll, forwards.

The Warrington men will probably not forget that they owe Hull a thrashing. If two balls had been in use at Hull Warrington would have won there, but the Efull men got ahead, and punched the. only ball out of the ground at every opportunity, thus wasting very valuable time. This is hardly sportsmanlike but it is one way of obtaining League points. The • e will be a plentiful supply of footballs at Wilderspool to-day.

The "A " team had an easy practice gallop with Salford St. Barts' last Saturday, Knight kicking three goals, and Berry running in three tries. The latter is improving in his pace and knowledge of the game, but he has not yet learnt the art of" nursing " his wing man. On Saturday it probably paid him to go on, as both wings were like milk and water—very weak! The tall youth has a good deal of promise in him. A new Welsh threequarter was given a trial at centre also, but beyond his remarkable likeness to J. Cross, the old-time Warrington centre, he did not startle anybody. Like most Welsh ,backs, he could handle the ball well, but he had little speed or clever- ness in his legs. Probably the last has been seen of him.

Hockey. The Stockton Heath first eleven played a draw with Timperley at Timperley, but on the days' play the visitors were decidedly the better side, and with a little luck might easily have been victors by three or four goals to none. In the first half S. Baxter hit the up I right with a fast ground shot, while later R. Pierpoint sent in a terrific shot which the home goal keeper just managed to keep out. The score at half-time was 1-0 in favour of Stockton Heath, W. Richardson being the scorer.

The second half was more evenly contested, both sides doing an even amount of attocking. Close on time the Timperley outside right, who was waiting in an off-side position, received the ball, and made the scores level, the referee allowing the goal.

The home side were certainly lucky to make a draw, and this speaks well for Stockton Heath seeing that Timperley this season have beaten such clubs as Bowdon Northern' Huyton, and Brooklands. For Stockton Heath J. Richardson and L. Fairclough at half were very good, while E. Pierpoint and E. E. Woods played a sound game. The Stockton Heath forwards were very effective at times, and with luck more goals might have been added.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

Sr. MARY'S GUILD.—The annual tea meeting in connection with St. Mary's Mission Women's Guild, was held in the Infant's schoolroom on Thursday night. The members turned up in strong force, and for sometime the waiters were kept busily employed attending to their wants. A committee of ladies consisting of Mesdames Aitkin, Owen, White and the Misses Tinsley, and Bolton were responsible, with the Vicar, for arrange- ments. After tea a very enjoyable concert was held,and one feature was that only local artistes were,present and the fact that they kept the audience interested from start te finish was evidence of their ability as entertainers. The singers were Miss A Daunt, who charmed the audience with her two songs ; Miss Annie Summerfield and Miss Belle Davies, acquitted themselves very creditably, and Mr. A. Goulden and Dr. Batchan, scored success. Mr. W. H. Ireland's singing was well received.A banjo and piano duett was also given by Mrs. White and Miss M.White,and an instrumental trio,(two violins and piano), by Misses Jeans, Jones and White. Mr. James Ray also attended with his fine gramophone, and gave interesting selections at intervals. The humorous element was in the hands of Messrs. Harry Mainley and E. Davies, and their various efforts were much appreci- ated. Mr. J. B. Aitken also addressed the meeting, and delighted the audience with an interesting recital of Indian folk lore. Rev. J. R. Jones presided, and Miss White officiated as accompanist. OLD FOLKS' TREAT.—The annual gathering engineered by the Penketh and Sankey District Old Folks' Treat and Relief Committee, took place last Friday, the Wesleyan schoolroom being the scene of the operations. The room was profusely decorated with flags, &c., and its bright and attractive appearance was favourably commented upon. The invited guests were to arrive at 6.30, and as the time approached, the road to the school presented an animated appearance as the old folks wended their way to the long looked-for treat. The good work of the committee can be judged from the fact that 81 persons sat down to *ea, and 31 were unable to be present through illness and other causes. During the year, also, deserving cases brought to the notice of the committee, are investigated, and if found worthy, help is given where required. This of course could not be carried on without the co-operation of subscribers, and the thanks of all are due to those who give so readily to bring a little sunshine into the lives of these people in their declining years. The committee also, are worthy of the greatest praise for their self- denying efforts, to make each treat better than its pre- decessor. We may add that this treat was first commenced in 1897, and has been held annually since. The arrival of the 'bus, provided for the Sankey con- tingent, completed the party, who at once sat down to a substantial tea, which had been tastefully prepared by a committee of ladies. Good things there were in abundance, and the old folks showed their appreciation of the fare, in unmistakable manner. After grace, the party removed to the large room, where a splendid entertainment was provided. Seldom has a concert gone off with the vim and enjoyment that characterized the proceedings of this particular ftwation, both artistes and audience being in splendid sympathy. The chair was taken by Mr. George Thompson president of the committee, and a well-known worker for the public good. The accompanist was Mr. T. Taylor, and he opened the proceedings with a lively march " Under the double eagle." Mr. E.Pownall's two songs, " Durable Dum Deary " and "The old brigade,"were well rendered,and the latter song seemed to bring back to the minds of the sprinkling of old army veterans in the company, the days of yore. Miss Jones gave a brilliantly executed violin solo, "Welsh Airs," with much taste. Mr. W. H. Ireland was in line voice, and his renderings of "Mary of Argyle," and Sally in our alley," delighted his hearers so that they insisted on his re-appearance each time. Mr. and Mrs. P. Jefferson gave a well acted duet" Very saspicious,"and at a later period Mr. Jefferson sang" All the comforts of a home." Mr. A. 0. Clay recited, "The Irish Fire Brigade," which amused the audience mightily. During intervals in the programme Master Hepple Dodds gave selections on the splendid gramophone kindly lent by Mr. Dodds. Mr. James Emson is an established favourite with the old folks, and his appearance was hailed with pleasure. His songs were vociferously en- cored, and he responded willingly each time. During the proceedings the Chairman conveyed the hest wishes of the late Vicar, Rev. E. S. Jackson, to the audience and a letter of regret from Rev. Father Ryan, who was un- able to attend. He thanked on behalf of all, the sub- scribers who had so liberally supported this function, and referred feelingly to the absence of many,who twelve menths ago had been present. He concluded by wishing all a very happy new year, and expressed the hope that. they might meet many more times at these treats. The Rev. J. R. Jones also addressed the gathering in his breezy style, and his remarks were much appreciated. The ministers of each denomination are annually invited and the Rev. John Gunnell was also present and watched the proceedings with evident interest and enjoyment. At the conclusion of the entertainment the services of the ladies and artistes were eulogised by Mr. Thompson, who asked the audience to show their appreciation of their services. The Vicar, Rev. .I. R. Jones supported those remarks and they were carried with acclammation. Mr. Ambler responded on behalf of the ladies and said they considered it an honour to be present on this !occasion. Supper being now laid,the tables were lined with the contented liguests and their wants quickly ministered to. A package containing llb tea, 11b. sugar, and ilia. coffee was handed to each lady rind each man received a package of tobacco and a pipe. Prior to the breaking up, one of the guests, Mr. B. Hobson, made a speech, thanking the committee and ladies for their kindness and remarking that he was particularly pleased to see that many of the committee had stepped into the places vacated by their fathers, who aforetime carried on the good work. His remarks were endorsed by his associates, and Mr. R. Routledge responded on behalf of the committee and called 'for three cheers for Mr. Thompson, which were heartily given. The 'bus being in waiting for the Sankey people, the gathering broke up, thoroughly satisfied with the evening's plea- sure. The committee responsible for all arrangements were Messrs. Geo. Thompson (president), J. J. Ambler (chairma.), W. Taylor, H. Mainley, W. H. Ireland, F. Jefferson' E. Pownall and R. W. Floughton, bon. secre- tary ; R. Rontledge, hon. treasurer.
Deaths. HANKEY—On the 10th inst., at 7 Southern-street, Stockton Heath, John Hankey, aged 75 years.

ST. HELENS. ST. HELENS PASSIVE RESISTERS. The second sale of goods of the St. Helens passive resisters took place at Messrs. Leach's salerooms Hard- shaw-street, on Tuesday morning. The lots of goods had been seized by Inspector Strong, and they were sub- mitted for sale by Mr. J. B. Leach. The passive resisters concerned were present, and one or two lady brokers had attended, evidently with the idea of adding to their experience of auction sales, and probably with the idea ot snatching a bargain, but Mr. Walter G. Smith, who agai* acted as buyer in, took care to avoid anything of the kind occurring.—Mr. Leach briefly stated the business on which they were met. He had every sympathy with the passive resisters, and said he I proposed to charge nothing either as commission or for the room.—The property was then put up and sold, after which Mr. Leach was thanked for his sympathetic con- duct on the motion of Dr. Best, seconded by the Rev. F. W. Clarke, and supported by the Rev. W. A. Eyre. A BRAVE Boy. An inquestpon Nathan Liptrot, aged four, was held at Marshall's Cross, St. Helens on Tuesday, by Mr. Jones. Charles the brother of deceased, aged ten, said that on Saturday morning they were playing in a field, and his brother slipped and fell into some water. Witness took his clothes off and went in to rescue him, but the water was too deep. The body was recovered by a man named Peter Gilheeney, who dived for it.—The 'Coroner said that the boy was very brave indeed for his age, and the jury asked the coroner to recommend Gilheeney to the Humane Society for some reward.—A verdict of Acci- dental death" was returned.
